item.title: Toward Agentic Runtime Healing
item.dc:creator: Zhensu Sun, Haotian Zhu, Bowen Xu, Xiaoning Du, Li Li, and David Lo
item.description: Using LLMs as runtime error handlers could be a promising pathway toward achieving the longstanding goal of creating truly adaptive and self-healing software systems.
item.content:encoded:
Runtime error handling37 is a critical aspect of software reliability engineering. It requires developers to anticipate potential errors and implement corresponding error handlers in advance. Unanticipated runtime errors, which lack corresponding handlers and are naturally uncaught, can lead to severe consequences, such as unexpected program crashes, exposure of sensitive information, and other critical issues.8 To mitigate such risks, significant efforts have been made to identify potential errors in source code through techniques such as software testing and verification.19,41 However, identifying all possible runtime errors and providing corresponding exception handlers remains a challenging and often impractical task.

Key Insights

  • Traditional self-healing systems rely on predefined rules (e.g., restart, rollback), which cannot adapt to the diverse range of unanticipated runtime errors. Large language models offer a fundamentally different approach: generating bespoke error-handling code in real time by reasoning over error context.

  • Without any fine-tuning, GPT-4 can continue execution in 73% of runtime error cases and produce correct results in 39% of them, demonstrating that LLMs already possess substantial capability for runtime error recovery.

  • The primary barrier to practical adoption is not effectiveness but trustworthiness: 75% of LLM healing behaviors follow recognizable, auditable patterns, suggesting that safety mechanisms like behavior whitelisting can make this approach viable.

Given the near inevitability of unanticipated runtime errors, minimizing their impact requires dynamic countermeasures. This necessity has driven the development of self-healing systems,12,28 a longstanding research area focused on enabling software to automatically recover from abnormal states and restore functionality. Importantly, healing a program execution does not involve patching the code to fix an error but rather revising the runtime state, such as variable values and environment configurations, to recover the program’s execution. A successful healing process should not only prevent unexpected termination but also correct the runtime state so the program can continue meaningfully. The core challenge for self-healing systems lies in the fact that specific errors and their locations are unknown in advance, requiring real-time responses. Consequently, these systems rely on predefined heuristic strategies, such as restarting,4 rolling back to a checkpoint,5 trying alternative methods,6 modifying input,23 reusing existing error handlers,13 preparing default error handlers,29 or combining multiple strategies.7 Despite decades of exploration, the reliance on rule-based strategies limits the adaptability of self-healing systems in handling the diverse range of runtime errors that can occur. The complexity of defining adaptation rules further complicates their implementation in real-world applications. A large-scale industry study highlights this challenge, emphasizing the need for more flexible and adaptive approaches to self-healing.38

Recently, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) has introduced new opportunities to revolutionize this field. LLMs have demonstrated exceptional performance in code-related tasks,14 such as the AlphaCode2 model,3 which outperformed 85% of human participants in a programming competition. These models possess the ability to understand both source code and natural language, and can generate a piece of source code within seconds. These abilities align well with the requirements of runtime error handling, for example, comprehending runtime error contexts, such as error messages and program states, and generating tailored solutions for unanticipated errors in real time. Specifically, when an unanticipated runtime error occurs, an LLM can be invoked with the runtime error contexts in the prompt and generate an appropriate code script. This script is not merged into the original program but rather is executed dynamically to recover the program from its faulty state. Thus, we propose that using LLMs as runtime error handlers could be a promising pathway toward achieving the longstanding goal of creating truly adaptive and self-healing software systems.

In this article, we take the first step toward this ambitious goal by demonstrating its feasibility. Specifically, we designed a framework, Healer, for LLM-driven runtime error handling and experimentally evaluated its effectiveness. To illustrate how Healer facilitates runtime error handling, in Figure 1 we present a motivating example from an open source tool for collecting system logs, SOS32 (v4.5.5). The extracted code is designed to create a temporary directory in which to save collected logs. However, when executed in a race condition where os.makedirs() is called after the directory has already been created, the code crashes at line 2179, resulting in the loss of collected logs. When such unhandled runtime errors occur, Healer can be invoked to handle the error. It gathers relevant information and instructs its LLM to generate a healing code snippet that seeks to avoid termination caused by the error, enabling the program to continue execution with a corrected state. For this example, the healing code renames the output directory to a new name, avoiding a conflict with the existing directory. Once generated, the healing code is dynamically executed to produce a new program state, allowing the program to continue execution with the updated state.

Following the design of Healer, we implemented a prototype for Python and evaluated its effectiveness. The evaluation was conducted on four different code datasets, containing a total of 1,185 (code, test case) pairs, where the code raises runtime errors with the test case. We tested Healer empowered by three state-of-the-art LLMs: two closed-source LLMs, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and one open source LLM, CodeQwen. Initially, we investigated whether Healer, under a zero-shot setting, could effectively avoid interruption and correct faulty program states for runtime errors during execution. The results show that without any fine-tuning, GPT-4 could continue execution in 72.8% of the instances and produce correct results in 39.6% of them. This demonstrates that, even without sophisticated measures, LLMs are capable of correctly handling runtime errors, revealing their great potential for this task. Additionally, we created an instruction-tuning dataset using the (prompt, healing code) pairs generated in our experiments and fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and CodeQwen to assess the effectiveness of fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the performance of GPT-3.5 and CodeQwen improved by 31.7% and 23.1%, respectively, in instances free of interruption, and by 26.8% and 65.8% in instances yielding correct results. Notably, the fine-tuned GPT-3.5 achieved performance comparable to GPT-4. We thus conclude that using LLMs for runtime error handling is a promising direction with great potential.

Although Healer has shown promising results, there are remaining challenges that must be addressed before LLMs can be applied in practice. The foremost challenge is the trustworthiness of LLM-generated code, as the generated code is executed directly, and LLMs may produce incorrect results, introducing potential risks to the program. To better understand this trustworthiness issue, we empirically investigated the healing code generated by GPT-4 and observed some risky behaviors, such as ignoring key logic in the original code, which could lead to unexpected program behaviors. Therefore, how to mitigate potential risks from the black box of LLMs is a challenging and important problem. Fortunately, there are many promising solutions to address these risks. For example, we can predefine a set of “safe” functions, such as a function for data saving, and only allow the LLM to use these functions to perform the healing. With such measures, we may not be far from achieving a fully self-healing system.

Proposed Framework

Healer handles errors relying on an integrated LLM, which generates a piece of code, named healing code, by understanding the error context. The integrated LLM refers to a model that is logically incorporated into the automated runtime error-handling loop, regardless of its physical deployment. It enables the use of diverse back-end models (either local or remote) based on computing resource availability. The workflow of Healer is illustrated in Figure 2. To ease understanding, we assume the framework is being applied to an interpreted programming language, such as Python or JavaScript, where the code is executed line by line, and the runtime environment automatically persists program state between each execution step. Formally, consider a program P with n lines, represented as P={L1,L2,...,Ln}. If an error E occurs at line Li without an available error handler, Healer is activated. Healer first collects the error context, including the error message, the program state S, the entire code snippet, and the erroneous line, to construct a prompt. The integrated LLM is then instructed with this prompt to generate a piece of healing code Li‘. This code is executed under the state S of the original program. If the execution of Li‘ is successful, the resulting program state S‘ is updated back to the original program state, allowing the program to continue from line Li+1. Notably, while the state is corrected for the current session, the original program is not permanently fixed and the bug will still need to be reproduced and fixed in future development. If the execution of the healing code still raises errors, the program is terminated and the error is reported, following traditional error-handling mechanisms.

The Healer framework consists of three main components:

  • Runtime information collector. Once Healer is activated, the runtime information collector gathers necessary information from the runtime environment. Specifically, Healer collects four types of information: the source code, error message, error location, and program state before the error is raised. This information is essential for a human developer to understand the error and write the healing code; thus, Healer collects it to prompt the LLM effectively.

  • Large language model. As illustrated in Figure 3, Healer interacts with the LLM using a structured prompt template that combines task instructions with relevant context fields. The instructions outline the task description, goals, and constraints, supplemented by an example to guide the LLM’s generation. Following this, the template is populated with the collected error context; specifically, the entire source code, error message, and program state are inserted into their respective fields. Adhering to OpenAI’s best practices for prompt engineering,25 each field is clearly demarcated by a section title, including “Error Message,” “Program State,” and “Buggy Code.” Notably, the error location is not designated as a standalone section. Instead, we highlight the error-raising logic by wrapping the error-raising block within <error> and </error> tags directly in the source code. Due to space limitations, the full prompt is provided in our artifacts.a

  • Healing runtime. The healing code generated by the LLM needs to be executed to produce a new program state. We refer to the runtime that executes the healing code as the healing runtime. A straightforward approach is to execute the healing code in the same runtime as the original program. However, to mitigate potential security risks associated with LLM-generated code, alternative runtime environments can be used. For example, the healing runtime could be a new session, a sandbox, or a virtual machine, depending on the required security level. Notably, the execution does not re-run the original program from the beginning but rather executes the healing code with the program state that existed before the error occurred.

Evaluation of Healer

We further evaluated the effectiveness of Healer in handling runtime errors. To conduct this evaluation, we implemented a proof-of-concept Python code executor that accepts source code strings as input and executes them using the Healer process.

LLMs can effectively handle runtime errors.  We evaluated Healer on four benchmarks: CodeNet16 for human-written code; HumanEval+, MBPP+,22 and LiveCodeBench17 for LLM-generated code; and DebugBench34 for code with implanted bugs. For CodeNet and DebugBench, we executed the code samples with the provided test cases and retained the (code, test case) pairs that raised runtime errors, yielding 228 and 436 instances, respectively. In the documentation for HumanEval+ and MBPP+, multiple LLMs are evaluated, and the code snippets generated during the evaluation are publicly available.10 We adopted the code snippets generated by six different LLMs, including GPT-3.5 (ChatGPT),24 GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview),1 CodeLlama (34B),30 CodeT5+ (16B),36 Mistral (7B),18 and StarCoder (15B),20 then followed the same execution-then-selection process to obtain the instances. Finally, we obtained 295 instances from HumanEval+ and 226 instances from MBPP+. Similarly, we collected the error-raising code snippets generated by GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) from LiveCodeBench as a control group that was free from any potential data-leakage issues, resulting in 47 samples. For each instance, we executed its code snippet with the paired test case and handled the runtime errors using the three LLMs, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and CodeQwen, following the framework described in Figure 1. We recorded the final execution status of each instance and computed the three metrics: CORRECT, PROCEED, and FAIL, respectively indicating whether the program finally produced correct results expected by the test case, whether the program could continue its execution, and whether the healing code still raised errors.

The results, shown in Table 1, demonstrate that Healer can effectively heal runtime errors, thereby improving program availability. On average, across all benchmarks, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and CodeQwen can proceed with 73.0%, 48.3%, and 35.1% of the executions, respectively, and help 38.7%, 23.5%, and 13.0% of the programs produce correct results. This provides compelling evidence that using LLMs to handle runtime errors is a feasible and promising direction. Among the LLMs, GPT-4 consistently achieves the best performance across all benchmarks, with the highest CORRECT and PROCEED metrics. For example, on the DebugBench benchmark, GPT-4 successfully completed the execution of 338 instances and corrected the faulty states for at least 177 instances, accounting for 77.5% and 40.6% of the total errors. Even for code snippets generated by LLMs, such as those in HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, Healer improved the execution outcomes. For instance, GPT-4 enhanced the execution results of the code it generated by successfully correcting 11 additional instances in HumanEval and one additional instance in MBPP. Moreover, Healer achieved comparable performance on LiveCodeBench, demonstrating the negligible impact of potential data-leakage issues. This illustrates that LLMs can be used to mitigate the runtime errors caused in their own generated code.

While we primarily focus on comparing different LLMs, it is worth contextualizing these results against traditional self-healing strategies, such as restarting, retrying, and steamrolling (i.e., logging the runtime error and continuing execution despite it). In the context of our benchmarks, the runtime errors are deterministic errors (e.g., IndexError, AttributeError, NameError) instead of environmental failures. Consequently, traditional strategies like retry or rollback would yield a 0% success rate in proceeding execution, as re-executing the same erroneous logic without adaptive healing would lead to the same crash. Similarly, an error steamroller2,9 might allow the program to survive, thereby improving the PROCEED metric. However, it cannot correct the program state to complete the task, resulting in an extremely low CORRECT rate. For example, when we adopted an error steamroller that exceeded the code execution anyway, the CORRECT metric was only 4.3%. This underscores Healer’s unique value in bridging the gap between simple crash avoidance and functional recovery.

Takeaway 1:Healer can effectively handle runtime errors and improve the availability and reliability of programs. Notably, GPT-4-based Healer can continue execution in 73.0% of the instances and produce correct results in 38.7% of the instances.

Fine-tuning further improves Healer’s effectiveness.  Using the data points that produced correct results in the previous experiment, we created an instruction-tuning dataset to fine-tune the LLMs for runtime error handling. This dataset consisted of 586 (prompt, healing code) pairs, generated from samples across all benchmarks except the human-written benchmark, CodeNet, which is reserved as the test set for the fine-tuned LLMs. Specifically, we ran GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to handle the runtime errors in each instance from the selected benchmarks and recorded the healing code. If the healing result was CORRECT, we paired the prompt with its corresponding healing code as a sample in the dataset. With this dataset, we fine-tuned two LLMs, GPT-3.5 and CodeQwen, while using GPT-4’s performance as a reference. Specifically, GPT-3.5 was fine-tuned via the commercial API provided by OpenAI, where the hyperparameters follow its default settings. CodeQwen was fine-tuned on our machine using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique,15 with its hyperparameters available in our artifacts.a After fine-tuning, we evaluated the fine-tuned LLMs on CodeNet.

The results, presented in Table 2, show that fine-tuning effectively enhances the LLMs’ performance in handling runtime errors. Both GPT-3.5 and CodeQwen exhibit substantial improvements, with GPT-3.5 achieving 26.8% more CORRECT instances and 31.7% more PROCEED instances, and CodeQwen achieving 65.8% more CORRECT instances and 23.1% more PROCEED instances. Remarkably, the fine-tuned GPT-3.5 successfully produces 90 CORRECT instances, closely approaching GPT-4’s performance of 96 CORRECT instances. Similarly, the fine-tuned CodeQwen also achieves competitive results comparable to GPT-3.5. This indicates that fine-tuning can be a powerful approach to developing task-specific LLMs for runtime error handling, potentially surpassing general-purpose LLMs in effectiveness. Therefore, a domain-specific LLM for runtime error handling is a promising direction.

Takeaway 2: Fine-tuning significantly improves LLM performance in handling runtime errors. GPT-3.5 demonstrates a 26.8% increase in CORRECT instances and a 31.7% increase in PROCEED instances on CodeNet, achieving performance comparable to GPT-4.

Remaining Challenges

Healer operates autonomously, executing code generated by LLMs to handle runtime errors without human intervention. However, research has shown that LLM-generated code can exhibit unintended behaviors, introducing risks when executed.27,39 This issue has also been highlighted in other studies that execute model-generated code directly, such as LExecutor,33 raising concerns about the reliability of Healer. For instance, one might ask, “What if the LLM deletes my database?”

LLMs can introduce unexpected behaviors.  To better understand the risks, we collected all the incorrect healing code (i.e., the healing code that successfully proceeds the execution but finally produces incorrect results) generated by GPT-4 on the DebugBench. This process yielded 204 pieces of healing code. Healing code that failed to execute in the Healer runtime was excluded from the analysis, since it did not affect the original runtime environment. Two authors, each with more than three years of experience as Python developers, manually examined these collected instances to identify the behaviors that LLMs might introduce when healing runtime errors. The goal was to empirically discover the behaviors an LLM could cause during the healing process. Specifically, the two authors reviewed each healing code snippet together and discussed the behaviors introduced compared to the original error-raising code. The identified behaviors were incrementally added to a list. Note that we did not aim to create a comprehensive taxonomy of all possible behaviors but rather to provide a quantitative demonstration of Healer‘s behaviors.

In total, we identified 19 distinct behaviors, detailed in Table 3. Some of these behaviors, such as omitting part of the context (2.4%) or omitting return statements (2.9%), are risky and can disrupt the expected flow of data, leading to unexpected execution paths. Therefore, without further constraints, the recovery performed by Healer is not guaranteed to be correct or safe. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that these risks are manageable because the majority of these behaviors follow distinct patterns that can be precisely identified through rule-based comparisons between the healing code and the error-raising code. Specifically, 75% of the investigated samples exhibit recognizable behaviors, such as changing variable values (21.0%), initializing undefined variables (10.2%), adjusting types (5.9%), or importing new libraries (27.3%). These behaviors can be identified through static checks based on a predefined whitelist. In this way, Healer can be conservatively configured to perform only behaviors that are not risky to the guarded program. While these restrictions may limit Healer‘s capabilities, they significantly reduce the uncertainty associated with its operation.

A trustworthy future?  Humans also make mistakes. However, with techniques such as software testing, we can identify and mitigate these risks to an acceptable level. Similarly, in addition to developing more powerful LLMs, supporting mechanisms for Healer are crucial for ensuring reliability. As a newly proposed idea, the ecosystem for Healer is currently underdeveloped. Below, we discuss potential methods to help LLMs behave more reliably. By implementing these strategies, we can move closer to a future where Healer operates reliably and safely within software systems, minimizing risks while maximizing its potential for automated error recovery.

Safety checks.  Behaviors such as context omission (skipping parts of the original logic) or return omission (omitting a return statement) can significantly disrupt the expected flow of a program. Mechanisms like static checkers can be used to prevent the execution of potentially harmful code. For example, we can define a whitelist of behaviors that Healer is allowed to perform and use static checkers to ensure that the healing code does not contain any behaviors outside this whitelist. Additionally, techniques used for source code, such as dynamic testing, static analysis, and verification, may also be applicable to the healing code.

Healer-aware programming.  Traditional software systems are fundamentally deterministic, and the uncertainty introduced by Healer can sometimes be unacceptable. To better accommodate Healer, software systems need to be designed with its potential interventions in mind. For example, since Healer may change variable values, the system should include additional mechanisms to handle these changes, such as warning users to be cautious about the system’s outputs or maintaining detailed error logs for future bug fixing. Moreover, it is important to establish a “comfort zone” for Healer within the system, where its interventions are acceptable and unlikely to cause significant harm. This comfort zone could encompass non-critical modules or components, such as user interface elements, where the potential side effects of Healer‘s operations are more tolerable. By confining Healer‘s activities to these safe areas, developers can benefit from automated error recovery without exposing more sensitive parts of the system to unnecessary risk.

Reliable skillsets for LLMs.  Inspired by practices in AI agents for software development,35 a possible solution is to provide a toolkit as a skill set for the LLM. The LLM inside Healer would then be restricted to using only the functions in this toolkit. For example, the toolkit could provide a predefined data-saving function, and the LLM could use this function to save data that might otherwise be lost. Since these functions are predefined, the behaviors of Healer become predictable, thereby mitigating risks.

Discussion

Here, we discuss some potential issues with Healer, including its deployment implications and extension to other programming languages.

Infrastructure and deployment implications.  Technically, Healer requires access to runtime state information (e.g., stack traces and variable states), an execution environment (e.g., a sandbox, container, or lightweight virtual machine) to properly execute LLM-generated healing code, and access to an LLM service, either via a remote API or a locally deployed model. Among these prerequisites, the LLM service imposes additional requirements on the software, where the choice between remote APIs and local deployment involves distinct architectural trade-offs. Using remote APIs requires stable network connectivity to the server-hosted model. Conversely, employing a local model requires the hosting device to possess sufficient computational power to support inference. To address this, various techniques, such as model compression31 and quantization,21 have been developed to enable inference on user devices. For example, LLAMA.cpp11 can efficiently run gpt-oss-20B26 on a single M3 Ultra MacBook. As the field advances, we anticipate further reductions in the resource requirements for LLMs.

Healer in real-world systems.  To effectively apply Healer in real-world applications, some engineering challenges need to be addressed. For instance, real-world software systems can contain millions of lines of code, the majority of which are irrelevant to any single runtime error. Consequently, for LLMs, reading through the entire codebase for every error is inefficient. This necessitates a targeted context retrieval strategy to identify code segments relevant to the error trajectory, methods that are already widely studied in repository-level tasks such as bug localization41 and repository code completion.40 Furthermore, Healer must integrate seamlessly with existing error-recovery mechanisms. For example, it should function alongside traditional rollback strategies (e.g., snapshot restoration) so that if Healer fails to resolve the error, the system can default to these predefined backup measures.

Extension to other programming languages.  While our current experiments implement Healer in Python, the underlying framework for handling runtime errors is designed to be language-agnostic. Interpreted languages (e.g., Python, JavaScript, Ruby) naturally fit Healer because they natively support dynamic code execution. In contrast, compiled languages (e.g., Java, C++, Rust) require a compilation step prior to execution, introducing architectural complexity to the dynamic execution process. However, this barrier is not insurmountable through specific language features. For instance, Java provides the Java Compiler API to compile code fragments at runtime, and C++ allows for dynamic loading of shared libraries. While some engineering effort is required to achieve this, extending Healer to these languages is promising. We look forward to exploring these extended implementations in our future work.

Conclusion

AI-driven runtime error handling represents a promising approach to enhancing the reliability of software systems and could serve as a new pathway toward achieving self-healing systems. For the first time, we propose this idea and provide a proof-of-concept implementation to demonstrate its feasibility. Through our implementation, we demonstrate that Healer can handle runtime errors with a high success rate. However, significant challenges remain, particularly regarding the uncertainty of LLM behavior and the compatibility of such systems with existing software architectures. We hope this work will inspire further research in this area and pave the way for the future of AI-driven runtime error handling, ultimately leading to more robust and resilient software systems.

item.title: AI and the Future of Accessible Work
item.dc:creator: Anne Marie Piper, Darren Gergle, Cynthia L. Bennett, Maitreya Shah, Chancey Fleet, Ali Abdolrahmani, Ariana Aboulafia, Stacy M. Branham, Sharon Koppman, Arielle Silverman, and Erik B. Sudderth
item.description: Work practices shaped by AI adoption and policy can both support and restrict disabled people's participation in the workforce.
item.content:encoded:
Many countries have legislation that prohibits discrimination against people with disabilitiesa in the context of employment. For example, the U.S. Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA),b the U.K.’s Equality Act of 2010,c and European Union policyd prohibit employment-related discrimination and require employers to provide reasonable accommodations or adjustments so disabled employees can perform their jobs. More broadly, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD)e has influenced legal frameworks across the globe. Despite these anti-discrimination policies, disabled people remain significantly underrepresented in the workforce. Employment gaps between disabled and non-disabled people exist globally.28 Among blind and low-vision Americans, for instance, only 44% are employed compared to 79% of those without disabilities.f Only 54% of d/Deaf peopleg in the U.S. are employed, compared to 70% of hearing people.8 These discrepancies are worse for multiply marginalized disabled people. For example, employment rates for disabled women are significantly lower than rates for disabled men.21

Key Insights

  • A reliance on AI for accessibility may result in increased pressure to use imperfect solutions, leave workers unable to hold companies accountable for accessibility barriers, and obscure the root causes of inaccessibility.

  • The positive framing of AI for accessibility can mask important issues related to privacy, potential harms, and the need for rigorous evaluation and ethical considerations.

  • Moving forward requires in-depth research into the real-world use of AI, ensuring a range of accommodation choices beyond AI, and including disabled people in the auditing and development processes.

While many discussions focus on the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance worker productivity and performance, AI can also improve the accessibility of work for disabled people. AI-based innovations enable many assistive applications, including real-time meeting captioning for people who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, image alt-text generation for blind people (e.g., Microsoft Seeing AIh), dictation support for people with speech-language disabilities,i and task management for neurodivergent people.j AI-enabled tools are also marketed as a way to make digital information accessible, such as via accessibility overlays.k Subsequently, AI-based tools are being adopted in workplaces to help address issues of accessibility, with promises of greater autonomy for disabled workers and lower costs of accommodations and compliance for employers.28

The exciting potential of AI-powered access technologies, however, may mask essential questions regarding how AI technologies may create additional barriers for disabled people in the workplace and other contexts of use.33,37 For example, errors and hallucinations in the output of AI models and tools (for a review, see Huang et al.20) challenge their use for accessibility in work situations where accuracy is critical.1,2,36 Digitized hiring assessments, such as AI-scored video interviews, can also be discriminatory toward disabled workers, who may have non-normative speech or body movement patterns, thereby restricting workforce entry.16,24 Automated tools for accessibility compliance—such as accessibility overlays—may not work as intended or advertised, making websites more difficult to use and introducing privacy issues.26

In this article, we aim to widen the ambit of accessible work by articulating social, organizational, and policy issues that emerge at the nexus of AI, accessibility, and employment for disabled people. We conceptualize accessible work as not only the practical ways in which technology and workplaces are made accessible to people with disabilities but also the ways in which work practices, which are shaped by technology and policy, can both support and restrict disabled people’s participation in the workforce. What makes understanding the potential benefits and harms of AI for accessible work challenging is its situated use and embedding within complex organizations with their own evolving norms and policies for both the use of AI and accommodations. Accessibility-related practices and policies are infrequently made public by organizations, and employees may be bound by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), preventing them from sharing their work-related experiences. Further, employers may require people to disclose their disability to receive workplace accommodations, yet disabled workers may avoid disclosing out of fear associated with stigma or negative repercussions related to job security or promotion opportunities.34 What’s more, disabled people may be required to disclose their disability to AI tools in order to receive useful outputs, such as a blind or autistic person telling an LLM about their disability to get a useful response.10,22,36 These ongoing challenges become even more complex in light of the increasing rhetoric around AI as a panacea for inaccessible information, technologies, and workplaces.

In what follows, we present a synthesis of the concerns and recommendations raised by researchers, practitioners, and policymakers as part of a one-day workshop on the future of accessible work and AI. Forty-four people participated in the event. Attendees were invited to represent a breadth of expertise and affiliations. Most attendees (n=43) were from U.S.-based organizations, although multiple had experience living and working outside the U.S. Attendees were from academic departments (n=31), including computer science, information science, communication, organization and management, and law schools; industry research labs and product teams (n=7); and nonprofit and government organizations (n=8) that serve people with disabilities. Multiple attendees held appointments across organization types. More than one-third of workshop participants identify as disabled, including people who are blind or low vision, neurodivergent, or who have motor disabilities, chronic illness, or multiple disabilities. Participants also had expertise in accessibility for d/Deaf and hard of hearing people, neurodivergent people (e.g., autistic, ADHD, learning disabilities), and people with cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia).

While discussions considered accessibility and disability in a broad sense, the workshop had a particular focus on the experiences of blind and low-vision people. Workshop presentations and discussions focused on the following motivating questions:

  • What is the current state of workplace accessibility given the widespread use of digital productivity and collaboration tools and increasing integration of AI into these tools?

  • What are key technical challenges and emerging approaches to AI that have the potential to transform accessibility and the future of work?

  • What organizational, policy, legal, and ethical issues are central to creating an accessible future of work as AI continues to evolve?

The resulting themes below were derived by analyzing meeting transcripts and notes, presenter slides, and follow-on conversations with workshop participants who are experts in accessibility, AI and machine learning, organization science and work studies, and disability and AI policy. Our analysis focused on identifying cross-cutting themes that emerged during discussion, grounding them in concrete examples offered by participants regarding their lived experiences with issues of AI and accessibility in the workplace. Workshop attendees were made aware that the meeting discussions were being transcribed and would be analyzed as part of preparing a public report on the workshop’s findings. This project was deemed “non-human subjects research” by the lead author’s university IRB. To avoid identifying individual participants, we do not provide detailed demographic data and present our findings in aggregate below. Given the limitations of our sample of participants, we contextualize the consequences and recommendations discussed below by presenting them alongside related academic research and policy efforts and enrich them with first-person accounts of how disabled workers experience these challenges in practice.

Consequences of AI for Accessible Work

The consequences of AI for accessible work are not merely technical, such as model biases, errors, and hallucinations in output that can be misleading and problematic when used in the workplace. They are also structural, including the potential for increased and systemic discrimination of disabled workers; organizational, through evolving workplace norms and policies on the use of AI and accommodations; and social and emotional, through how AI-powered technologies have the potential to affect experiences of workplace acceptance and belonging. Below we articulate six consequences of AI for accessible work.

Workers are likely to feel pressure to use AI-based accommodations.  Disability policy, particularly in the U.S., U.K., and EU, provides disabled people not only the right to reasonable accommodations but also the right to refuse an accommodation if they so choose. Yet we know that disabled people already report hesitancy in telling their employers if or when they need accommodations, for fear of backlash or retribution.34 Multiple participants explained that, with the promises of AI for accessible work, there is likely to be increased social and organizational pressure for people to use AI-based technologies to meet their access needs, even if the technologies are less ideal than human support. For example, one blind participant explained that blind and low-vision people can feel pressure to use an AI image-description tool, such as Seeing AI, rather than ask a human for a visual description, even if the AI-based tool is imperfect and contains inaccuracies. Participants raised the parallel issue of d/Deaf and hard of hearing people feeling pressured to use relatively inexpensive automatic captioning in place of more accessible, yet more expensive, human sign language interpretation or human-generated communication access real-time translation (CART) captions. This increased pressure is likely to stem from employers wanting to cut costs, and from employers and disabled workers having different perspectives on what constitutes “reasonable” accommodations, particularly as AI-based accommodations become widely used in certain work contexts. Moreover, participants cautioned that when employees feel pressured to adopt AI-powered accommodations rather than the tried-and-true solutions they find most effective for given work tasks (such as human assistance), AI may ultimately become the de facto accommodation. Participants called for accommodation processes to be participatory, individualized, and determined according to what will foster an accessible workplace.

Disabled workers may be unable to hold employers accountable for inaccessible AI-based applications.  While current policies in multiple countries provide legal mechanisms for workers to hold employers accountable for accessibility in the workplace, enforcement of that accountability is not straightforward. Multiple participants emphasized that even if a worker feels comfortable pointing out accessibility issues in their workplace, some countries have loopholes or exceptions that allow businesses to skirt responsibility. Referencing U.S. policy, one person explained that if a blind worker cannot access a timekeeping application, but the timekeeping application is a third-party software created by another company, the worker has no legal recourse for ensuring accessibility through their employer.l Other loopholes exist for small businesses or when accessibility compliance would place an undue financial burden on the business. For instance, in the EU Employment Directive, there exists a “disproportionate burden” exception to the mandatory reasonable accommodations provisionm that allows for cost considerations in employer decisions.

Participants, primarily those from industry and with legal/policy expertise, raised concerns that many software products and services that integrate AI exist within those loopholes, making it difficult for workers to hold employers, or anyone else, accountable when an AI tool is inaccessible or creates accessibility problems. The challenge is not only that workers may have no legal recourse, but also that the companies disabled people work for may need to spend time tracking down where the accessibility issue originated—and who is responsible for fixing it—before remediation can happen. This problem gets exacerbated in countries like the U.K., where the law does not prescribe a definite timeframe within which employers must make reasonable adjustments for employees.n Several participants emphasized that the closed-box designs of many AI systems and stochastic nature of generative models make it difficult for even the manufacturers of AI products to identify what is creating the access barriers, let alone companies or individual employees working with third parties to try to diagnose the issue.30 Collectively, participants expressed concern that AI employed as a workplace accommodation has the potential to rapidly scale these issues, leaving disabled workers unable to hold employers accountable and enabling businesses to avoid direct responsibility for creating inclusive environments.

AI promises to resolve accessibility issues without addressing the root causes.  One key promise of AI for accessibility is to remediate—or resolve—accessibility problems in a variety of situations, from inaccessible meeting environments to websites and software. For example, many accessibility overlays use AI to re-render digital content in an attempt to make websites and applications more accessible for disabled users.o Related approaches improve mobile application accessibility by generating missing metadata based on visual screenshots,40 a feature that was added to Apple iOS VoiceOver.p Despite the potential of AI to remediate inaccessible digital experiences, multiple participants highlighted that accessibility overlay companies have overpromised the potential of this approach to resolve accessibility issues, resulting in litigation and significant fines (e.g., AccessiBeq) Even worse, accessibility overlays may increase challenges for some assistive technology users by blocking keyboard input or failing to accurately detect document structure.26,31

Multiple discussions emphasized that turning to AI to resolve accessibility issues also has the potential to leave the root cause of inaccessibility unaddressed and create other problems. Accessibility overlays, for example, can threaten user privacy, misapply semantic structure, mislabel elements, and fail to detect nuance in graphical information.26,31 Workshop participants raised concerns around how disabled users will verify real-time remediation, such as a blind person needing to understand whether the presented overlay is the correct equivalent of the visual layout. While AI-based techniques for remediation will continue to improve, turning to AI as a post-hoc fix does little to ensure that software and Web content abide by the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)r from the start. Instead, participants explained that AI-based remediation may create the perception that AI will be there to “clean up” inaccessible code, reinforcing a mindset that coding with accessibility standards in mind is optional and reducing market pressure for companies to make technologies accessible from the beginning.

Participants suggested that the perception that AI will be there to fix and clean up inaccessible technology has the potential to derail more than two decades of social, educational, and technical efforts to build accessibility awareness among different stakeholders. Natively accessible software and Web content is not only important for equal access and ensuring a consistent user experience for all people, but is also tomorrow’s training data. One participant pointed out that when inaccessible code is used as training data, it allows inaccessibility to propagate through and be reinforced by AI-based coding tools. A recent experiment that used an LLM to generate website code similarly showed that 84% of generated websites contained accessibility violations.3 What’s more, novice developers using AI for programming support may fail to prompt for help with accessibility or miss crucial steps required for making code accessible.27 As AI becomes normalized as a way of resolving accessibility issues in code, participants emphasized the importance of considering the consequences of this mindset on the entire ecosystem of development tools, coding practices, and software review guidelines.

A reliance on AI may undermine the collective effort required for access.  Accessible work requires more than simply ensuring digital experiences pass certain accessibility benchmarks (e.g., WCAG compliance). Creating accessible workplaces and work practices involves ongoing awareness and understanding of access needs among one’s colleagues and organization.6 Similar to developers relying on AI to clean up inaccessible code, workshop discussions emphasized that an overreliance on AI for making work accessible has the potential to undermine the human efforts and mutual understanding that are crucial for effective collaboration among ability-diverse teams in the workplace (see also Branham and Kane,9 Cha et al.,11 and Das et al.12). Multiple workshop participants noted that with greater reliance on AI for making work accessible, coworkers may perceive AI as meeting a disabled coworker’s access needs and feeling less need to adapt their own behavior to support workplace access. Thus, accessibility is further pushed onto the disabled worker as an individual burden rather than a collective effort.6 One example discussed by participants involves using AI to make virtual meetings more accessible by providing captioning and auto-generating meeting notes. While this may, in fact, be helpful to neurodivergent, d/Deaf and hard of hearing, and blind or low-vision workers, meeting accessibility involves more than technology. All meeting attendees must be aware of and uphold accessible practices, such as being mindful of turn-taking when speaking and distributing meeting agendas and materials in advance to allow time for review.14 Workshop participants emphasized that while AI may ultimately shift some of the labor of access from humans to machines, we have yet to understand the consequences of that shift in terms of who is viewed as responsible for creating access—whether it is AI, employers, coworkers, or disabled employees themselves. Multiple participants described how disabled people are often expected to “bring their own accessibility” or individually take on the work of figuring out how to ensure their access needs are met. Thus, the normalization of AI as a one-stop shop for accessibility may ultimately put more social pressure on disabled people to sort out their own access needs rather than shifting the pendulum toward access as a collective phenomenon.6

Disabled workers may be unable to opt in or opt out of using AI.  Workshop discussions highlighted the ways in which AI-augmented workplace tools promise to support new ways to generate and refine content, derive insights from data, and engage with customers, ultimately boosting worker productivity and performance. As such, participants shared stories of organizations rapidly adopting new AI-augmented workplace tools, often ushering in new tools without fully checking their accessibility compliance. One participant shared their experience as a blind U.S.-based employee joining a new team at work. The team uses an AI-augmented digital whiteboard tool, such as Miro, to coordinate tasks and track project deliverables, yet this tool is not fully accessible to them. Not only is it tedious to add and modify content with their screen reader, they face difficulty maintaining both local and global understandings of the collaborative workspace given its highly visual nature. When monitoring a team’s status and coordinating tasks depends on understanding inaccessible visual representations, they are unable to effectively do their job. Rather than the AI-enabled tool bolstering productivity, it may instead directly hinder their ability to participate, with consequences for their actual and perceived job performance.11 Moreover, the employee is faced with the impossible situation of either asking their team to change their tool selection to accommodate their needs, with the potential for backlash and being viewed as not a “team player,”12 or to shoulder the burden of finding workarounds that may still limit their participation.

As AI becomes normalized as a way of expediting work and offloading certain tasks, participants explained that disabled workers may feel increasing pressure to use AI just to keep up. One attendee shared the example of a worker, when feeling particularly fatigued or overwhelmed, deciding to offload a task to AI, such as gathering information across a range of websites rather than spending hours sifting through partially accessible content. They explained that the better these tools get, the easier and more tempting that decision is for all people—but especially for people with disabilities, who are dealing with elevated levels of friction every single day because of inaccessibility. To further complicate matters, multiple participants emphasized that disabled workers may fear becoming overreliant on AI to support their work and then having their access revoked. Certain companies or roles may not allow its use, such as when working on a proprietary and confidential code base, or may change their policies around the use of AI tools and suddenly prohibit the use of a tool that has become integral to one’s workflow.10,11 Workplaces are rapidly adopting new AI applications, and in parallel evolving policies for their use, creating ongoing tensions that may result in disabled workers being unable to opt in or out of using AI for access.

The beneficence of AI for accessibility may elide possible future harms.  Throughout workshop discussions, participants highlighted the potential for AI to make a positive social impact by increasing access to information and giving disabled people more choices for meeting their access needs. The beneficence of AI for accessibility is a powerful message and marketing tool, explained one participant, positioning subsequent advances as not only a necessity but also a human right. Participants warned, however, that this perspective can obscure or elide concerns over the implementation and use of AI tools, such as how data protections and privacy are managed, as well as how even accessible AI tools can discriminate against people with disabilities in other ways. The trade-off between privacy and access is not new to disabled people, as they are routinely forced to give up their privacy to secure access or give up access to maintain their privacy.35 A poignant question one participant posed to the group is whether accessibility as a use case for AI nudges people toward accepting a technology that until now would have felt highly invasive.

Another key concern raised during discussion involves whether the normalization of AI among youth means we are socializing the next generation of workers to accept such technologies in contexts where similarly invasive technologies would be unwelcome. For example, if AI tools are socialized among youth as appropriate within classrooms—a sensitive context of use—future generations of workers may come to accept such technologies in equally sensitive contexts within the workplace, such as private meetings and discussions. Multiple participants emphasized that we must be mindful of how the promise of AI to improve accessibility, whether in workplaces or classrooms, has the potential to normalize surveillance culture and obfuscate potential harms.

Another consequence of the beneficence of AI for accessibility is that certain requirements and review processes may be relaxed or fast-tracked when motivated by narratives of social good, with participants sharing examples of this already happening in their organizations. That is, participants noted that accessibility as a use case may be leveraged to skirt technology reviews or lessen requirements around data retention and privacy. Several participants expressed that within an employment context, the risks are exacerbated for disabled workers, who may need to use fast-tracked, minimally tested AI tools to meet their access needs. Multiple participants with legal expertise noted that these same tools may reveal a worker’s disability status to their employer, among many other potential harms.38 Data that captures the way people walk, talk, look, and interact can all be used as proxy data to infer disability status, potentially exposing protected disability information in an employment context.

Toward Responsible AI for Accessibility in the Workplace

How AI will shape accessible work for disabled people—for better or worse—presents more questions than answers at this stage. The use cases, norms, and concerns of AI for the future of work are rapidly evolving, creating new considerations for disabled workers, who may simultaneously depend on and deplore AI tools. Policies and regulations on both AI and disability vary locally and globally, are being actively negotiated, and are often in tension, yielding continually shifting currents that disabled workers must navigate. Grounded in our findings and related literature, we make four recommendations for moving toward responsible AI for accessible work.

Understand the situated uses of AI in the workplace among disabled people.  Studying the ways in which AI technologies are adapted and appropriated within a wide range of workplaces and settings is essential to understanding their immediate and longer-term impacts on disabled workers’ ability to secure and maintain employment. Use of AI technologies must be contextualized within organizational settings to understand how it may both alleviate and create new tensions for disabled workers. It is well known both that disabled people are early adopters of technologies and that newly introduced technologies often have unanticipated negative effects on workers. For instance, organizations have implemented algorithmic systems in the workplace to improve coordination and decision making, yet these algorithms have similarly intensified work and managerial control, leading to negative consequences such as increased stress, job precarity, and loss of privacy.23 It is also important to go behind the scenes and actually see how AI is being used in practice. New technologies are often valued more for what they symbolize than how they are actually used.4 As a result, there is often a gap between the two. For example, one study found that hospitals promoting their use of surgical robots in marketing campaigns actually kept these robots locked away in storage closets,5 while another found that startups often exaggerated the effectiveness of new software algorithms to secure funding.32 Given the widespread hype surrounding AI, and AI for accessibility in particular, there is likely a substantial gap between what firms say AI-enabled tools can accomplish and how they are used on the ground. The fines against AccessiBe for overpromising their ability to make websites accessible may be the first of many examples.q

Prior work shows there are certain situations where disabled people prefer and disprefer using AI as an accessibility tool (e.g., Adnin and Das,1 Carik et al.10), yet what is missing is an understanding of how workplace expectations and norms, which vary across countries and cultures, may increase the pressure to use AI and its associated risks. Working in collaboration with disabled people to study the situated uses of AI for accessibility in the workplace also has the potential to identify practical evaluation metrics or benchmarks. For example, even if AI performs well on general benchmarks evaluating its average performance, it will be a poor-quality accommodation if the model or resulting applications contain biases around disability or cannot remediate certain content. Benchmarks must therefore be contextualized and applied according to spectra,17 considering factors such as task importance, the tool’s utility to provide reliable information, and whether it is used alongside other accommodations (e.g., human verification). Situated studies of AI for accessibility will not only help identify meaningful benchmarks but also reveal potential harms and shortcomings, such as how errors or model hallucinations may affect job performance, or the follow-on human labor required when AI tools only partially remediate inaccessible content. As AI is assessed for its effectiveness and suitability as an accessibility accommodation, it is essential to directly involve a wide variety disabled people, including multiply marginalized disabled people, as primary stakeholders. Their perspectives are crucial to understanding how well AI tools function in situ and to identifying potential harms, ranging from personal and data privacy concerns to impacts on worker self-efficacy, across diverse workplace contexts.

AI-powered accommodations should not be the only option.  While disabled workers in many countries have the right to reasonable accommodations in the workplace, the proliferation of AI-based accessibility tools is likely to complicate what is considered “reasonable” by various stakeholders. AI-based accommodations can be empowering to people with disabilities by giving them more agency and privacy to do their work, and they can be more cost-effective for workplaces needing to provide accommodations. Yet many AI-based access technologies exist to remediate content that was not born accessible, thus serving as an imperfect ad-hoc solution that, in many cases, is better than nothing but still lacking. As AI becomes an accepted accommodation option, we must be mindful of how AI will be perceived as a “reasonable accommodation” by various stakeholders in certain contexts and as wholly inadequate and inappropriate in others. When accommodations are inadequate, employees are often left with the only option of filing an individual lawsuit against an employer, which is time-consuming, expensive, and puts the burden of proof on the employee. Policies and monitoring mechanisms should proactively consider the implications of AI on accommodation processes.

Moreover, accommodations are not one size fits all, but legally and pragmatically should consist of multiple solutions that employees may leverage depending on the task demands. For example, a blind employee may prefer to use an AI-enabled tool to draft content and choose a first round of images to put into a presentation, but then consult a human visual interpreter when refining the presentation. Neurodivergent workers may prefer AI for some social communication tasks and not others.10 As AI becomes more normalized as an accommodation, it is critical that workers maintain the ability to fluidly move between accommodation options depending on the task, context, and what is at stake. Though AI can be a valuable accommodation option, it should not be the only option.

There is a growing need for a range of both human and automated accommodation options, especially in situations where users cannot independently verify a tool’s output. While disabled people often rely on human assistance to confirm critical information produced by AI tools,1,2,36 an increasing reliance on AI raises concerns about how scalable and sustainable this verification process is. Contemporary LLMs and VLMs remain prone to errors, and much of their practical success in application stems from their ability to quickly and easily generate “initial” content that can be verified and refined or edited by a human. Given the high cost of human verification, one approach could be for AI tools to signal uncertainty, although even the most advanced AI models today struggle to reliably assess how confident they are in their own outputs.39 Further complicating verification, many scenarios of use have no single “correct” answer, such as an autistic worker needing to evaluate the quality of job-related advice from an LLM.22 Across the broader spectrum of disability, we know even less about how workers with intellectual disabilities (e.g., Down syndrome) or mild cognitive impairments (e.g., early dementia) understand and ensure the quality of output, particularly when recommendations from AI and human experts diverge.22

Involve disabled people in efforts to audit AI technology.  Early work on accessibility and AI called for greater involvement of disabled people in the development of AI systems, including sourcing data to build models and surfacing issues of fairness.37 Related efforts infuse disability perspectives into AI development pipelines with disability data, for example, by releasing disability datasets18 and proposing infrastructures for accessible data collection.29 These efforts, while a valuable step forward, do not fully engage disabled people in efforts to audit AI technology. Participatory AI (PAI) is gaining momentum in HCI and AI communities.19 A component of PAI, community-based auditing, empowers the people most impacted by AI to lead in evaluating it. However, accessibility research has long pointed out discrepancies between calls for participatory design processes and their success when applied in disability communities. For example, the methods and tools used in these processes may themselves be inaccessible (e.g., sticky notes,7 digital whiteboards13). A first step in community-based auditing of AI in the workplace is to ensure that the auditing process and training in foundational machine learning (ML) and auditing concepts are accessible. For example, researchers who evaluated AI-generated images depicting disability provided image descriptions to blind evaluators;25 one challenge in making this material accessible concerns when people do not have access to AI outputs without them being translated, and when AI itself is serving as an accessible remediation of inaccessible “ground truth.” Additionally, if workplace technologies are being audited, extra care is required to ensure employees are not obligated to conduct these audits in ways that protect corporate interests, and that they are free to audit the AI honestly. Engaging third parties to facilitate audits may be necessary. Companies could alternatively sponsor community organizations to lead audits; this could be an opportunity for multiple organizations using similar AI capabilities to benefit from a public audit. Disabled workers should also be empowered to audit AI-enabled tools not just for accessibility, but also for other barriers that may lead or contribute to disability discrimination in the workplace.

Finally, static and discrete notions of disability challenge the very concept of auditing as it is commonly configured in ML research. As disability is dynamic and every person’s experience of it is affected by their unique position, and since people’s diverse accessibility needs require information to be presented in multiple formats, audits will need to be flexible to capture evaluations by disabled people, as compared to benchmarks with only predetermined metrics with closed-ended response options.15,25 What’s more, we are all enmeshed in a global work product, which is the unseen labor of tuners, moderators, data refiners, and others. We know little about who is doing this work and whether they are fully representing the disability community. The people making decisions at this level may not be people with lived disability experience, and if they are, they are bringing their own disability culture to bear on decisions. Moving forward, another open question is how well existing accessibility audit tools,s which are useful for assessing many types of content and experiences for a broad range of users, extend to and align with emerging AI auditing processes and frameworks.

Disability must be a key consideration in AI governance and policy.  AI can provide unique benefits to people with disabilities, and these benefits should be considered whenever policies are developed, particularly when they limit disabled people’s use of AI. For example, policies within organizations may restrict employees from using certain AI products, even if those same products provide useful accommodations for a disabled employee. While AI should not be the only option for accommodations, its use should also not be limited when there is benefit as an accommodation, particularly without a compelling reason (like worker safety or security). In contrast, if there are certain cases where AI is limited to accessibility use cases, policy must also outline how someone justifies usage and whether that requires disclosing disability, which presents additional barriers. Conversely, accessibility should not become a loophole for inappropriate usages of AI, such as by companies fast-tracking use cases of AI for accessibility and circumventing rigorous review.

One way forward is to take a dual track approach, in which disability is included in mainstream AI governance policy and AI is included in core disability policy. The EU AI Act makes progress toward AI governance and policy that attends to disability.t It prohibits developing systems that exploit disabled people, emphasizes making systems accessible for disabled users, and encourages developing codes of conduct that assess and prevent the negative impact of AI systems on accessibility for disabled people. As another example, in the U.S., the New York Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Act proposes third-party auditing of AI-based hiring tools with attention to discrimination based on gender, race, disability, and other protected classes.u While these policies provide an important step forward, working toward meaningful AI governance and policy that includes disability is challenging, due to limited population-level data on disability and the underrepresentation of disabled people and associated data in AI models.

Conclusion

The consequences of AI for accessible work extend beyond mere technical considerations, shaping and being shaped by organizational norms and impacting the social-emotional experiences of disabled workers. Throughout this article, we highlight not only how technology and workplaces are made practically inaccessible, but also how work practices—influenced by AI adoption and policy—can both enable and constrain disabled people’s participation in the workforce. The pressure to adopt AI-based accommodations, the challenges of accountability for inaccessible AI, the erosion of collective responsibility for access, and the obfuscation of potential harms all necessitate a cautious and critical approach. While we surface many ongoing and future challenges of AI for accessible work, more research is needed to fully understand how such issues manifest for various groups of workers across the globe. Our sample is limited in that participants were primarily U.S.-based, and those coming from industry are from larger technology firms or nonprofit organizations. Additionally, blind and low-vision people were more heavily represented than other disability groups. Moving forward, more research is needed to ensure that a diverse range of disabled workers from across the globe are actively involved in surfacing issues regarding contextualized use of AI for work, the auditing of AI technologies, determining evaluation metrics and benchmarks, and developing robust governance and policy frameworks. Only through such concerted and holistic efforts can we hope to harness the transformative potential of AI in a way that genuinely empowers disabled people and fosters inclusive and equitable workplaces.
