item.title: Computing Is Changing; How Should ACM Change with It?
item.dc:creator: Elisa Bertino
item.description: ACM's president Elisa Bertino vows to help ACM become even better at connecting people, disciplines, and ideas.
item.content:encoded:
I have been an ACM member for more than 40 years. During this time, ACM has given me opportunities to learn, to meet great colleagues from around the world, to present and publish research, and, perhaps most importantly, to be part of a community. I am deeply grateful to ACM; serving as its President gives me an opportunity to give something back to an organization that has been an important part of my professional life.

As I begin my term as President, I have been thinking about a fundamental question: Computing is changing—how should ACM change with it?

Let’s consider how computing has evolved. We moved from algorithms and programming to networked and distributed systems, and then to cloud computing, mobile computing, and data-intensive systems. Today, AI is changing how we develop hardware and software, secure systems, manage data, conduct research, and interact with computing systems. AI-based systems increasingly sense, reason, communicate, and act in the physical world. Quantum technologies may require our community to revisit some of the foundations of today’s computing infrastructure. Computing is also moving into new environments, from autonomous vehicles and robots to UAVs and space systems.

This evolution leads to another fundamental question: What is computing today?

I believe ACM should help our community and more broadly our societies to answer this question, and, more importantly, help shape what computing will become.

One of my priorities is to make sure ACM remains at the technical forefront of computing. We have already started several initiatives in areas I believe to be critical today and in which ACM should have a key presence. These include a new conference on agentic AI and the ACM AI Leadership Summit—which we would like to evolve into a continuing initiative rather than a single annual event, as well as plans for activities in physical AI, including embodied AI.

In the area of quantum technologies, I have co-founded the ACM Conference on Post-Quantum and Quantum-based Security (ACM PQQS)—ACM’s first quantum-related conference—and I believe we should explore a broader technical community and additional activities in this area.

Robotics and autonomous air and space computing are other areas in which many important computing challenges are emerging. These areas also show a trend that today is more important than ever. Interesting problems no longer fit neatly within a single computing discipline. Autonomous air and space systems, for example, require AI, networking, distributed systems, security, real-time computing, software engineering, data management, and human-computer interaction. Physical AI similarly brings together AI, robotics, systems, sensing, and interaction. ACM has communities with expertise in all these areas. One of our great opportunities is to bring them together.

Another important priority is the ACM Digital Library (DL). The DL is an extraordinary repository of computing knowledge, but I believe it can become much more. In particular, we should ask how it can better serve practitioners and educators in addition to researchers. AI provides opportunities for new services that can help people discover, connect, understand, and use computing knowledge. We should explore these opportunities responsibly while preserving the quality and trust associated with ACM content. We also need to think about the long-term sustainability of the DL, including new partnerships and a funding campaign to support its future development.

A third priority is open research in computing. Openness means more than making papers accessible. Computing research increasingly depends on datasets, benchmarks, software, models, and experimental infrastructure. We should explore creating a journal dedicated to datasets and benchmarks across computing—not only in AI. At the same time, AI poses particularly difficult questions for experimental research. Much leading research—both on AI itself and on computing systems that incorporate AI—is conducted in industry using proprietary models, datasets, and computational infrastructure that cannot readily be made available to the broader research community. How should such work be evaluated? What should reproducibility mean under these conditions? What information and evidence must researchers provide so that their results can be independently and meaningfully assessed?

I believe ACM can bring academia and industry together to develop new methods and standards for rigorous experimental research in the AI era. This effort should also address access to AI models and other essential resources, and how greater openness can be reconciled with legitimate concerns about security, intellectual property, cost, and responsible use.

To pursue initiatives such as these, ACM itself must be able to move quickly. We need mechanisms that make it easier for our communities to create conferences, summits, and visioning workshops around emerging topics. We should also consider organizational structures that allow ACM to focus on important multidisciplinary areas that cross the boundaries of existing SIGs. This does not mean replacing our existing communities. On the contrary, it means making it easier for their expertise to come together when new challenges require it.

None of this can be accomplished by a President—or even by the ACM Council—alone. ACM’s greatest strength has always been its community and its volunteers. During my more than 40 years as a member, I have seen what ACM volunteers can accomplish when people with different expertise, experiences, and perspectives come together around an idea. My goal for the next two years is therefore not simply to launch a collection of new initiatives. It is to help ACM become even better at connecting people, disciplines, and ideas.

I look forward to listening to your ideas and working with all of you. Together, I hope we can help ACM continue to serve our community and contribute to shaping the future of computing.

item.title: Governing Social Media as a Public Utility
item.dc:creator: Christoph Mueller-Bloch and Raffaele Fabio Ciriello
item.description: The proposed public utility model combines law-driven removal of illegal content with ranking systems that curb the visibility of harmful material without deleting it.
item.content:encoded:
While social media connects billions, it also fosters discord, with algorithmic amplification of misinformation linked to polarization,5 violence, and mental health decline.4 Amid these challenges, a key question is often overlooked: Who should govern social media? As social cohesion erodes, the need for democratic oversight grows more urgent. Corporations such as Meta have repeatedly prioritized engagement and ad revenue over the public good, even when aware of the harm their practices cause.4

In the U.S., governance is shaped by Section 230 and the First Amendment, limiting state intervention and relying on counterspeech to combat falsehoods.13 The European Union’s Digital Services Act imposes more direct obligations for content moderation.a Yet both approaches ultimately defer to corporate discretion, perpetuating a conflict of interest: misinformation drives user engagement, and engagement drives profits.

This dynamic constitutes a negative externality—private actions imposing societal costs akin to environmental pollution—which justifies corrective intervention to prevent market failure.14 The “Bullshit Asymmetry Principle” captures the challenge: refuting misinformation takes significantly more effort than producing it.15

Treating social media as a public utility curtails profit incentives for misinformation and enables public oversight of content moderation. Like water, electricity, and broadband, social media is critical public infrastructure, serving as a dominant news channel and forum for societal discourse.9 Building on prior proposals for public alternatives to corporate platforms,10,11 we develop a model centered on democratic oversight, transparent moderation, legally bounded content removal, and institutional protections for free expression. While ambitious, this proposal seeks to expand what is politically imaginable by reinforcing the democratic foundations of social media governance. Our framework can accommodate private alternatives under public regulation and is adaptable to diverse democratic contexts. Even though the U.S. exemplifies how partisan government intervention offers no viable path towards replacing commercial freedom with civic responsibility, countries such as Germany, Canada, the U.K., and Australia offer proven non-partisan governance models to draw on.

Adapting the Public Utility Model to Social Media Governance

Governing social media is challenging due to its ever-evolving nature, which defies established regulatory frameworks. While Internet and public broadcasting regulations offer principles—universality, equitable access, quality standards, and resilient funding—these must be adapted to social media’s distinct challenges. Chiefly, effective governance requires institutional safeguards to protect free expression and prevent autocratic control.

Social media platforms, whether public or private, face a trade-off between free expression and civil discourse. People value freedom of expression but also freedom from harmful expression, posing a dilemma when one person’s expression harms another. A state monopoly on truth is incompatible with free democracy.14 So, how can state-governed social media mitigate negative externalities while upholding democratic opinion forming?

Our proposal distinguishes between content removal and content ranking, with democratically defined and authorized editorial rules. AI can enhance moderation efficiency by detecting illegal content, but auditability and open source algorithms are essential for trust and accountability.

Content removal should be limited to illegal material, enforced by courts. For instance, U.S. First Amendment protections exclude obscenity, child abuse material, incitement to imminent lawless action, true threats, fraud, defamation, and false advertising. Legal misinformation, however, should be addressed through content ranking, not removal, to safeguard free expression.

Content ranking should prioritize social connections and user interests over engagement to curb misinformation. Platforms such as Reddit12 use up- and downvotes to rank content, which can curtail misleading yet technically legal “gray-area” content more effectively than simple flagging.1 Thus far, countries such as the U.S., U.K., Canada, and Germany regulate only illegal content. While this avoids a state monopoly on truth, it fails to address harmful but lawful expression. Our proposed public utility model combines law-driven removal of illegal content with ranking systems that curb the visibility of harmful material without deleting it. This approach limits amplification without censorship or government overreach. Decentralized identifiersb can prevent vote manipulation while preserving privacy. Self-sovereign identitiesc enable cross-platform data portability, reducing platform dependence.

Any ranking system entails a trade-off between group preferences and societal cohesion. Conservatives may upvote content that liberals downvote. An algorithm marketplace could enhance in-group satisfaction and reduce inter-group conflict, but risks deepening echo chambers. Aggregated preferences may mitigate fragmentation but marginalize outliers. For public social media, prioritizing consensus through aggregation may be preferable. This approach sidelines, but does not censor, extreme content and leaves it accessible to those who seek it. Integrating social graphs and user interests, such a system supports civil discourse while maintaining an open marketplace of ideas.

Checks and balances are essential to prevent partisan capture by insulating content ranking policies and funding decisions from partisan control. The German public broadcasting model offers a valuable precedent. Germany’s constitutional court has repeatedly upheld that public broadcasting must be pluralistic and independent. Politicians are barred from controlling editorial or funding decisions. Regulatory boards that determine funding and editorial policy are legally required to include members chosen by designated societal groups (for example, unions and religious organizations), not politicians.

Australia’s Online Safety Act 2021 offers a complementary pathway. It empowers an independent eSafety Commissioner to mandate the removal of illegal or clearly abusive material across digital services. While it expands regulatory capacity, it does not address “harmful but lawful” expression or algorithmic ranking. Nonetheless, it demonstrates how liberal democracies could build on existing institutions to move toward a public utility model of social media.

Like public broadcasters, public social media should follow content ranking standards overseen by independent institutions to ensure accuracy, impartiality, and educational value. This may require constitutional amendments to create safeguards against partisan interference. Financial independence can be supported through a mix of fees, donations, and revenues from advertising and premium services.

Public and private social media platforms can coexist, much like private TV stations do alongside public broadcasters like the BBC. However, private platforms must be subject to regulatory oversight to ensure responsible ranking and curb engagement-driven harms. Independent regulators—modeled after the U.K.’s Ofcom—could assess compliance using metrics such as attention allocation (how algorithms allocate user attention), revenue attribution (how attention is monetized), and impact measurement (societal consequences of content amplification).8 Regulatory tools could range from attention trading mechanisms14 to more forceful measures such as expropriation, antitrust action, or shutdowns in cases of persistent non-compliance.

Another approach—fully compatible with our proposal—would mandate a shared infrastructure supporting multiple ranking systems.13 Bluesky’s marketplace of algorithmsd is one such model, allowing users to choose their preferred ranking systems. A default public-interest algorithm could coexist with commercial alternatives, provided they meet regulatory standards for misinformation control.14 However, having a multitude of competing social media infrastructures, including a public one, would be preferable, as a unified infrastructure would introduce a single point of failure and make social media as a whole more vulnerable to partisan takeover. Having a public option alongside private social media would be best suited for supporting a pluralistic and democratic society.

Weighing Alternative Options

Alternatives to the public utility model abound. In response to mounting calls for accountability, Meta established an external “Oversight Board” in 2020 to review content decisions and adjudicate user appeals. Likened by CEO Zuckerberg to “a Supreme Court,”7 the board remains structurally and financially dependent on Meta, ultimately leaving policy control in corporate hands. Without accountability beyond Meta itself, the Oversight Board functions more as a PR stunt than a genuine system of checks and balances.3 By contrast, the public utility model assigns such oversight to actual democratic institutions—courts and parliaments—instead of corporate-appointed, pseudo-independent bodies that remain accountable to shareholders rather than citizens.

Recently, Meta shifted from fact-checking moderation to crowdsourced moderation, citing concerns over scalability and the neutrality of fact-checking organizations. However, this shift sidesteps the core issue: Meta retains both the incentive to promote engagement-boosting misinformation and unilateral control over content ranking and removal. Crowdsourcing may broaden participation in moderation, but it does not resolve structural power asymmetries or the absence of public oversight.

Another proposal, information fiduciaries, would impose legal duties of care on platforms.2 Critics6 caution that this model requires platforms to balance the conflicting interests of shareholders and society. Because engagement simultaneously drives profit and societal harm, fiduciary platforms may struggle to navigate this conflict of interest, limiting their effectiveness. The public utility model offers a stronger solution by removing profit incentives and aligning operations with societal goals such as equitable access, content integrity, and harm reduction. It also ensures democratic oversight by courts and legislatures, with international cooperation addressing the longstanding regulatory evasion by global corporate platforms.

Recent efforts by President Trump to defund PBS and stack its board with political allies highlight the risk of partisan capture,e yet they also showcase the relative resilience of democratic institutions: PBS has retained editorial independence, supported by citizen donations and legal protections. In contrast, Meta’s content policies rest entirely on executive discretion, requiring no approval beyond Zuckerberg. While imperfect, democratic governance may offer stronger safeguards than corporate self-regulation.

Another proposal envisions a wave of smaller, self-organizing platforms enabled by targeted regulation to address misinformation.16 While promising, profit-driven smaller platforms funded by advertising would still prioritize engagement, and thus retain incentives to amplify misinformation. A public utility model may address this more effectively by aligning incentives with the public interest.

The Road Ahead

Despite its promise, the public utility model faces challenges. More than anything, social media’s resilience to capture depends on institutional safeguards rather than on technical design. In robust democracies, public oversight can reinforce accountability and make capture costlier, warranting serious experimentation with the public utility model. Funding may require taxes—a trade-off justified by their contribution to a democratic society. Reconciling national autonomy with global standards remains complex.

Safeguarding free expression and privacy requires robust institutions resilient to partisan or corporate capture. Such capture occurs in many forms: state control, as seen in VKontakte in Russia, WeChat (Weixin) in China, or attempts of the U.S. government to limit enforcement of the European Union’s Digital Services Act in Europe, and corporate influence, as evident in the algorithmic moderation and platform bans shaping discourse in Western democracies. These are not opposite extremes but variations of the same problem: concentrated power over online speech. Private platforms have also been weaponized by governments, such as during the Duterte administration in the Philippines, while public ones may be less likely to amplify coordinated misinformation and less vulnerable to interference by foreign governments. Introducing public platforms alongside private ones could diversify the social media landscape, making it less corruptible overall.

Just as today’s private platforms are fragmented, so too might public alternatives fragment along jurisdictional lines if they lack interoperability, weakening network effects. Countries will understandably seek to retain editorial control and fiscal sovereignty. Content removal laws vary widely: Holocaust denial is illegal in Germany but protected in the U.S., while abortion service ads are restricted in some U.S. states but permitted in others. A global enforcement framework, akin to SWIFT, could enable cross-border functionality within domestic legal constraints. Without such coordination, divergent regulations may erode cohesion and effectiveness.

Conclusion

While politically contentious, governing social media as a public utility offers a viable path toward a more equitable and resilient digital society. Drawing lessons from robust democracies (such as the U.K., Germany, Canada, and Australia), we propose a model rooted in non-partisan democratic oversight, law-bounded content removal, and transparent moderation. Although the model alone does not guarantee resistance to partisan capture, particularly if constitutional safeguards are lacking, it does resonate with values shared across ideological lines: free expression, checks and balances, rule of law, sovereign infrastructure, and public accountability. Its purpose is not to empower any party or leader, but to strengthen democratic institutions with sovereign digital infrastructure. If social media is to serve the people, it must be accountable to the people.

item.title: Who Owns the Wai (Water)? AI, Power, and the Public Trust
item.dc:creator: Josiah Hester
item.description: Can we build AI without replicating familiar patterns of environmental injustice where benefits flow upward to a privileged few while harms are imposed locally and endure?
item.content:encoded:
AI’s environmental impact is no longer theoretical: it is showing up in people’s lives. Across the U.S. and soon around the world, the rapid buildout of AI datacenters is driving up energy demand, draining water supplies, and reshaping communities, often without their consent. What was once framed as a technical scaling problem has become an environmental justice issue, playing out in zoning hearings, regulatory meetings, and angry town halls, as residents grapple with higher utility bills, constant noise, and contaminated or depleted water.

The shift into public view has been swift. Viral videos, front-page headlines, and even local elections now center on the real costs of AI infrastructure—rising electricity rates, water scarcity, air pollution, and falling property values. The promised benefits of AI—helping people live better, healthier, more productive lives—remain largely unrealized, even as its environmental and social costs are imposed on communities with little say in the matter.

Yet the industry’s response is depressingly familiar: promises of future fixes, vague assurances of community benefit, and ever more fantastic claims about what AI will someday deliver for everyone. In practice, those promises are often paired with aggressive accounting and legal maneuvers that obscure present-day harm: land quietly purchased through shell companies to avoid public scrutiny, or state and local officials required to sign nondisclosure agreements before they are even allowed to ask basic questions about water use, power demand, or emissions. We have at least three reasons to be skeptical of claims this AI infrastructure buildout will all be for the best.

First, for more than a decade, a small but persistent community has documented computing’s—and especially AI’s—escalating climate and environmental impacts, arguing that unchecked growth would lead to precisely this moment.7 Communications itself echoed that warning in the Opinion column “Our House Is on Fire,” rejecting “digital exceptionalism”—the belief that computing’s benefits justify unlimited expansion.5

Second, while AI is often promoted as a powerful tool for climate action—and it can be—its climate benefits must be weighed against both the direct costs of the infrastructure required to support it and the additional emissions enabled by AI-driven productivity gains, which recent modeling suggests may exceed the emissions AI helps avoid.1 Investment and talent have largely shifted away from conservation and sustainability work toward scaling AI capabilities themselves. At the same time, the impacts that matter most to communities are systematically left out of industry reporting. Independent research from Hugging Face has shown that the metrics companies emphasize—energy use and greenhouse gas emissions—capture only a narrow slice of AI’s footprint, ignoring water extraction, land use, air pollution, labor impacts, and community displacement.6 When these broader harms are accounted for, the picture changes dramatically: efficiency gains and AI-enabled climate tools are overshadowed by the physical and social costs of building and operating AI at scale.

Third, the question is not whether AI can be useful—it can—but whether we can build it without replicating familiar patterns of environmental injustice, where benefits flow upward to a privileged few while harms are imposed locally and endure. Given the incentives shaping today’s tech industry, skepticism is warranted. As Cory Doctorow has argued, digital systems tend to follow a predictable path of enshittification: first optimized for growth, then for monetization, and ultimately for extraction at all costs.3 That logic now governs AI infrastructure, where value is increasingly extracted not just from users as in the first Internet platforms (Facebook, Gmail, and so forth), but from land, water, air, and public resources. There is little reason to believe these systems will suddenly become more accountable simply because companies promise they will.

The argument is this: the physical costs of AI need public governance. Who owns the infrastructure, who directs its growth, and who bears its costs cannot be left solely to private firms. Digital services are not immaterial: they are built from land, energy, labor, and water, or wai in the Hawaiian language. Treating AI as private infrastructure with public consequences is no longer tenable if AI is meant to deliver shared prosperity. AI must be governed as part of the public trust: the principle that essential shared resources are held in stewardship for the public, protected from exclusive private capture, and managed for present and future generations. For AI infrastructure, that means transparency about water, energy, land, and emissions; requiring large users to bear the costs they impose on public infrastructure; meaningful community authority over siting and resource use; and public or community-controlled alternatives where critical infrastructure has become too concentrated. This idea is an ancient one. In Hawaii, Kānāwai—water law—recognized water as a communal trust to ensure all people could grow food, with dire consequences if someone took more than a fair share. Achieving this shift requires more than optimization. Computing professionals must build and defend new technical and institutional alternatives—free and open source systems, repairable and maintainable hardware, distributed and community-controlled infrastructure, and mechanisms that align power with accountability—while standing alongside Indigenous and frontline communities as leaders in governance. I tell the story of wai through two stories from my home in Atlanta, GA, and my homeland of Hawaii, because they reveal what is already unfolding everywhere and offer us historical and current perspectives on the impacts of privatizing AI infrastructure. This moment of attention is an opportunity we must seize to determine AI, and our, future.

Your City: The Next Datacenter Megalopolis

During the past five years, the U.S. has experienced an unprecedented datacenter buildout, foreshadowing the global expansion now underway. In my home in Atlanta, GA, and the surrounding metropolitan area, we are seeing it in a transformative way. With approximately 1.46GW of datacenter capacity built, and another 2.08GW under construction, concerns about noise, property values, water availability, and power rates are on the minds of many. These developments carry real public health risks, including degraded air quality that disproportionately affects people with asthma.11 In nearby Newton County, GA, national attention followed reports of household wells running dry and tap water turning brown after a new Meta datacenter came online (Meta disputes they caused well problems).

Communities have not been passive. Neighborhood planning units, local academics, and environmental groups have pressed city and state leaders to require datacenter developers to pay for the power infrastructure they need, rather than shifting those costs onto residents. Advocates have pushed for higher electricity rates for datacenters as large industrial consumers and have successfully blocked new facilities near dense neighborhoods and sensitive watersheds. Consumer groups such as the People’s Power Union and Science4GA have challenged the outsized lobbying influence of Georgia’s energy sector after years of rate hikes. Legislative victories, however, have been elusive: a bill to increase energy payments from new datacenters stalled despite broad support, while another to suspend generous tax breaks was vetoed by the governor.

The most consequential decision came in December 2025, when the Georgia Public Service Commission approved an unprecedented $15 billion, nearly 10,000-megawatt expansion of power infrastructure to meet projected AI and datacenter demand. The vote occurred during the final days of a lame-duck commission—after voters had ousted two incumbent commissioners over affordability and energy concerns in a nationally covered election with record-breaking voter turnout, but before their replacements could be seated—leaving ratepayers potentially on the hook for decades of higher costs and increased climate burden. Anger has been palpable. Since 2023, the commission has approved six Georgia Power rate increases, raising the average household bill by at least $43 a month, or roughly $500 a year, even as the company’s profits rose by 40 percent. For many Georgians, the message is clear: the benefits of AI infrastructure flow elsewhere, while the costs are being paid at home.

First it was Northern Virginia, then Atlanta, and now the buildout is global. Singapore, despite its challenging climate and limited land, is converting land for datacenter use; in Southern Italy, a “Mediterranean AI Hub” is being developed; and in India, Microsoft and others are investing billions in new datacenters. The scale of this expansion is staggering: the IEA projects global datacenter electricity consumption to nearly double, from approximately 485TWh in 2025 to approximately 950TWh by 2030. Across these locations, consumer and environmental advocates are refusing to let Big Tech treat climate responsibility as a branding exercise or a series of accounting tricks. Efficiency improvements often trigger rebound effects: when a technology becomes more efficient and cheaper to use, total consumption tends to increase rather than decrease, ultimately exacerbating resource demand and environmental impact.9 In the context of AI and datacenters, making computing “greener” without limiting overall growth simply accelerates energy, water, and land use rather than reducing harm, even when offset by credits, which are often fraudulent.10 For many Georgia residents, these were abstract connections. Now, we are seeing in real time how our own water, land, and tax dollars are being used to support AI use everywhere except here. If allowed to continue, we as individuals, as communities, as parents, as employees, as renters, as homeowners, as citizens, will see our lives negatively impacted in the near term.

What Can We Do?

Data Center Watch, a research project from 10a Labs that tracks grassroots opposition to datacenter development across the U.S., reported that by early 2026 more than 800 active opposition groups were organizing across 49 states, with approximately $130 billion in datacenter projects blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone through community meetings, classrooms, local policymaking, and activism led by those who often bear the brunt of climate impacts: Indigenous communities, black communities, and other communities of color. It is clear that communities are pushing back, and we should be paying attention.

Our key question is how we, as computing professionals, support this grassroots effort. I take hope from people already using computing in radically different ways—practitioners working alongside environmental justice groups, leveraging technology not for extractive industry goals but for genuine public good. This is not a new fight: decades ago, communities pushed back against landfills being placed only in black neighborhoods, and now we are seeing similar battles play out over the placement of datacenters and the draining of local resources. Meaningful change requires collective action that moves beyond technical optimization and brings together consumers, policymakers, and community organizations to force industry shifts. What is needed now are morally ambitious people willing to steer the direction of computing and AI at every level. So what can be done? Several existing efforts point toward what this can look like:

  • Community-governed, place-based computing for stewardship. Direct partnerships such as the STRONG Manoomin Collective in the Great Lakes region and the CEAR Hub in Brunswick, GA, show what community-governed, place-based AI can look like in practice. Working alongside federally recognized Ojibwe tribes, STRONG Manoomin develops sensing and AI systems to preserve wetlands and assert tribal sovereignty, utilizing data for stewardship, advocacy, and cultural restoration, rather than as benchmarks.8 In Brunswick, youth and researchers co-deploy water-level sensors, climate curriculum, and flood modeling in neighborhoods experiencing rising flood risk. In both cases, computing is embedded in local knowledge and lived experience, serving community resilience rather than extractive innovation.

  • Indigenous-led technology and ancestral stewardship. In Hawaii, the Purple Mai’a Foundation works at the intersection of Indigenous knowledge, computing, and entrepreneurship, co-developing technologies with Native Hawaiian youth and communities to restore and protect ecosystems. Their programs train a new generation of technologists grounded in ancestral stewardship. The Nation of Hawaii, too, leverages sensors, mapping tools, and networked infrastructure to monitor and protect āina (land) from overdevelopment. At a recent event, called Build4’Āina, computing professionals from Big Tech companies, academic computing researchers, and local artists and practitioners gathered to build AI and sensor systems to directly support community conservation, traditional food production, and community action, eventually demoing these systems to state government agencies.

  • Carbon transparency and literacy for developers: Tools such as GreenPT and CodeCarbon can help developers see the resource costs of AI workloads, challenging the illusion that computing is zero-impact.

These efforts need more hands—now. Every computing professional has a role to play in shifting AI from extractive infrastructure to community-governed systems, tools for resilience, land stewardship, and self-determination, not harm.

Lessons from Hawaii’s past for AI’s Future

I conclude with a warning from the past, and a vision of hope for our shared future. My people (Native Hawaiians) have a proverb taught to almost every child: I Ka Wā Ma Mua, I Ka Wā Ma Hope—the future is in the past. Other indigenous cultures describe this as moving backward into the future—the belief that past experiences, traditions, ancestral knowledge, and learning will guide us today in making forward-looking and just decisions.

My Polynesian ancestors voyaged across the Pacific to the Hawaiian islands more than 1,000 years ago and built extraordinary, whole-island wai (the word for freshwater, the most important resource on an island surrounded by ocean) engineering works called ahupua’a to sustain themselves. They developed a system of laws called Kānāwai, which ensured a careful, place-based framework for food production, water protection, and people’s well-being. The fresh water stream was life, and wealth—called waiwai, as in much water—was measured not in extraction or accumulation, but in the ability of water to support everyone. At its peak, this system supported more than 700,000 people’s needs, while today, most food is imported to Hawaii, and the Hawaiian islands and their people are at extraordinary risk from climate degradation.

The story of Hawaii’s transformation from a self-sufficient, 1,000-year-old advanced sovereign nation to a subjugated state with the highest cost of living in the U.S., and dire food and water insecurity, is a complex one. However, one particular period in the Hawaiian Kingdom’s history mirrors our current time.

Water as a public trust resource was codified in written law in 1840. Even as sugar plantations expanded and profits from foreign investors overrode local concerns, systems were in place to regulate water withdrawals (via large ditches and built infrastructure) to ensure that small farmers could access water alongside the enormous sugar plantations. Water commissioners from the region were tasked with weighing impacts, scheduling withdrawal times, and preventing total enclosure of resources. The system was rooted in Hawaiian values that emphasized the perpetuation of land and water for future generations, as well as the local knowledge that the water cycle influenced everything from wildfire frequency to fisheries and lei making. Disruption would harm all; water was a public trust, not a commodity. My own ancestors were part of the commissioning body that adjudicated water management at the time, listening to oral testimony from farmers, plantation representatives, and long-time residents, to ensure fair use. Often, the stream diversions benefited small farmers, who could take advantage of the large infrastructure projects undertaken by sugar plantations. The Hawaiian kingdom leveraged revenue from sugar plantations during this time to build public works, educate the population, pay for roads, schools, and hospitals, ensuring the public trust.2

This robust public trust framework collapsed half a century later with the overthrow of the monarchy by sugar plantation leaders supported by the U.S. Marines, eager to exploit a fraught time in global history, and ride industrialization to drive huge profits. The consolidation of rights over nearly all water on the islands into the hands of “The Big Five,” descendants of missionary families and other businessmen, concentrated in corporations, wrested control away from community stewardship. Sugar production skyrocketed, and water became scarce (it takes approximately 1,000 liters of water to produce one pound of sugar). By the time plantations eventually shut down, well into the 20th century, the water and land were already broken. Today, Hawaii imports most of its food, and the legacy of diverted streams still haunts the islands.

I see in this history a warning, but also a guide for how we govern AI. Hawaii’s Big Five consolidated the infrastructure of sugar—the land, water, finance, and transportation on which the industry depended—and with it, the power to redirect shared resources toward private profit. Today’s hyperscalers are consolidating the infrastructure through which AI is built and delivered. At the end of 2025, hyperscale operators controlled nearly half of global datacenter capacity, and Amazon, Microsoft, and Google alone accounted for roughly three-fifths of hyperscale capacity. The danger is not concentration alone, but what control of infrastructure allows its owners to control upstream: access to energy, water, land, public investment, and ultimately the terms under which communities participate in the AI economy. As that control concentrates, decisions about shared resources move away from the communities that bear their consequences. Just as plantations diverted streams to maximize production while while leaving communities dry, today’s tech giants today’s tech giants divert energy, water, and public resources to feed their own system. If we build AI the way sugar captured water—extractive, consolidated, and dismissive of community voice—we will inherit the same legacies of scarcity, inequity, and disempowerment. But if we treat AI like wai, belonging to the public trust of land, water, and air, we can chart a different course.

British-American computer scientist and technology entrepreneur Andrew Ng said, “AI is the new electricity.” I disagree. AI is water, AI is wai. Literally, because we transform water into computation in datacenters, and figuratively, because AI, like water, should be a public trust resource, available to all. In Hawaiian, waiwai means both water and true wealth. AI can become waiwai—shared abundance. To avoid repeating Hawaii’s history, we as computing professionals must empower and collaborate with communities, especially indigenous ones, who have safeguarded water and other vital resources for generations, reimagining these systems, harnessing this extraordinary moment of consciousness about AI’s impacts, to build a better future for us all.

item.title: Bounded Minds, Generative Machines
item.dc:creator: Jiqun Liu
item.description: An emerging line of work motivates a research pathway that connects design, evaluation, and governance to reduce AI harms and bias risks in practice.
item.content:encoded:
Conversational AI systems are entering the mainstream as a primary interface for information seeking and decision making. Yet most systems, evaluations, and implicit user models still presume idealized users who can carefully weigh evidence and notice implausible claims. In reality, human cognition is bounded by limited time and attention, uneven domain knowledge, and reliance on heuristics that evolved to support fast judgments under uncertainty.9 Heuristics such as anchoring, availability, confirmation, authority, and scarcity are not failures of reasoning but adaptive mental shortcuts. When paired with fluent, personalized, and confident generative responses, however, these shortcuts become a double-edged mechanism that can systematically skew judgment.

Researchers in human-computer interaction, cognitive science, and behavioral economics have long studied these biases, and there is growing recognition in AI ethics and safety communities as well.2 However, mainstream design practices and system evaluations still emphasize correctness, relevance, and narrowly defined utility while leaving cognitive impact underexplored.5 In multi-turn dialogue, a single confident response can anchor users, vivid anecdotes can dominate base rates, repeated agreement can reinforce expectations and misbeliefs, and even neutral layout or ordering choices can introduce framing effects that alter trust and preference.

The risk is not merely that conversational AI fails to mitigate these biases; it is that systems can exploit them for scalable behavioral manipulation, which aligns with the unacceptable-risk framing under the EU AI Act.a In advertising, persuasion, and political microtargeting, systems already optimize engagement by aligning with predictable vulnerabilities.1 As generative models become more adaptive and personalized, subtle steering becomes easier to produce and more difficult to detect.

The challenge, then, is not simply higher factual accuracy. It is to build conversational systems that recognize how users actually reason through heuristics that can be adaptive or distorting depending on context, individual differences, and system choices (see the accompanying figure).

An emerging line of work, sometimes described as machine psychology, studies how generative models exhibit and interact with cognitive shortcuts and how systems might support better reasoning rather than amplify bias.8 This motivates a research pathway that connects design, evaluation, and governance to reduce AI harms and bias risks in practice.6

Why this becomes a research pathway now?  Bounded rationality has long been studied, but its implications become substantially more urgent with large language models (LLMs) and agentic conversational systems being widely deployed. Unlike earlier information systems, conversational AI can adapt natural language turn by turn and influence reasoning over longer horizons, amplifying cumulative effects of framing, anchoring, and heuristic reinforcement. During the next decade, this makes cognitive impact a first-order design concern rather than a peripheral issue.

Designing for Heuristics, Not Against Them

This work does not argue for a single design solution. Instead, it highlights recurring cognitive dynamics that define a broader research pathway for conversational AI as heuristics unfold across multi-turn interaction. Once we recognize that people rely on heuristics rather than mathematically rational utility calculation, the research challenge is to understand how these shortcuts behave when responses are generated fluently, adaptively, and at scale across varying tasks. What once appeared as subtle laboratory effects can accumulate across everyday exchanges, where small shifts in wording, sequencing, and emphasis reshape judgments, comparisons, and preferences.

According to Prospect Theory,9 people evaluate outcomes relative to reference points and weigh losses more than equal gains. In conversational settings, reference points are often established implicitly through language, ordering, and tone, and early framings can persist across turns. Over time, path-dependent agreement can narrow exploration even without introducing factual errors.

The structure of option sets also reshapes outcomes. When comparisons are generated on the fly, dominated alternatives may appear and quietly steer choices. For example, a student asking an LLM for study resources might see a free open textbook, a reasonably priced course, and an overpriced “platinum package” with little added value; the decoy makes the paid course look like the safe and balanced choice. Similar dynamics arise with anchoring, vivid anecdotes, authoritative tone, scarcity cues, and confirmation-seeking language, which can co-occur and reinforce one another in conversational information retrieval and recommendation.5

These dynamics explain why surface-level accuracy cannot be the only standards for judging conversational AI. A response may be correct yet still entrench loss aversion, amplify overconfidence, or channel decisions through hidden framing. The research question shifts from whether an answer is correct to whether an interaction supports sound reasoning within bounded cognitive limits: Does it broaden perspectives, calibrate uncertainty, and reduce vulnerability rather than compound it? Because interactions unfold turn by turn and are context-dependent, this pathway calls for design and evaluation centered on cognitive impact in addition to quality-focused effectiveness.

Detecting and Intervening in Bias Risks

Conversations are where reasoning develops between human and machine, and also where it can quietly bend. This pathway requires monitoring how exchanges unfold and identifying signals of bias risk: narrow framing, unbalanced emphasis on benefits versus costs, overconfident claims without uncertainty, comparisons that hide baselines or include redundant options, and rapid user acceptance without examining evidence. Such signals suggest measurable features that future systems could track, including viewpoint diversity via source entropy,4 calibration failures in expressed probabilities,3 and turn-level traces that enable later audit.6 Additional behavioral and physiological signals may help in some settings, but generalizable, privacy-aware signals remain a core research challenge.

Once signals are detected, systems could explore lightweight interventions before presenting a final response: surfacing a clear baseline, framing outcomes symmetrically in gain and loss terms, and representing uncertainty as ranges rather than single numbers.3 Retrieval can supply base rates and counterexamples.4 A dominance check can flag or remove decoys, and an anchoring guard can introduce a second estimate after baselines are shown so the first number does not dominate judgment.10 These interventions can be implemented through structured outputs, function calls, and lightweight critics that review drafts before answers are returned.7

Illustrative scenarios can clarify the goal. In health advice, a vivid patient story presented first can dominate evidence from clinical trials; pairing anecdotes with prevalence rates can rebalance judgment. In e-commerce, a high-priced decoy can make a mid-range product appear reasonable; detecting and labeling dominated options reduces hidden steering. Similar failures can arise in legal guidance and news summarization through redundant options, problematic framing, or anchoring order. These cases show how heuristics can turn from shortcuts into vulnerabilities and why small interventions may keep conversations more balanced under bounded rationality.

Evaluation also has to evolve. Accuracy and topical relevance remain necessary but are no longer sufficient. Systems should be tested on whether interactions improve calibration after uncertainty is shown,3 broaden perspectives, and reduce susceptibility to dominated options and decoys.6 Scenario sets that vary framing, priors, and time pressure can stress test interventions, while online experiments can compare policies through stability of choices and reduced repeat queries.7 Counterfactual logging and interleaving can evaluate alternative baselines safely, and tuning can incorporate penalties when high-risk turns pass without intervention.6,7

Open challenges.  Detecting cognitive vulnerability in real time is subtle, context-dependent, and heterogeneous across users and domains. Interventions must balance effectiveness with intrusiveness, since excessive safeguards may increase cognitive loads and reduce trust or usability. Integrating detection, intervention, evaluation, and governance into a coherent conversational pipeline raises unresolved questions about transparency and generalizability. These challenges are central to the research pathway rather than solved engineering tasks.

From Principles to Practice

Turning these ideas into practice does not require reinventing conversational AI, but it does require reframing priorities. Many building blocks exist, yet their effective integration and evaluation remain open research problems. Function calls, structured outputs, and long-context modeling can support baseline surfacing and uncertainty representation; retrieval-augmented generation and reasoning can supply diverse perspectives with grounded sources;4 and lightweight critics can flag missing baselines or overconfident tone.7 Recent model developments make these capabilities increasingly feasible, but feasibility alone does not guarantee cognitive benefit and safety.b

Open research questions and roadmap.  This pathway suggests several actionable questions: How can systems detect moments of cognitive vulnerability reliably across tasks and populations? Which interventions, such as contrastive framing, baseline surfacing, or uncertainty representation, work best under different heuristics and contexts? How should success be evaluated beyond accuracy, especially in calibration, stability of judgment, and resistance to manipulation? What governance mechanisms and audit trails are needed to make such systems accountable at scale?

Evaluation can be reframed around these goals. Instead of asking only whether an answer is correct, we can ask whether interaction improves calibration, reduces anchoring, and broadens perspectives.3,6 Scenario sets that vary framing, priors, and time pressure can test robustness, while online experiments can compare policies through stability of choices and reduced susceptibility to decoys.7 Over time, such measures can complement accuracy and latency with benchmarks for decision quality and cognitive robustness.

Practical safeguards also depend on governance and transparency. Cognitive-impact reviews can become part of release practice alongside privacy and security checks. Policy and model cards can disclose guardrail scope and known limitations, while audit trails can log which options were shown, what baselines were included, and which interventions were triggered.6 Practical audit trails can include retrieval queries, ranking choices, cited spans, and the system’s internal plan behind high-stakes answers.c Such documentation may feel burdensome, but it enables reproducible traceability for accountability.

Taken together, these directions outline a credible and timely research pathway for building conversational AI systems and evaluation pipelines that work with bounded human minds, support robust reasoning, and reduce the risk of hidden harm and cognitive behavioral manipulation.

item.title: ACM as a Professional Society: The ACM Volunteer Database
item.dc:creator: Jeanna Matthews
item.description: The Volunteer Database could be a comprehensive record of volunteer service.
item.content:encoded:
I have been co-chair of the Communications Opinion section for more than four years. As I write this, Chiara Renso and I are transferring this role to new leadership: Vivek Sarkar is taking the reins. In our time as co-chairs, I am told that the Opinion section has grown to receive more submissions than the entire magazine did before we started. It was a big job, but we have loved serving, especially together.

When I first started, I wrote an Opinion piece, “Embracing Critical Voices,” to express what I hoped to accomplish. As I wrap up my responsibilities as co-chair, I am writing a series of columns expressing my hopes for ACM as a professional society, informed not only by my role here in Communications, but as co-chair of the Global Technology Policy Council, former chair of the SIG Governance Board, and one of the longest-serving members of ACM Council.

As Communications Editor-in-Chief Jim Larus expressed in a recent Opinion piece, “Wither ACM? Publish and Perish?,” ACM seems to vacillate between being a publisher and a professional society. Over the years, in the context of arguing for Open Access, I have repeatedly argued that “Whenever there is a conflict between being a publisher and a professional society, ACM should be a professional society every day and twice on Sunday.” Why? Very simply, every good thing ACM has to offer the world is the direct result of authors, volunteers, and community members. The staff and volunteers in ACM publishing serve ACM members in key ways, amplifying their influence, highlighting their contributions; but to ever be a publisher in opposition to the will of members would be to choke the only true source of value ACM brings.

I agree with Larus that it is “time for ACM members to debate what kind of organization ACM should be and how to remake it into the society they want to belong to.” I hope to spark conversation around specific ideas and recommendations for change. Many of my recommendations boil down to simple principles—do not surprise members, involve members substantively in the big decisions facing ACM, create processes that respond to member requests, and help members organize around areas of shared concern.

In this first column, I would like to talk about publicly celebrating members’ volunteer service in an expanded Volunteer DB.

In June 2022, as a member of ACM Council, I suggested that ACM create a Volunteer Database to connect volunteer leaders with other people who have served in the same roles. The original goal was to increase the continuity of volunteer leadership. Without this, one generation of volunteer leadership may push for change; then the next generation comes in fresh without awareness of this history and starts from ground zero to discover the problems for themselves and push for similar change. With volunteer leadership terms relatively short, it is possible that no generation accomplishes the changes. Former Communications Editor-in-Chief and columnist Moshe Vardi discussed some of these concerns in his Opinion article, “The Agency Trilemma and ACM.”

I am happy to say that the existing Volunteer DB has already made it easier for volunteers to sustain the push for key community initiatives such as the transition to Open Access, but it could be so much more. The current Volunteer Database contains only a small subset of ACM volunteers, and many important roles are missing.

The ACM Digital Library is a comprehensive record of author contributions and similarly, the Volunteer DB could be a comprehensive record of volunteer service. It could provide an authoritative source members could use to document their professional service to share in the context of searching for a job or documenting impact for tenure, immigration, or other purposes.

Have you volunteered for ACM as a reviewer, distinguished speaker, program committee member, program chair, general chair, editor? Look yourself up in the Volunteer Database. Is your record complete and accurate? I’d love to know. If yes, great! If not, one way for ACM to serve members well as a professional society would be to receive reports of missing service and work diligently to improve the database. In time, the Volunteer DB could remind you of roles you forgot rather than the other way around.

There may be problems documenting historical service with sufficient evidence to confidently add a record. That is understandable, but going forward ACM could keep better records documenting and celebrating the varied volunteer service of its members, helping members document and brag about their important work.

item.title: The ASML Monopoly: Platform and Ecosystem Leadership in EUV Lithography
item.dc:creator: Michael A. Cusumano
item.description: Why ASML and its technology have been so difficult to replicate, and what China is doing about it.
item.content:encoded:
Generative AI software requires a semiconductor stack that is increasingly constrained at multiple levels: Nvidia dominates GPU designs.8 TSMC dominates advanced chip manufacturing.9 High-bandwidth memory is dominated by SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung. But another critical bottleneck is one layer deeper: the equipment used to fabricate the most advanced chips. At the center of that other layer is a company known as ASML.

Based in the Netherlands, ASML (the acronym name is derived from Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography) is Europe’s most valuable technology company. It produces approximately 90% of all lithography tools and is the only supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) systems, a critical manufacturing technology.29 ASML has a market value of approximately $677 billion, with more than $37 billion in FY 2025 revenues, $11 billion in profits, and 44,000 employees. But the company’s de facto monopoly is not based on a single breakthrough innovation. Rather, it results from decades of foresighted investment combined with extraordinary platform leadership and ecosystem management skills.11 No competitor has yet been able to reproduce the core technology or the full stack of system capabilities needed for EUV lithography.

Since 2019, following U.S. policy, the Netherlands has prevented export to China of the most advanced ASML machines. This ban has provoked in China a Manhattan Project-type of response. This column examines how ASML has come to dominate EUV lithography, why the company and the technology have been so difficult to replicate, and what China is doing about it.

Technology and Company Origins

Photolithography uses light to “print” billions of microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers treated with photosensitive coatings. The technology resembles photography and dates back to the 1950s, invented for the U.S. military and commercialized by firms such as Fairchild Semiconductor and Texas Instruments. By the early 1980s, Geophysical Corporation of America (GCA) had as much as an 85% market share in lithography machines. By the later 1980s, however, Nikon and Canon overtook GCA (which shut down in 1993) and came to dominate the industry.19,38

ASML began in 1984 as a joint venture between Philips, the Dutch electronics conglomerate founded in 1891 (and an early investor in TSMC), and ASM International, a small Dutch semiconductor manufacturing equipment firm founded in 1964. The goal was to commercialize Philip’s in-house photolithography technology. However, ASML’s first product, the PAS 2000 (PAS stands for “Philips Automatic Stepper”), was unreliable and a failure.35 In 1988, ASML became independent. Its next product line, the PAS 5500, introduced in 1991, was highly successful, using a modularized architecture, precision optics from Carl Zeiss AG of Germany (based on a partnership started in 1983), and “near” ultraviolet light to produce denser chip designs.2,39 PAS 5500 in the mid-1990s added “Deep Ultraviolet” (DUV) capabilities, which the Japanese were also perfecting.

The challenge for European and U.S. lithography producers in the 1990s was to find a way to leapfrog Nikon and Cannon. One way was to establish an early leadership position in the next generation of the technology.12 DUV had physical limits and experts believed the shorter wavelengths and higher photon energy of EUV would be necessary to produce denser chips. The problem was how to generate and control EUV light for mass production. There were other candidate technologies (X-rays, electron beams, ion beams, and charged particles), but none offered the potential speed and cost advantages of EUV.17

Successful commercialization of EUV lithography is one of the greatest stories in the history of science, engineering, and business. That said, the success took roughly two decades, $11 billion in R&D, and a global effort coordinated by one firm—ASML.24 The history goes back to 1985, when Hiroo Kinoshita, a researcher at Japan’s NTT labs, adopted multilayer mirror research from the Soviet Union to project the first EUV images. He used Mercury-vapor lamps, which produced ultraviolet light of 365 nanometers (nm). Kinoshita’s presentation at a 1986 Japanese optics conference was met with skepticism but prompted other researchers around the world to study EUV lithography.13

By 1994–1995, ASML executives had concluded EUV was indeed the future of lithography. Martin van den Brink (later president and CTO), a technology executive with a strong physics background, had led development of the PAS 5500. He championed the effort to explore EUV and put another senior manager, Jos Benschop, in charge.13,34 In 1998, ASML and Zeiss formed a European industrial consortium named EUCLIDES for “Extreme UV Concept Lithography Development System.”13 Similar consortia appeared in the U.S. and Japan, but only EUCLIDES succeeded.

In 2000, convinced they could overcome the scientific hurdles, ASML created a small team to build a prototype EUV stepper. ASML also benefitted from U.S. military R&D after it bought the last surviving U.S.-based lithography company, Silicon Valley Group (SVG), also in 2000.19 The prototype took six years, completed in 2006. ASML worked closely with key suppliers and universities as well as IMEC, the Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre in Belgium, which served as a laboratory and equipment testing ground for the European semiconductor industry. In 2009, ASML opened a new EUV R&D facility at its headquarters in Veldhoven, Netherlands.13

Another important milestone occurred in 2012. Three key customers—Intel, along with Samsung and TSMC—agreed to become investors in ASML to share the R&D costs and help resolve the technical challenges.13 Intel’s investment of $4 billion (a 15% stake—several times larger than TSMC and Samsung) was especially significant.18 Intel was the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturer and this decision signaled a major commitment to EUV. ASML began shipping EUV prototypes in 2010 but needed help to produce a commercially viable system, which it did by 2013. Machines perfected for mass production took until 2017 and were priced at $100 million.3,29

Despite its early backing of EUV, Intel decided to delay commercial introduction until the next generation because of the high cost. Unfortunately, this delay (until 2025) caused Intel to fall behind TSMC and Samsung in advanced manufacturing capabilities. It also has led to severe financial and reputational difficulties, from which Intel is only now starting to recover.1,7 Samsung would go on to ship the first EUV-enabled product (using what is referred to as a “7nm” node process) in August 2019 for its Galaxy Note 10 smartphone.13 TSMC shipped its first EUV-enabled products (also with the 7nm node process) in October 2019 for multiple customers, including Huawei in China.30

Why ASML’s EUV Machines Have Been So Difficult to Copy

In semiconductor manufacturing, to shrink circuit feature sizes depends fundamentally on the wavelength of light used in lithography: shorter wavelengths enable finer patterns and denser packing of transistors. For decades, the industry has relied on DUV systems operating at 193nm, and these machines are still widely used. EUV reduced the potential wavelength to 13.5nm. This is a dramatic improvement, though mass production required significant advances in a range of complementary technologies.14

For example, EUV light cannot pass through air or conventional glass, which eliminates traditional lens-based approaches. Instead, ASML’s EUV machines rely on highly specialized multilayer mirrors, fabricated with sub-nanometer precision by Zeiss, to reflect and focus the EUV light. Generating and controlling EUV light is another complex physics problem. ASML uses a high-powered laser produced by TRUMPF GmbH, a German company, to strike microscopic tin droplets at 50,000 times per second. This creates a plasma about 200,000 degrees centigrade (40 times hotter than the surface of the sun) that emits the required wavelength.23 The laser module alone is said to contain 457,329 parts.19

The wafer masks are another critical component. Semiconductor foundries create the masks but work closely with electronic design automation (EDA) tools companies such as Cadence and Synopsys. The chip manufacturers use EDA tools to generate data for the 50 or so alternating layers of silicon and molybdenum in each mask, which must be perfectly compatible with the EUV optics, light system, and the stepper’s numerical aperture.10 To make sure each EUV machine can print the mask patterns and produce functioning semiconductor devices also requires special test engines and many rounds of simulations, done by the EDA firms and the foundries.33 Other firms handle final assembly and packaging of the semiconductor devices, with processing steps almost as complicated as the core EUV technology.6

The challenge for potential competitors is that no one component defines performance of the whole system. The light source, optics, wafer, mask, and control software all come from different specialist firms, and their modules must all function as a tightly coupled system and operate in a vacuum under extreme thermal, mechanical, and computational constraints. Each component has required scientific and engineering advances in different fields, achieved over decades, in plasma physics, precision optics, mechanical engineering, materials science, and software engineering. ASML also holds the rights to thousands of patents that protect its technology.5

EUV machines weigh approximately 400,000 pounds, are the size of a double-decker bus, and require three Boeing 747s to transport.20 ASML charges around $200 million for less sophisticated versions and $400 million for the most advanced versions (“2nm” and denser node processes). Each system contains more than 100,000 modules from some 800 suppliers, which have thousands of additional suppliers in their supply chains. ASML’s strategy has been to outsource 90% of the modules and act as the R&D leader and system integrator.20,28 This strategy leveraged the R&D and capabilities of many outside firms, but has limited ASML’s control over manufacturing capacity. In 2025, ASML shipped just 48 EUV systems out of 327 ASML lithography machines of all types.16 The company plans to ship 60 EUV systems in 2026 and 80 annually in future years.15

EUV machines and advances in chip design have enabled the semiconductor industry to continue on the path laid out by Moore’s Law and produce increasingly advanced microprocessors, GPUs, and memory chips. The price tag limits the market for EUV machines but, as Intel discovered, due to their power, precision, and speed, using EUV to make the densest chips has become cheaper than workarounds with creative three-dimensional chip designs and DUV equipment.34

The cost and complexity of ASML’s EUV machines help explain why the industry’s leading manufacturing firms—Intel, TSMC, and Samsung—chose not to develop EUV lithography themselves but instead to invest in ASML. The cost and complexity also help explain why companies that mastered DUV lithography—particularly Nikon and Canon—gave up on EUV. They also fell behind ASML in advanced DUV machines, where ASML holds between a 60% and 85% market share.20,31 It probably had some impact that the Japanese did not have direct access to U.S. military and national laboratory research, which ASML did through its SVG acquisition.19

Future Competition: Spotlight on China

ASML illustrates a unique type of monopoly—a dominance rooted not in a single proprietary invention but in a technology platform and ecosystem strategy used to integrate a complex system of components and skills provided by hundreds of partners, suppliers, and customers. ASML subsidiaries also maintain tight control over critical technologies: HMI—mask pattern verification; Cymer—light sources; and Berliner Glas—optics.25 This platform-ecosystem structure is useful to understand why ASML’s main customers became investors and why competitors face a challenge that looks increasingly like a nation-state effort. The Russians have been trying to develop EUV technology for years but appear to be as much as two decades behind ASML.4 The Chinese are more advanced and investing heavily, spending an estimated $50 billion per year on semiconductor manufacturing technology.25

China’s leading foundry, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), founded in 2000 as an attempt to build a TSMC-like foundry in China, had been a large ASML customer.19 However, SMIC and other Chinese firms since 2019 have been prohibited from importing not only EUV machines but also the latest DUV machines produced by ASML as well as Canon and Nikon. SMIC and other foundries have extended DUV technology by using “multi-patterning” to add extra lines on the masks with multiple passes. Though costly and slow, this approach has enabled the production of 7nm and 5nm node devices, which SMIC has done mainly for Huawei.10,27

To produce its own EUV machine, China launched a project that is supposed to be a state secret. As reported by Reuters, in early 2025, former Chinese ASML engineers completed a prototype at a Shenzhen laboratory using components from older ASML machines available in secondary markets. The prototype is operational and undergoing testing. Observers believe it will take until at least 2030 for commercial production.22,26,37

China’s effort differs from simple reverse engineering. The Central Science and Technology Commission is overseeing the project, with Huawei as the system integrator. The Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (SIOM) as well as several other private companies are involved as well. They are using solid-state lasers for EUV light generation, an approach ASML determined was inadequate for mass production. The Chinese still need Zeiss mirrors (also banned for export to China) or a substitute. In addition, Huawei is developing a Laser-Induced Discharge Plasma (LDP) technology that uses high voltages to generate extreme ultraviolet light.32 LDP should use less energy than ASML’s tin-based approach but still generate the 13.5nm EUV light.36

Perhaps the biggest challenge for China is to produce EUV machines that are suitable for mass production, though initial cost is probably a secondary concern. For example, for 7nm chips using DUV technology, SMIC reportedly had yields less than 50% and wafer costs 40% to 50% more than TSMC, but at least it was able to make these advanced devices.32 Another challenge is that the target is moving: ASML and its customers are already introducing technology for sub-2nm fabrication.21,29 At some point, the laws of physics will limit ASML’s approach and a better technology will emerge, but we are not there yet.

item.title: Non-Volatile Memory Renaming for Safe Batteryless Computing
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Bhattacharyya, Abhijith Somashekhar, and Joshua San Miguel
item.description: This work addresses backups caused by idempotency violations, a critical challenge in energy-harvesting intermittent systems.
item.content:encoded:
Abstract

Batteryless devices powered by energy harvesting face frequent interruptions due to unstable power, requiring them to save their progress and resume later. These devices rely on non-volatile memories, such as Flash or FRAM, to preserve their state across power losses. However, saving data to these memories not only consumes significant energy, making frequent backups expensive, but can also lead to data inconsistencies and incorrect program execution when not handled appropriately.

This work introduces NvMR, an architecture that addresses these challenges by renaming non-volatile memory addresses to prevent inconsistencies. NvMR minimizes the need for backups, ensuring they occur only when absolutely necessary. It also simplifies the backup process, freeing it from program-specific constraints, and reduces energy consumption by 20%–40% compared to current state-of-the-art. These improvements make NvMR a significant step forward for energy-efficient and reliable operation in batteryless devices.

1. Introduction

By 2030, the proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices is expected to reach staggering levels, with forecasts estimating more than 29 billion IoT-connected devices globally, growing at a compound annual rate of 13% from 2024.21 This growth is driven by advances in connectivity technologies, such as 5G, low-energy Bluetooth, and sophisticated applications like machine learning, alongside expanding use cases in industrial automation, healthcare, smart homes, and urban infrastructure. A majority fraction of these devices relies on batteries, which are less eco-friendly because they wear out quickly due to frequent recharging. They are also inconvenient to replace in remote deployments, driving interest in batteryless devices that harvest energy from ambient sources, such as solar, RF, wind, or piezoelectric systems.6,8,15,18

Batteryless devices store energy in supercapacitors (higher recharge cycles but less dense energy storage) but face challenges due to unpredictable power supply. To ensure forward progress, they rely on intermittent computing (IC), where the system backs up application and processor states to non-volatile memory (NVM) before energy depletes completely. Once recharged, the system restores state and resumes computation. The constraints of an IC system pose unique challenges that are normally not encountered in a continuously powered system.

1.1. Challenges in IC.

Inconsistency due to idempotency violations.  Unexpected power losses during program execution in batteryless devices can cause an incorrect processor state. To illustrate, in Figure 1 we show the execution of a loop with the iterator stored at NVM location A, the instruction LD A initially reads a value of 0 from address A and stores it in register r1. ADDI then increments the value in r1 by 1, and ST A writes the value of r1 back to address A in NVM. However, if a power outage occurs after the store, re-executing the program causes LD A to read the updated value of 1 from NVM and the subsequent ST A storing a value of 2, resulting in skipping an iteration, which can ultimately lead to incorrect behavior. This inconsistency in the result of LD A from the result prior to power failure is referred to as an idempotency violation, an artifact of write-after-read (WAR) dependency between LD A and ST A.

Expensive conservative backups.  IC systems require backups to ensure data consistency during power failures. Backup schemes can be broadly classified as hardware- or software-based. Hardware-based approaches2,10 use an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to constantly monitor supply voltage and trigger a backup just before power failure. To ensure correctness, backups must be atomic (Figure 2a). Software-based methods5,12 decompose programs into atomic tasks, with backups at task boundaries (Figure 2c). While these approaches ensure consistency, they often impose unnecessary backups due to conservative policies or static task decomposition.

Clank9 and DINO12 highlight the trade-offs in idempotency handling. Clank uses buffers to classify addresses as read-first or write-first, triggering backups on idempotency violations caused by store operations (Figure 2b). Although effective, this approach results in frequent backups, even when sufficient energy is available. Our experiments with Clank show that such violations account for more than 30% of total energy consumption in common embedded benchmarks. DINO, on the other hand, enforces task-level idempotency with privatization buffers, but static task decomposition limits flexibility and increases programmer effort. The challenge is to balance backups for correctness with forward progress. An ideal solution would ensure program correctness while optimizing energy efficiency.

We propose NvMR, an IC architecture that overcomes these challenges by dynamically renaming NVM addresses of violating persist stores (Figure 2d), decoupling backup policies from program characteristics, and allowing energy-efficient backup policies under varied conditions.

2. Intermittent Persist Dependencies

Most of the previous works have built models to characterize the efficiency of IC, but none provide generalized models addressing the persistency constraints required for correct execution under intermittent power. Persist dependencies, essential for ensuring programs behave as if running on a continuously powered system, remain unexplored. While memory-persistency models17 in shared-memory multiprocessors address orderings between persists to an external persistent data structure, this work introduces the first persist dependency model tailored for addressing the persist orderings imposed by IC.

Previous studies proposing correctness models for IC assume architectures with no dirty data buffering, such as write-through caches.23 In contrast, we consider an architecture with a volatile write-back cache, which reduces costly NVM writes by reusing dirty data. Thus, there is a good chance that the persists for backups and stores can get reordered. Execution resumes from the last persisted backup after power loss. Any instructions executed after the backup must be re-executed. This work aims to provide a theoretical framework for understanding persist dependencies and their impact on intermittent execution.

2.1. Requirements for correct IC. 

Correct execution in traditional intermittent architectures relies on three key requirements:
