  1. Code Progress. Stores to the same address must be persisted in program order, and backups must be persisted in the order they are triggered to ensure the program completes if the device sustains energy for at least one backup.

  2. Data Progress. A store to NVM address X must be persisted before the backup following it, ensuring data remains up to date across power losses.

  3. Idempotency. After a backup, if the first access to an address X is a load, subsequent stores to X must not be persisted until the next backup. This prevents data corruption from unbacked instructions after a power loss.

2.2. Persist ordering model.  

To ensure correct execution in intermittent systems, it is essential to define the order of persist operations, including backups and stores. Current systems often enforce overly conservative constraints, limiting efficiency. We aim to characterize the minimum persist dependencies required for correctness, balancing flexibility and reliability. Specifically, given a program and a set of backups invoked during its execution, what are the minimum ordering constraints for correct persists? Each backup captures the volatile processor state, including registers and the program counter, and persists it into NVM. Similar to stores, persisting the backup can be decoupled from its execution as long as the persisted register contents match what they would be at the position in program order at which the backup was triggered. The processor may trigger a backup and continue executing instructions after it; however, if power is lost before the backup is persisted, the processor must revert its state to an earlier backup. A backup must be persisted atomically via double buffering.

We formally describe persist dependencies using happensbefore relations between persist operations, expressed as {p1,rel,p2}:

  • p1 and p2 are persist operations in program order (e.g., store or checkpoint).

  • rel represents the persist order between a pair of persists with the order direction.

For example, st,→spo,st is the relation between a pair of persist stores to the same address, representing the necessary ordering between them to maintain program order (Requirement 1). We color-code the various relationships that exist in an intermittent execution and list them alongside the requirements they satisfy in Table 1. The ordering, st,→spo,st, is also needed for correct program execution in continuously powered systems, while the other orderings are specific to IC systems. backup,→bpo,backupordering is necessary in multi-backup schemes only.20

Figure 3 shows the necessary persist dependencies for any general program execution, characterized by read-dominance and write-dominance, focusing on the symbolic NVM location X. We ignore the dependencies in instruction execution and assume they respect program order. We also ignore loads and assume the most up-to-date values are readily available in the write-back cache, except immediately after a power loss; in that case, a load must fetch the value from NVM. Backups can be invoked at any arbitrary point in the program, but when invoked, they introduce a set of happensbefore orderings and atomicity constraints with surrounding stores.

Understanding persist orderings in IC.  The backup point also decides if an address location X is read-dominated or write-dominated in the next intermittent code section.

Read-dominance. A location X is read-dominated if the first load after the most recent checkpoint occurs before the first store in program order. Figure 3(a) models the dependency pattern when all stores access read-dominated addresses. To ensure data progress (Requirement 2), each store must persist before the next backup persists. Otherwise, if the next backup were persisted first and power is lost, the most up-to-date value of X would be lost. Simultaneously, to ensure idempotent execution (Requirement 3), each store must not persist until the next backup persists. Otherwise, if the store were persisted first and power is lost, the program would re-execute from the prior backup and incorrectly load the later store’s value of X. These constraints combined imply that all stores to a read-dominated address must atomically persist with the next backup. This is a unique, fundamental challenge in IC systems.

Write-dominance. A location X is write-dominated if the first store occurs before the first load. Figure 3(b) shows that for the same program, with a simple shift of when backups are invoked, X becomes write-dominated. As a result, the dependency pattern changes dramatically. Now only Requirements 1 and 2 need to be enforced, which is done by persisting backups in program order and ensuring stores are persisted before the next backup. Stores no longer must wait until the next backup to persist, eliminating the atomicity constraint. In fact, stores after a backup may even be persisted before the backup persists. Since X is always write-dominated, whenever power is lost, regardless to which backup system it reverts, X will always be overwritten first, nullifying the last persisted store.

Why non-volatile memory renaming?  Idempotency is essential for correct intermittent execution and can only be violated by WAR dependencies on NVM locations. Our architecture addresses this by dynamically renaming read-dominated NVM addresses, inspired by similar techniques used in out-of-order processors for registers. NVM renaming ensures idempotent execution (Requirement 3) regardless of backup timing.

The key insight is: renaming transforms all NVM addresses into write-dominated ones. As shown in Figure 4, renaming eliminates dependencies such as st,→spo,st, backup,→bpo,st, and st,←irpo,backup  from Figure 3(a).

This approach achieves the theoretical maximum efficiency by only persisting stores immediately preceding a backup, satisfying Requirement 2 (data progress). Backups must still be persisted in the order invoked to ensure Requirement 1 (code progress). Thus, renaming minimizes persist constraints, allowing backup decisions to be decoupled from program correctness requirements.

3. NvMR Architecture

Based on insights from our previous analysis, we propose an intermittent architecture, non-volatile memory renaming (NvMR), that efficiently detects idempotency violations due to persist stores in hardware and renames their NVM addresses. Figure 5 is a high-level block diagram of NvMR. Map table and free list are two software data structures allocated statically in NVM at compile time. Map table keeps a record of the old (original or most recently persisted) mappings. Free list is a queue of available mappings. Four hardware components are important for NvMR’s renaming mechanism:

  1. Write-back, write-allocate (WBWA) data cache that exploits data locality and tracks dirty blocks

  2. Global bloom filter (GBF) that logs the composite state (Unknown=0 or Read-dominated=1; discussed later) of a block when it is evicted from the cache

  3. Local bloom filter (LBF) array, tightly coupled with cache data array, with one LBF per block that logs the state of each word in a block (Unknown=00, Read-dominated=01, and Write-dominated=10)

  4. Map table cache, a volatile cache for map table (analogous to a translation lookaside buffer for page table) that saves energy and time by reducing the number of trips to NVM. Apart from the old mapping, it also holds the new (latest) mapping. Since it is also a WBWA cache, for each block there is a dirty bit along with a valid bit and a tag.

3.1. Intermittent execution in NvMR. 

Figure 6 explains NvMR’s renaming mechanism in a concise flowchart. To explain NvMR’s microarchitecture in more detail, we divide intermittent execution in NvMR into five disparate events and explain them with a running example.

Idempotency violation.  Figure 7 shows a cache block X with a tag, Xtag. This block was fetched from NVM because of a read-dominated access to word [C]. Later, as word [A] is updated to [Anew], the block is marked dirty and the corresponding LBF states of [C] and [Anew] are set as R and W respectively. Only when a dirty block is evicted is the composite state of the block calculated by OR of the LSBs of the LBF states of the constituent words. If the composite state is 0 (block is write-dominated), there is no idempotency violation. Otherwise, it should be flagged as an idempotency violation since it is dirty and read-dominated (violates Requirement 3). Thus, NvMR flags an idempotency violation (A1) when block X is evicted. The composite state is logged in GBF.

Renaming.  Eviction of an idempotency violating block triggers a lookup in the map table cache to find its new mapping. In case of a hit, the new mapping is used to persist the block. In case of a miss, map table is looked up. If the map table lookup is successful, the old mapping is fetched into the map table cache. Otherwise, a new mapping is popped from the head of the free list and fetched into the map table cache. The block is persisted using the fetched mapping. Thus, the old mapping of the persist store is renamed to a new mapping. In Figure 7, block X incurs a miss in both map table cache (A2) and map table (A3). Thus, NvMR fetches mapping 710 from free list (A4) and inserts a new dirty map table cache block (A5), renaming 200 to 710. The contents of block X are written to the renamed address 710 (A6).

Cache miss.  In Figure 8, a store request for cache block X attempts to write [Bnew]. Since the block was recently evicted, the lookup results in a cache miss (B1). The cache controller then looks up the map table cache to find the latest mapping in NVM. As address 200 was renamed to 710 and this entry exists in the map table cache, the lookup is a hit (B2). The block is fetched from 710 in NVM, updated with [Bnew], and marked dirty (B3). NvMR then checks GBF to determine the block state. Since block X is read-dominated (1), all associated LBF states are set to R (B4). For blocks in the U state, LBF states are marked R or W based on the type of request. A map table cache miss triggers a lookup in the map table, which lies in the critical path. We assume the map table lookup can be done in parallel to fetching the application data, since both reside in separate regions of NVM.

Backup.  NvMR initiates a backup in three cases: (1) when a dirty map table cache entry is evicted to ensure the map table in NVM reflects the latest mappings, (2) based on a user-defined backup policy to guarantee forward progress, and (3) when an idempotency violation occurs and either the map table is full or the free list is empty, making renaming impossible. Like other intermittent architectures, NvMR snapshots general-purpose and special registers (e.g., the program counter), but these are omitted in Figure 9. With a write-back data cache, NvMR persists all dirty blocks during backup. If a cache block was renamed, NvMR fetches its latest mapping from the map table cache or the map table; otherwise, the block is stored at its program address.

For cache block X, the map table cache lookup is a hit (C1), and the dirty data is persisted at the new mapping 710 (C2). The dirty bit of block X is cleared after the write-back. NvMR writes the new mapping 710 to the map table (C3) and appends the old mapping 200 to the free list tail (C4), indicated by the orange arrow for the write pointer. Once all updates are completed, the new mapping is copied to the old field in the map table cache, and the dirty bit is reset. Finally, GBF and LBF arrays are cleared (C5).

Restore.  After a power loss, an IC system state is restored to the most recent backup and execution resumes. In NvMR, restore is pretty simple: The program counter and other registers are restored from the most recent snapshot saved in NVM. Moreover, only the read and write pointers of the free list need to be restored.

Reclamation.  The map table, being a limited hardware resource, can fill quickly for applications with frequent idempotency violations, especially in energy-harvesting devices with small non-volatile memory. To address this, we introduce reclamation (a popular technique in garbage collection), which reuses the original mapping—the program’s cache block address. When the map table is full after a backup, NvMR reclaims an entry using a cache-like replacement policy. This involves atomically moving the old mapping to the free list’s tail, invalidating the entry, and copying data from the freed mapping back to the original mapping. NvMR also invalidates the corresponding map table cache entry on a lookup hit. Reclaiming reduces backups after a full map table but decreases the free list’s effective size, as original mappings cannot be added. To compensate, the free list requires more mappings to avoid shortages.

4. Methodology

We extend a cycle-accurate C++ simulator20 to model an intermittent ARM Cortex M0+1 (3-stage in-order pipeline) executing ARM Thumb ISA instructions. Voltage traces sampled at 1kHz from prior work14 are used to compute the charge across the supply supercapacitor. Dynamic and leakage power for added volatile components are modeled using CACTI,16 and NVM energy values are taken from the STM32L011K4 MCU data sheet.22

We compare NvMR with two IC architectures: a) a modified Clank9, augmented with local and global bloom filters, and a write-back data cache, an idempotency violation-aware hardware solution, and b) HOOP4, a software transactional memory solution with hardware support with similar semantics to a task-based IC architecture. We use the configuration listed in Table 2 for all our results except for the sensitivity analysis because it is pareto-optimal. Since NvMR decouples the backup policy from the memory access patterns of an application, we show the impact of NvMR using three backup schemes:

  • Just-In-Time (JIT) is an oracle that accurately estimates when a power loss will happen and triggers a backup just before it.

  • Spendthrift uses a lightweight neural network (trained offline with two inputs, available ambient energy, and supercapacitor voltages at a particular time to an accuracy of 97%) to predict backups,13 representative of JIT schemes deployed commercially.

  • Watchdog timer is the most naive out of the three and invokes a backup every 8,000 cycles.9

The benchmarks we chose are from MiBench7 and PERFECT3 benchmark suites, representing applications typically found in ultra-low-power IoT systems with a high number of idempotency violations.

5. Evaluating NvMR

To understand the benefits offered by NvMR, we compare it with the chosen baseline IC architectures by looking at the energy savings in each architecture with different backup schemes. In addition, we analyze how sensitive NvMR is to variations in system configuration. Further, we discuss the minimal overheads incurred with NvMR. All results are averaged over 10 voltage traces.

5.1. NvMR vs. Clank. 

Figure 10 presents the percentage of energy saved in NvMR compared to Clank. With JIT, NvMR saves on average about 20% energy compared to Clank. The energy savings can range from 2% to 37% based on the application. With spendthrift, NvMR saves about 15.6% energy on average. Since Blowfish and dijkstra spend the least amount of energy on backups due to idempotency violations, they marginally consume more energy in NvMR. With watchdog timer, NvMR saves on average 9% energy on average. stringsearch and hist perform worse than in Clank because a significant portion of energy (6.5%–7%) is wasted in re-executing instructions after a power failure (dead energy20).

We take a deeper dive by analyzing the breakdown of normalized energy consumption of Clank and NvMR with JIT backup scheme in Figure 11. The total energy consumption is split into four components—forward progress, backup, restore, and dead energy.20 NvMR incurs additional energy overhead for forward progress and restore due to dynamic and leakage energy from the map table cache, extra NVM accesses for the map table and free list, and reclamation-related energy.

JIT backup scheme eliminates dead energy, and NvMR’s restore energy is minimal, involving only the retrieval of CPU registers; hence, these are omitted from Figure 11. The benchmark stringsearch performs worst, with nearly 90% of its energy spent on forward progress due to minimal idempotency violations during string list searches. NvMR incurs forward progress and backup overheads, along with additional energy for reclaiming. Forward progress energy is higher in NvMR than Clank for some benchmarks, since persisting data to renamed addresses is included in forward progress rather than backup energy. Reclaim energy is significant only for benchmarks such as blowfish, dijkstra, and qsort, where frequent idempotency violations fill the map table. Overall, renaming and reclaiming add just 3% to NvMR’s total energy, a small cost for reducing backups by 185x on average.

5.2. NvMR vs. Hoop. 

HOOP, a log-based architecture, performs out-of-place updates to an NVM region, optimizing write efficiency and triggering backups when its buffer or mapping table fills up. Table 3 outlines the HOOP configuration used for the results in Figure 12. Components, excluding the mapping table (idealized as infinite for no energy usage), are sized to match NvMR’s on-chip area and memory overheads (Table 2). With JIT, NvMR saves 40% more energy on average, except for benchmarks stringsearch, picojpeg, and basicmath, where HOOP excels due to high store locality, allowing its buffer to reduce NVM writes. For watchdog timer backup, NvMR achieves 19.4% average energy savings, although less than with JIT due to the naive nature of the timer scheme. (Spendthrift results are not shown since they were not part of the original paper.)

5.3. NvMR sensitivity. 

Map Table Cache.  Energy savings in NvMR improve with larger map table caches, as seen in Figure 13b, since evictions of dirty entries (and the associated backups) reduce. Associativity has minimal impact on energy efficiency after reaching four-way; savings plateau at around 0.2% with full associativity, as shown in Figure 13a. These results use a map table with 4,096 entries and JIT backup for consistency.

Map Table Size.  Increasing the map table entries from 1,024 to 8,192 shows a modest 1% energy saving (Figure 13c), primarily benefiting benchmarks prone to idempotency violations, such as blowfish, dijkstra, qsort, and dwt. Given the large Flash requirements for small gains, 4,096 entries represents a balanced choice, aligning with the constraints of energy-harvesting devices.

Capacitor Size.  NvMR’s energy savings grow as capacitor size increases, with a 7% improvement from 500µF to 7.5mF and a slower 2% rise up to 100mF (Figure 13d). Larger capacitors extend active periods, leading to more idempotency violations, which NvMR exploits to reduce backups. However, the rate of savings diminishes beyond 7.5mF, reflecting diminishing returns on larger capacitor sizes.

5.4. Benefits of reclamation. 

Reclamation minimizes backups caused by idempotency violations when the map table is full, but only a few benchmarks encounter this issue with the configuration in Table 2. As shown in Figure 14, reclaiming provides minimal energy savings, averaging just 1%, without diminishing NvMR’s overall efficiency qsort (9%) and dwt (1%) benefit, while dijkstra, blowfish, and 2dconv incur slightly higher energy consumption). Nonetheless, reclamation can be particularly valuable for devices with limited NVM, where allocating large map tables and free lists is impractical. Our experiments reveal with a map table of 1,024 entries, reclaiming saves about 9% more energy compared to the “no reclaim” scenario.

5.5. NvMR overhead. 

The hardware cost of NvMR is limited to the map table cache, with McPAT11 estimates indicating a modest 6% on-chip area overhead for the configuration in Table 2. NvMR’s software and hardware structures can be tailored to application requirements, constrained only by the available memory onboard. The memory footprint for the reserved region is approximately 6% of the 2MB Flash (typical size of Flash in commercial MCU boards19). However, if the NVM is byte-addressable, NvMR’s renaming mechanism provides a significant advantage by reducing wear-out, achieving an impressive 80.8% average decrease in maximum writes per location compared to Clank.

Conclusion

This work addresses a critical challenge in energy-harvesting intermittent systems: backups caused by idempotency violations. While prior research has improved backup efficiency, unnecessary overhead from these violations persists. Our key insight is that backups should stem solely from energy or hardware constraints, not program inconsistencies. By analyzing unique persist dependencies in intermittent execution, we show that renaming NVM addresses of violating persists minimizes backups. Based on this, we propose NvMR, an energy-efficient hardware architecture that enables productive use of harvested energy and decouples program correctness from backup policies, paving the way for advancements in intermittent system design.

item.title: Technical Perspective: NVMR for Batteryless Computing
item.dc:creator: Brandon Lucia
item.description: Opening the door to more capable batteryless systems.
item.content:encoded:
It has been 10 years since we first wrote about intermittent computing, and research in this area has come a long way to make batteryless devices more capable. The accompanying paper on the NVMR architecture opens the door to more capable, correct batteryless systems. Intermittent computing has not always been in the research zeitgeist, so here is an overview. An intermittent computing device is a batteryless hardware/software system that harvests energy from its environment into a tiny capacitor. The system computes until energy is exhausted, when the system abruptly stops to collect more energy. After collecting enough energy to do more work, the system turns back on and the cycle continues. A system can operate indefinitely harvesting solar, RF, or mechanical energy for a range of use cases, such as environmental sensing, wearables, and smart buildings.

Intermittent computing devices operate without batteries, allowing deployment to environments where batteries are infeasible: inhospitable environments like space and glaciers, and operationally infeasible environments with unacceptable costs for battery production, maintenance, and disposal. The abundant uses for these systems are an exciting vision, but it isn’t free.

Intermittent operation causes problems for programmers. Programming languages and developers assume continuous operation, but intermittent operation is different. If the system samples a sensor now and calls a function to process the data immediately in the code, the sensor data might be hours old when it is processed, because power could fail before processing completes? A power failure every 100ms can leave the state of the system murky: “What was I doing before power failed?” Reasoning about program behavior is harder when power may fail any time.

Memory consistency is particularly challenging and is the focus of the NVMR paper. Parts of memory are non-volatile, and some dependencies can leave non-volatile memory (NVM) inconsistent when power fails. As the paper describes, if a program “persists” (i.e., commits to NVM) a value, but then reverts to an earlier checkpoint, NVM is left inconsistent. A read to that persisted location in a re-execution of the region sees the wrong value; similar problems arise if cache writebacks or checkpoint backups persist out of order. These subtle persistent ordering conditions all lead to incorrect behavior when a program re-executes from a checkpoint. Instead, regions between checkpoints should be idempotent, meaning re-execution always produces the same result.

Idempotence is where NVMR’s solution to the persistent ordering problem comes in. The paper nicely characterizes these dependencies and shows that some lead to incorrect execution if left unaddressed. NVMR has a nice insight: rename the memory locations being written, uniquely in each re-execution. That way, if power fails and a read in a re-execution attempts to access a location that was persisted in a prior execution attempt, the read does not see the persisted value and the program re-executes idempotently. NVMR is a set of hardware extensions that track memory accesses and persist actions. When a memory access could violate idempotence, NVMR’s mapping table redirects the access to a different, safe NVM location. When remapped locations are no longer needed, NVMR reclaims their mapping state.

The simple technique in this paper works extremely well to avoid idempotence violations with low cost, because problematic accesses are replaced by idempotent writes to “fresh,” renamed locations. The hardware cost is acceptable and the net effect of NVMR is to save 10% to 30% energy on average that would have gone to bookkeeping and moving data into and out of NVM. Energy is everything when you’re running from a capacitor, so these savings translate to more capable intermittent devices.

The NVMR paper is part of the community’s steady progression toward more capable intermittent computing devices with reasonable, basic correctness properties. These properties are now becoming formalized [Surbatovich-dissertation1], and the community is turning a corner to face the next great challenge in batteryless devices: energy efficiency. A concerning and even puzzling aspect of computing “at the low end,” especially in intermittent systems, is that devices continue to be built around relatively inefficient von Neumann processors. Despite the addition of vector units, NPUs, DSP cores (and cool spoilers and racing stripes), these architectures are still hampered fundamentally by the inefficiency of instruction supply, control, and data movement in the von Neumann model. For the last decade of intermittent computing, including the great work in the NVMR paper, the focus was “How do we make an intermittent system do anything useful?” The success of systems approaches now clears the path for the future to be defined by a different question: “How much more can an intermittent system do?” This future will be defined by a new wave of energy-efficient architectures [RipTide (Gobieski), Monza (Efficient Computer), Ultra-Elastic CGRAS] that tap into what we have learned about correctness and bring to bear the benefits of efficiency to support intermittent applications that, even today, seem impossible. It is an exciting moment for the intermittent computing research community.

item.title: Cheating by the Rules
item.dc:creator: Dennis Shasha
item.description: Calculating candidate options.
item.content:encoded:
Suppose the political spectrum is analogous to a measuring stick numbered between 1 and 100 (where 1 is totalitarian and 100 is anarchy, with liberal democratic being approximately 50), Here are the rules: Any candidate must state his or her integral position value (some whole number between 1 and 100, inclusive) and no two candidates may choose the same value. Voters will vote for the candidate nearest their position. If there are two candidates at the same distance from a voter V, then voter V will not vote.

Now suppose that two parties are vying for power. Party A must introduce its candidates and their positions on this 1 to 100 spectrum. Party B then introduces its candidates and their positions.

The elections work in two rounds. At the end of the first round, the two candidates who receive the most votes face each other in a runoff. If several candidates tie, then the election commission arranges the second round between members of different parties when possible. For example, if party X has one candidate that wins the most votes in the first round and several other candidates tie for receiving the second highest number of votes, then the election commission will choose a candidate from a party other than party X.

Warm-Up: Can both parties guarantee to having at least one candidate in the run-off if each puts forth two candidates? Please remember that if there is a tie between candidates from the different parties, the commission will ensure that two parties are represented in the final election.

Solution to Warm-Up: Let’s say that party A puts its candidates at position 25 and 75. If party B puts a candidate at 24 and 26, then B will capture voters having positions 1–24 and 26–49. Party A will capture 51–100. So, the runoff will be between the party A candidate at 75 and one of the party B candidates chosen at random by the commission. Facing party A’s choice of 25 and 75, party B cannot prevent party A from having at least one candidate reach the runoff.

Question: Suppose there are three candidates from party B but still two from party A. Can B guarantee to have all runoff candidates be from B’s party when A goes first? Prove your answer.

Solution: In that case, B can guarantee that the runoff will be between B’s candidates. Let’s say party A puts its candidates at X and X+d, respectively. One possibility is for party B to put one candidate in the middle of the A candidates (at X + d/2). That candidate would receive approximately d/2 votes. B’s other candidates could go to X-1 and to 1+(X+d). This limits A’s candidates to approximately a fraction d/4 of the votes. Provided d/4 < X-1 or d/4 < 100-(X+d), B’s candidate in the middle and one of B’s other candidates will enter the runoff. We will call this middle-and-two-ends strategy Configuration 1.

If d is large, party B puts two candidates at X+1 and X+d-1 and the third candidate at X+d+1 or X-1 whichever gains that B candidate more votes (or at least no fewer). We will call this surround-one-candidate and inside the other candidate strategy Configuration 2.

For example, suppose X = 10 and X+d = 80. B places its candidates based on Configuration 2 at 11 and 79 and get roughly 34 each. Those two enter the runoff. B places another candidate at 81. A’s candidate at 10 will get 10% of the votes and A’s candidate at 80 will get 1% of the vote.

To show this works in general, note that party A has every interest to make X and X+d symmetrically distant from the ends, so X = 100 – (X+d). Otherwise, in either configuration, party B will take the bigger end (automatically in configuration 1 and by choice in configuration 2). This symmetry implies that 2X = 100-d. Recall that configuration 1 wins for party B provided d/4 < X-1. Given the symmetry condition, d/4 < ((100-d)/2) – 1 = 49 – d/2. So d < (4/3) x 49 = 66. For example, if d = 64, then party A places its candidates at X = 18 and X+d = 82. Party B places its candidates, under the configuration 1 strategy, at 17, 83, and 50. The candidate at 50 obtains all votes from 35 to 65. The A candidate at 18 obtains 18 through 34 inclusive or 17%. The A candidate at 82 will obtain from 66 to 82, also 17%. However the B candidate at 83 will obtain 18% and the B candidate at 50 will obtain 31% (35 to 65). So the B candidates will appear in the runoff.

Configuration 2 wins for party B if X < (d/2) – 1. So, for example, if d > 53, then Configuration 2 wins. In the case that d = 54, party A places its candidates at X = 23 and X+d = 77. Party B places candidates at 24, 76, and 78. The party B candidates at 24 and 76 each obtain 26% of the vote. The party A candidate at 24 obtains only 24% of the votes and the party A candidate at 76 obtains only 1% of the vote.

Thus, if d > 64, use configuration 1. Otherwise use configuration 2. In fact both configurations will work for d between 54 and 64, inclusive.

End of Solution

Upstart: Suppose that party X has C candidates and party Y has C’ candidates and C > C’, but X must place all its candidates before Y. For which values of C and C’ can Y still guarantee to field at least one candidate in the runoff? Are there any values for which Y can guarantee to field two candidates in the runoff?

item.title: Instruction Set Migration at Warehouse Scale
item.dc:creator: Eric Christopher, Kevin Crossan, Wolff Dobson, Chris Kennelly, Drew Lewis, Kun Lin, Martin Maas, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, Emma Rapati, and Brian Yang
item.description: How Google migrated a multibillion-line codebase from x86 to Arm.
item.content:encoded:
Migrating large codebases to a new instruction set architecture (ISA) is a major engineering challenge. Examples include Apple’s migration from PowerPC to x86 and later to Arm,3 as well as the adoption of Arm by major hyperscalers (such as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft). While there are anecdotal claims regarding the complexity and efforts required1,26,28 and several historical records of such migrations,23,33,34 to our knowledge, there is no systematic analysis of what these ISA migrations entail today and how they are impacted by modern technologies, such as improved software-engineering tools and AI. In this article, we perform such a systematic analysis for the migration of a multibillion-line codebase from x86 to Arm at Google.

When source code is available, as is often the case via open source or within large organizations, recompilation is preferred over techniques such as binary translation.a Contemporary ISAs are generally well-supported in upstream compilers, runtime libraries, and the Linux kernel. As a result, modern compilers mostly “just work” for a new ISA, and previous ISA additions have smoothed the path to packages supporting cross-compilation by default. For example, 98% of Debian packages build for RISC-V, although it only became an official Debian architecture in 2023.9

Perhaps surprisingly, this does not mean ISA migration is no longer a challenge in the presence of source code. We find that modern ISA migration involves many usually-simple, repetitive tasks such as updating build scripts or fixing floating-point issues. In contrast to historical migrations, the volume of simple changes is much higher today. This creates challenges but also presents opportunities for automation, including with AI. We focus on three research questions:

  1. What are the tasks involved in a modern ISA migration?

  2. Which tasks can be successfully automated with conventional methods?

  3. How can modern AI help automation, and what tasks remain challenging?

To answer these questions, we provide what we believe is a first-ever detailed breakdown and taxonomy of large-scale ISA migration tasks. Using state-of-the-art LLMs, we analyze and categorize a corpus of 38,156 commits that constitute our real-world migration. We quantitatively evaluate the capability of current tools, including AI models, to perform these tasks automatically. We systematically identify the strengths and weaknesses of current automated tools and highlight areas of future work and improvement. We believe this work highlights research opportunities for the academic community and revisits longstanding assumptions around ISA migrations.

Specifically, we contribute the following insights:

  • The complexity of ISA migrations involves a number of different tasks, many related to rewriting build and configuration files.

  • Many of these tasks are highly automatable.

  • Many of the tasks that are not automatable only need to be performed once when going from a single ISA to multiarch.

  • Of the remaining tasks, many can be performed by modern AI, but some challenges remain.

Background and Related Work

There are several reasons why organizations have performed large-scale ISA migrations. First, many ISAs have gone extinct over the years (e.g., Alpha, MIPS, SPARC, Itanium, VAX). Second, the proliferation of Android and iOS apps drove many codebases to be ported to Arm. Third, Apple Macs went through successive migrations from PowerPC to x86 to Arm. Finally, major cloud hyperscalers have also been migrating large codebases from x86 to Arm.

In this context, migration not only refers to getting software to build on a new architecture, but also to reaching parity in terms of performance, security, and stability. While ISA migrations go back more than 30 to 40 years,23,33,34 modern migrations are vastly larger and more dependency-heavy than these historical examples. The most closely related academic work falls into two categories.

First, there is a significant amount of work on static and dynamic binary ISA translation13,32 to address the long tail of a software ecosystem. Such systems are eventually deprecated to avoid carrying forward technical debt, as seen with Apple’s planned phaseout of Rosetta.1 In cloud computing, where compute is commoditized, recompiling onto the new ISA maximizes performance and efficiency. We thus forewent binary translation altogether.

Second, there is extensive research on automatically applying edits to code, such as for performance optimization,21 fixing security issues,17 or correcting bugs.4 As we will see, these are common tasks that are part of a successful ISA migration.

Google’s x86 to Arm Journey

We now analyze Google’s multi-year effort to port a substantial portion of Google’s server application ecosystem from x86 to Arm, enabling simultaneous support for both. We start by describing Google’s environment and provide a step-by-step analysis of our ISA migration.

Google’s software ecosystem.  Google’s codebase is organized as a monorepo containing billions of lines of code.29 Individual applications and libraries reside in various directories. These directories also contain metadata files, e.g., to indicate code owners or configure continuous integration (CI) testing.38 An overview figure of this internal ecosystem can be found in Henderson et al.15

Building with Bazel.  Builds use Bazel,6 a highly configurable build system. BUILD and bzl files describe how binaries, libraries, and tests are built from source files. Most code is covered by our primary continuous integration system, “TAP” [Test Automation Platform],19,24 which gates releases similarly to GitHub Actions or GitLab CI. Bazel’s builds and tests (including TAP) run on a shared set of machines called Forge,37 which provides a distributed build execution and caching service. Forge’s scale and cache enable Google to compile everything needed for a binary from scratch on every build, including fundamental dependencies such as the Python interpreter.

Creating releases with Blueprints.  Google distinguishes between compiled binaries and release packages (internally referred to as “MPMs” for the Midas Package Manager that stores them globally).6 These packages are bundles of binaries and static assets ready to be deployed in Google’s clusters, akin to Debian packages or container images. Releases are defined by “Blueprint” files, which serve as release configuration manifests (similar to Helm charts or Kubernetes manifests)25 to specify dependencies, environment settings, and build flags. An automated continuous delivery system called Rapid5 consumes these manifests, runs CI tests, and builds release packages.

Multiarch support.  Google’s fleet has supported dozens of CPUs over the years, and services run on machines that can be as much as 10 years old. During development, engineers can configure builds and testing across multiple architectures (e.g., Arm, K8, Haswell) in their Blueprints. Multiple architectures are also supported at release time, producing multiarch MPMs. Unless an owner adds specific constraints, a job can be scheduled on any machine with an architecture-compatible MPM, and owners expect to run on a mix of different kinds of machines with different performance profiles simultaneously.

Shifting down and large-scale changes.  Google has moved to a “shift down” approach to development,11 where developers only focus on one level of the stack and other issues are abstracted and/or automated for them. For example, the CI pipelines (e.g. Bazel, TAP, and Rapid) mean developers do not generally need to worry about the specifics of build systems or releases. In addition, a healthy automated testing culture means everyone can change code throughout the monorepo without frequent breakages. This enables large-scale changes (LSCs),38 monorepo-wide revisions that can change code owned by many teams over thousands of files at once. Low-risk LSCs can be approved centrally and submitted efficiently without asking individual teams. To manage code edits across many reviewers, Google has developed Rosie,38 an automated change-orchestration tool, which allows engineers to create a very large commit and shard it into tens, hundreds, or thousands of smaller commits split up by the owner.

Life cycle of an ISA migration.  Migrating an individual package from single-arch to multiarch support requires several steps:

  1. Test: Fix tests (and builds) that break when run with the new ISA.

  2. Set up multiarch CI: Modify the corresponding Blueprint files to ensure no additional regressions are introduced (often simultaneous with the next step).

  3. Configure releases: Modify Blueprint files to make releases multiarch by default.

  4. Roll out new binaries: Run the multiarch packages on machines of the new ISA and assess performance and stability, addressing issues as needed.

  5. Full production: Allow production jobs to be scheduled freely on machines of the new ISA.

While these steps are the same for all packages, the issues encountered within each step vary widely across applications and throughout the different phases of our ISA migration from x86 to Arm. This often involves creating performance-optimized code for the new platform, which can happen in parallel to these steps. We observe parallels to Uber’s reported porting workflow.22

Phase 1: Large users.  We started our Arm migration with a small set of large users, such as the Spanner,8 BigQuery,20 and Bigtable7 big data systems. These migrations were hands-on with a small team and required weekly meetings and tracking bugs. Once tests passed, rollout was manual, with very careful performance and load testing, and gradual scheduling constraint removal on a per-job basis. This first-phase work was done, by and large, by people rather than automation or AI.

During this phase, a number of issues in these workloads surfaced and were addressed. Examples include: x86-specific intrinsics; long double, which differs between x86 and Arm, with cross-platform equivalents; brittle tests (e.g., due to exact floating-point equality checks); x86-specific flags; memory ordering issues hidden by x86; out-of-memory errors, often due to heap limits being tuned for x86; multiarch release packages exceeding the capacity limits of our infrastructure; unsupported dependencies, and loading of unsupported dynamic libraries; jobs not getting scheduled due to legacy x86-only scheduling constraints, such as requiring AVX2 instruction support to target newer machines.

This list was surprising to the teams involved. Initially, teams perceived porting these mature codebases to Arm as a herculean task fraught with toolchain difficulties. However, as we gained experience, most issues involved simple changes, many of them in configuration files. At the same time, these changes were surprisingly pervasive, as evident by the 38,156 commits generated.

Generally, we found that the modifications required for software to compile and run on Arm differ from initial expectations. For example, while a package might completely fail to build initially, simple manual fixes to a number of shared dependencies often unblock many builds at once. We also made a few (≈10) systematic, automated changes, such as steering nearly all applications away from long double for numeric stability across architectures.

Phase 2: Everybody else.  To take full advantage of Arm in datacenters, migrating only the largest workloads is insufficient. To maximize the use of available capacity, the cluster scheduler needs to be able to schedule workloads flexibly across platforms, packing workloads large and small onto machines. If only a small subset of services can run on Arm, it will result in underutilization of those machines. We note that the distribution of workloads at Google is very flat: Although our top 50 binaries are very large, they only represent ≈60% of running compute.16 Addressing this long tail requires porting more than 100,000 packages and billions of lines of code. This makes the Phase 1 approach of working directly with customer teams infeasible. In fact, even just talking to each team would be prohibitively expensive. The second phase of the x86 to Arm migration therefore focused on automating and scaling the migration of these workloads, while minimizing involvement from the teams themselves. We found that effectively using Arm hardware did not require porting all workloads. It is this phase of Google’s x86 to Arm migration that we mostly focus on. So far, we have ported about 60,000 packages, accounting for around 75% of Google’s server CPU cycles. In this phase, we ramped down engineers working on individual tests or configurations, as it was not scalable. Instead, we used a range of human-operated conventional automation tools for a large fraction of commits. Toward the tail end of the process, LLM-generated changes via CogniPort began to emerge, though our analysis in the next section almost entirely focuses on the time before then. We will now describe this phase in more detail, as well as our automation process.

Analyzing an ISA Migration

To fully understand what is involved in an ISA migration, we now analyze the full range of tasks involved in Google’s x86 to Arm migration (Research Question 1). As a monorepo, any change—be it to code, configurations, or documentation—is tracked as a commit in our repository’s history. Further,  relevant commits marked with a keyword indicated they were part of this migration, allowing us to extract them after the fact. We thus identified a relevant set of 38,156 commits. The contents of the changes included code and fixes written almost entirely by humans and conventional (non-AI) automated migration tools, using large-scale changes. The vast majority of the dataset predates the rise of agentic coding tools.

Analyzing these commits manually would have been cost-prohibitive. Instead, we used a variant of Gemini 2.5 Flash18 (the latest model available at the time) to analyze these commits at scale:

  1. We passed the commit messages and code diffs into the LLM’s 1M token context window in groups of 100 at a time, and picked 20 categories for each batch.

  2. We passed all ≈400×20 categories into the context window and asked Gemini to consolidate them into 50.

  3. We adjusted the model outputs by hand for a final list of 16 categories (Figure 1).b

  4. We ran Gemini again to apply labels to all of the commits, sorting them into these 16 categories (as well as an additional “Uncategorized“ category for outliers, to improve stability). Figure 2 shows examples of each category.

At 38,156 commits, it is impractical to verify that every categorization is correct. We have examined ≈100 exemplars, and they appear correctly categorized.

Commits fall into four overarching groups: code changes, test changes, build and configuration files, and supporting processes and tools. In total, our commits updated around 700K lines of code. While the vast majority (84%) of commits are related to updating build or configuration files (Category 8), these commits account for only 19% of lines of codes updated. We also see a substantial number of lines (17%) spent on migration tooling. A large portion of this work is only required once and can be reused in future ISA migrations.

Code-related changes (Categories 1–5) only account for 1% of commits and less than 4% of lines of code, refuting the conventional wisdom26 that code translation accounts for most of an ISA migration. Later in this article, we analyze how automatable these commits are.

We also analyze the timeline of our ISA migration (Figure 3). We observe that at the start of the migration, most commits were in tooling and test adaptation, aligned with Phase 1. Over time, a larger fraction of commits centered around code adaptation, which can be seen as a phase when there is still a need to update code in common dependencies and address common issues in code and tests. Eventually, the fraction of these kinds of commits declined, and in the final phase of the process, almost all commits are configuration files and supporting processes. We also observe that in this later phase, the number of merged commits rapidly increased, capturing the scale-up of the migration.

Why so many configuration changes? Automated and manual flag flips enabled the Arm variant across tens of thousands of projects with simple releases. For projects with complex release testing or evaluation, reconfiguring needed more hands-on (or agentic) labor across multiple commits.

Finally, we want to understand how these different categories of commits differ from one another. We observe that median commits in most categories are less than 20 LoC, with many single-line commits. However, we also observe very large individual commits that change 10,000+ LoC and skew the averages. We manually inspected these commits to understand their origin and found these commits do not typically represent more work since they are conceptually similar to large numbers of simple, one-line commits. Overall, there are 19 commits that cumulatively account for 238,289 LoC (32.4%) of total lines changed and that are trivial. Examples include:

  • Remove a porting tool once it was no longer used—57K LoC (Category 12)

  • Update a list of microbenchmark targets—23K LoC (Category 11)

  • Add several very large test vectors for a coverage tool—15K LoC (Category 6)

In summary, we find most commits related to migration are small; larger commits often change very large lists or configurations and are not inherently complex. Finally, we observe that some of the commits (particularly in “Supporting Processes & Tools”) could likely be reused in a subsequent multiarch migration.

Automating ISA Migrations

Now that we have established the tasks that are part of an ISA migration, we can explore how automatable each of these tasks is (Research Question 2) and how novel automation approaches can facilitate them.

ISA migration automation at Google.  We already employ a number of (non-AI) automation tools at Google today, which automated a large portion of the ISA migration process (83.82% of commits and 14.15% of LoCs).

Large-scale changes.  A key piece to ISA migration automation is Rosie, a preexisting tool that allows us to programmatically generate large numbers of commits and shepherd them into the monorepo. Rosie orchestrates the testing, mailing, code review, and submission of each individual commit. Rosie managed a total of 31,984 commits, but these changes represented only 14.15% of the total lines changed in our dataset. Figure 1 shows the fraction of each category that was generated using automated tools. For one of the major large-scale automated migrations, we introduced the concept of variant projects to the continuous integration (CI) and continuous deployment (CD) infrastructure,15 which enabled the following single-line addition to configure Arm CI and CD in a Blueprint file:

arm_variant_mode = ::blueprint::VariantMode::VARIANT_MODE_RELEASE,

Sanitizers and fuzzers.  While not limited to ISA migrations, fuzzers and LLVM sanitizers such as AddressSanitizer,30 MemorySanitizer,35 and ThreadSanitizer31 are key enablers of our migration. Even before Arm adoption, Google routinely ran all TAP tests with these tools enabled, which turn latent errors such as memory corruption, memory leaks, or race conditions into debuggable faults. Application owners regularly triage and fix these faults, sidestepping many common differences in execution between x86 and Arm (e.g., a data race may be hidden by x86’s TSO memory model). Catching these kinds of issues ahead of time avoids debugging non-deterministic behavior when recompiling to a new ISA.

ThreadSanitizer (TSan), in particular, has proven to be effective in managing the memory model differences between Arm and x86. TSan can detect threading issues in nearly all code except for rare, lock-free algorithms. Programs typically use language-provided synchronization primitives, which fall under TSan’s purview and have the same guarantees on both x86 and Arm. Code that has passed TSan is extremely likely to use synchronization primitives correctly.

Although we saw few threading issues across the codebase, some made it through due to code that is not tested or not testable with TSan. Thread-related issues in such code were not easily detectable until we scaled up deployment significantly and saw a pattern of issues, such as crashes. One such issue was a bug in core JVM code27 caused by a thread race. In our production experience, running at full scale provides high confidence that no issues remain.

Continuous health monitoring platform (CHAMP).  The final step in our automation is CHAMP, an automated canary analysis and qualification system that monitors applications running on Arm hardware. It continuously monitors health metrics to detect whether behavior differs from x86 instances of the job (e.g., significantly higher RPC error rates or crashes). If so, it automatically marks the job as ineligible for Arm, files a bug for its owners to follow up, and tries again in 30 days. Following Google’s production principles, it scales up the fraction of Arm instances of the application incrementally to limit service-level objective risk. CHAMP is less important for new microarchitecture deployments (either x86 or Arm), as the behavior, performance differences, and associated issues are relatively minor. However, it was highly effective during the Arm migration and helped assure service owners who felt deploying to a new ISA was risky.

Using CHAMP, it is no longer necessary to manually shepherd every binary through qualification. Instead, after updating project configurations to build Arm releases, rollout is now automatic.

Reliability of the automation approach.  Combined, these tools allow for a mostly automated approach where LSCs enable Arm for different builds and releases, which are then automatically qualified using CHAMP. To understand the stability of this approach, we analyze LSCs targeting a particular standardized release management system that covers 49.6% of all binaries at Google. These LSCs modified release configurations to bring this system’s percentage of Arm-qualified applications from 4.8% to (at the time of writing) 78.89%. The rate of applications that were rolled back in early testing was 1.8% (which dropped to 1% after fixing bugs), and less than 0.8% in the final phase.

Early in the migration, after ≈300 release packages, we had a 5% refusal rate (code owners deciding not to migrate). During scale-up, this dropped to 0.6% after ≈600 additional packages. In the final phase, the commits were globally approved with no refusal. We found that acceptance rate was strongly influenced by careful workload targeting, users gaining trust in the automation, and messaging that anticipated worries and objections.

The remaining binaries that have not yet been migrated fall into various categories: ready and awaiting migration, uses complex and bespoke testing, has broken tests that have not been repaired yet, on its way to deprecation, uses unmigrated dependencies, is burdened by non-Arm-specific technical debt, has hardware requirements that current Arm servers don’t yet fulfill, to name a few. Some small portion of jobs are completely ISA-specific, but the vast majority are possible to migrate, and changes to fix them would be classified into our existing 16 commit categories. All of this remains future work for this ongoing project.

Automation of ISA Migrations with AI

While LSCs and CHAMP automate a large part of the process, there are limits to this approach. They can edit build and configuration files, as well as automatically qualify Arm binaries for deployment. However, standard LSCs are fixed-function pipelines. They are not flexible to respond to unexpected errors or other issues that occur at any stage of the process, be it during testing or in production.

Modern generative AI techniques represent an opportunity to automate the remainder of the ISA migration process. We built an agent called CogniPort, which aims to close this gap. CogniPort operates on build and test errors. If an Arm binary does not build or a test fails at any point in the process, the agent can step in to fix the problem automatically.

The agent consists of three nested agentic loops (Figure 4). Each loop uses an LLM to perform one step of reasoning followed by a tool invocation—that is, a function call. The tool’s outputs are then attached to the agent’s context. There are tools for building and returning logs, running test(s) and returning logs, heuristically fixing build file errors, searching through code, modifying code, and exiting the loop (finish).

The outermost agent loop is an orchestrator that repeatedly calls the build fixer agent and/or the test fixer agent depending on the state of the workspace. The build fixer agent tries to build a given target and makes modifications to files until the target builds successfully. The test fixer agent runs a given test and makes modifications until the test passes. In both cases, the agent can time out via a step limit or give up early by calling finish.

To evaluate the agent, we took historic commits from our dataset, reverted them, and then checked whether the agent fixed the introduced error(s). Note that not all our categories are suitable for this approach—it only applies to Code and Test Adaptation (categories 1-7). We further narrowed down our dataset to commits that can be cleanly reverted and that have identifiable build or test targets. This resulted in a benchmark set of 234 commits in categories 1, 2, 3, 6, and 7. We ran the agent twice for each commit: once with Gemini 3 Flash fine-tuned on a corpus of internal data (including code and documentation)18,c and again with out-of-the-box Gemini 3.1 Pro. We saw a best-of-both success rate of 73.5%. Test fixes, platform-specific conditionals, and assembly code porting had the highest success rates. Test Execution Environment was the most difficult but still had a success rate of 56%, with our fine-tuned model performing the best.

Note that we consider these results directional: While we analyzed an arbitrary subset of outputs to ensure result validity and confirm the absence of recitation from training, the evaluation is not perfect and may miss cases where, for example, a fix is incorrect but not caught by a test or where there is other information leakage (e.g., a subsequent commit made the original fix easier, or reverting only the commit itself makes it easier to root-cause an issue than if the entire fix was reverted).

Discussion and Research Challenges

Overall, we see that ISA migrations involve a wide range of different tasks shown in our taxonomy (Research Question 1). Many of these tasks are highly automatable. Build file and configuration changes are almost fully automatable, while code changes and tests are partially automatable with conventional techniques (Research Question 2). In addition, many areas scale across architectures and do not require additional work for each ISA. This includes multiarch support for build and test infrastructure, spinning up a new hardware platform whether or not it is a new ISA (e.g., categories 11 and 15), and deprecating old code (category 14).

We have released multiarch binaries covering 75% of server compute at Google, a cross-cutting, representative set of code. Historically, such a migration would have consumed immense human effort. Tools like CHAMP and Rosie combined with broad-based testing, liberal use of sanitizers, and focusing on simplifying the process enabled a large fraction of this migration to be automated. CogniPort and similar AI tools will further accelerate the process, making giant codebase migrations tractable at a fraction of the effort. This raises the question: What are the remaining challenges, and are there research opportunities in closing the remaining gaps (Research Question 3)?

By manually inspecting outputs, we find that categories such as build and configuration files, intrinsic and assembly code porting, and test logic are already largely automatable. However, category 7 (Test Execution Environment) proved to be significantly harder. While the details of these challenges are unique to ISA migrations, the root causes are similar to quality issues that arise when using agents to automate general software development. They are rooted in LLM context-window limitations and information-retrieval challenges.

At Google, we found that imperfect AI-based code generation combined with our extensive test and monitoring infrastructure and human code review is sufficient to reliably land large numbers of changes in production, even with a <50% success rate at the model level. For example, a system called ECO21 has been used to submit thousands of AI-generated code optimizations and less than 0.5% of commits had to be rolled back. The 73.5% CogniPort success rate in our study is already better than rates reported in the ECO paper. Techniques such as information retrieval on past commits (which ECO uses) and spec-driven development (SDD)12 to make agents more robust could both help further. Even so, we find that a number of open challenges remain:

  • ISA-Specific Vector Code: Writing ISA-specific, performant vector and matrix code is difficult. Previous research showed limited success.36 However, we and others14 observe that modern LLMs are starting to show promise on writing vector intrinsics.

  • Deep Performance Optimizations: This sometimes requires major refactors and algorithmic changes. Existing performance-focused AI tools, such as ECO, will also help.

  • Difficult Corner Cases: We saw a number of corner cases that require obscure knowledge beyond the code itself. For example, we saw commits that worked around an Arm compiler bug, addressed a hash function behaving differently on Arm and x86, and fixed bugs that were not triggered until the code ran on Arm.

  • Performance Tuning: Hyperparameters and feedback directed optimization (FDO) profiles sometimes must be regenerated for a new platform. An agent could configure testing harnesses, run workloads, and measure performance.

Meanwhile, we also found a number of examples not directly related to ISA migration tasks and that may not be completely automatable:

  • Multiarch tooling: A significant portion of this work includes implementing the automation itself (e.g., CHAMP), as well as simulation tools and dashboards. However, AI agents are rapidly advancing their capability to implement these components.

  • Resource provisioning: These are configuration changes that help human engineers manage physical hardware in datacenters and can include strategic or business judgement.

Our results demonstrate that the rapid adoption of agentic infrastructure by software engineers, including at Google, will also address ISA migration challenges. Future ISA migrations may require a limited amount of manual work, mostly focused on making new hardware available and adding the new ISA to our existing multiarch tooling and automation.

Conclusion

By analyzing a large-scale ISA migration at Google, we refute longstanding assumptions about such migrations. First, even in the presence of source code, migrations are not straightforward and involve a large range of multifaceted tasks, with no single task dominating. Second, many of these tasks are highly automatable, particularly using modern AI techniques. Finally, AI agents are rapidly improving, expanding the breadth of tasks that can be automated.

item.title: Why We Need Occupancy Intelligence during Emergencies
item.dc:creator: Vinton G. Cerf and Harsh Verma
item.description: If occupancy intelligence can become an important component of emergency decision making, how should it be represented, exchanged, and trusted?
item.content:encoded:
Today, billions of connected devices continuously observe our world. Satellites monitor storms from space. Seismic networks detect earthquakes within seconds. River gauges report rising floodwaters. Weather radar tracks tornadoes. Wildfire sensors identify rapidly changing fire conditions. Emergency alerts can now reach millions of people almost instantly through mobile phones, television, radio, and the Internet.

These advances represent remarkable achievements in engineering and global collaboration. We have become increasingly successful at answering questions such as: What is the Emergency? Where did it happen? How severe is it? When will it occur?

Other important questions, however, often remain unanswered: Where are the people and how many may need help?

As technology has evolved over the years, our modern digital systems, including emergency alerting systems, have been extraordinarily successful in describing hazards. The standards for alerting do not describe the dynamic human environment surrounding those hazards. That information is critically important during emergencies.

A magnitude 7.0 earthquake affecting a downtown business district at 3:00 am on a Tuesday presents a very different operational picture than one occurring at 3:00 pm on a Friday. A hurricane approaching a coastal city during a holiday weekend differs significantly from one arriving after a successful evacuation. The hazard itself may be identical, but the number of people exposed, their locations, and their ability to respond can vary dramatically.

Emergency managers make decisions based not only on the characteristics of the hazard but also on the characteristics of the affected population. Which hospitals may soon receive large numbers of casualties? Which transit stations are crowded? Which schools are occupied? Which evacuation routes are already congested? Which shelters still have available capacity?

During a U.S. Geological Survey Pilot Licensing Agreement pilot, Harsh Verma and his team were investigating how real-time crowding and occupancy modeling could complement Earthquake Early Warning systems. The objective was not to improve the hazard models themselves but to better understand their operational human impact. The exercise revealed that although modern alerting systems have become remarkably effective at characterizing hazards, they generally lack standardized ways to communicate information about the people who may be affected. If we already possess increasingly sophisticated methods for detecting hazards, why have we invested comparatively little effort in communicating their human context?

Hazard detection and warning systems evolved to measure physical events. Population information evolved within entirely different systems—transportation networks, building management systems, mobile devices, public safety operations, and countless other sources. Each serves its own purpose. Rarely were they designed to work together during rapidly evolving emergencies.

Ironically, the Internet facilitates the connection of much of this information. Cities are becoming increasingly instrumented. Public transportation systems, smart buildings, infrastructure sensors, and mobile technologies continuously generate information that helps us understand how people move through the built environment. The challenge is no longer whether such information exists. The challenge is to determine how it can be represented, exchanged, and trusted in ways that are useful during emergencies while preserving privacy and public confidence.

Occupancy intelligence should never be confused with surveillance. Emergency responders rarely need to know who is present. More often, they need to understand whether a location contains dozens, hundreds, or thousands of people; whether occupancy is increasing or decreasing; and how reliable that information may be. Properly designed systems can provide operational awareness using aggregated, anonymized, and privacy-preserving information without identifying individuals.

As our digital infrastructure continues to evolve, perhaps the Internet and other communication systems will be able to carry more than descriptions of hazards. Perhaps they should also carry reliable contextual information that helps responders understand the potential human consequences of emergency situations and hazardous conditions.

Achieving this objective will require careful consideration of data quality, confidence, timeliness, governance, interoperability, and, above all, trust. These are not merely technical challenges. They are questions for computer scientists, emergency managers, standards organizations, policy makers, public agencies, and technology companies working together.

The Internet and its applications have continually evolved by solving problems earlier generations could not fully anticipate. We improved routing as networks expanded. We strengthened security as new threats emerged. We developed mechanisms for establishing trust in increasingly complex digital environments.

Perhaps the next evolution is ensuring that the information we move provides the context needed to use it to make better decisions. Knowing where the earthquake will strike is important. Knowing where people are when it strikes may help save lives.

If occupancy intelligence can become an important component of emergency decision making, how should it be represented, exchanged, and trusted? Those questions are now beginning to be explored by researchers and standards communities alike. International emergency alerting standards are evolving to incorporate occupancy intelligence while preserving interoperability, privacy, and public trust. It seems to us that this is an area worthy of increased attention with the potential to offer significant life-saving returns.

item.title: If You Think You Can Do Real-World Text-to-SQL
item.dc:creator: Michael Stonebraker and Peter Baile Chen
item.description: Looking for systems and ideas me on how to make LLM/agentic AI technology work better on real-world business applications.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Stonebraker
Peter Baile Chen
DOI: 10.1145/3838721
https://bit.ly/45JJqeU

Data warehouses are often subject to a preponderance of ad-hoc queries. They came into existence in the 1990s to support historical data stores of customer-facing data, especially sales data. At that time, it was widely reported that they paid for themselves based on better stock rotation in less than six months. For example, if pet rocks are “out” and Barbie dolls are “in,” then discount the pet rocks and move them up front; tie up the manufacturer of Barbie dolls with a big order so competitors cannot get merchandise.

Although there are repeated queries (for example, “produce the weekly sales report”), much of the traffic is ad hoc in nature, including the above example. Historically, data warehouses were fronted by business intelligence tools such as Business Objects, Power BI, and Tableau. This allowed many queries to be coded by business users using a simple graphical interface. Obviously, one would like to query data warehouses and other large, structured data stores in natural language to further empower non-programmers. It would have the added benefit of not requiring familiarity with a bespoke user interface. With the advent of large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI, this becomes a real possibility, and there are public benchmarks with leaderboards that show promising results.

On Spider 1.0,1 the leaderboard had accuracy in the 80+% range, while on Bird-SQL,2 accuracy was above 90%. However, both benchmarks have the following issues:

  • The data is in “the pile,” so LLMs can train on it. It is widely known that an LLM can only find data it has seen before. Almost all data warehouses we know about are behind serious enterprise access controls and are not publicly available.

  • Real data warehouses exhibit “schema rot.” Inevitably, the warehouse begins life with a well-structured schema. However, the schema of a typical warehouse is updated as business conditions change, the company buys or sells business units, and regulations change. Often schema changes occur multiple times a year. It would be wonderful if enterprises spent the time to construct a well-structured replacement schema. Invariably this is not the case, and schemas “rot” over time. The result after a few such changes is non-intuitive table and column names. For example, there may be six different columns in various tables labelled “salary.” Such columns may have overlapping non-documented semantics; one salary column may be for “net after taxes and commissions,” while another one may be for “gross salary.” Materialized views may be used to speed up popular queries. These characteristics give an LLM multiple ways to solve a query, and to generate headaches.

  • Real data warehouses often have idiosyncratic data. For example, in the MIT administration data warehouse containing information on students, faculty, building, classes, etc., there are mentions of “J-term” (a one-month term in January between fall and spring semesters) and building numbers (MIT buildings are numbered, not named—Stata Center is officially Building 32). Such bespoke information is difficult for an LLM.

  • Real data warehouse queries are more complex than the student-generated ones in Spider and Bird-SQL. They rarely have just one join and often two or three.

Spider 2.03 has addressed the last issue, but not the first three. The leaderboard of agentic-AI solutions for this benchmark is in the 90+% range.

In our opinion, real data warehouses have all of the issues mentioned above. Hence, any text-to-SQL benchmark should address the difficulties of real-world data stores. Those that do not are of academic interest only and do not reflect reality.

Beaver Benchmark

For the last two years, we have been trying LLM-based text-to-SQL on real workloads from real data warehouses. We started with the above-mentioned MIT data warehouse, an Oracle data warehouse of 1,400+ tables that is queried by many units at MIT (including CSAIL). Typically, business users pose a question to IT personnel who translate the request to SQL, often with clarifying dialog between the two people. We got real queries from the Oracle log and generated the corresponding natural language with the assistance of real users. This generated a collection of (natural language, gold SQL) pairs. Later we applied the same methodology to three other data warehouses. With permission, we anonymized and extended the queries and the data to produce the Beaver benchmark.4 One should clearly note the four issues noted above are all present in this benchmark. As such, we do not expect to get the same high accuracy as Spider/Bird. More details on the benchmark are published online.5

On this benchmark, a pure LLM generated an accuracy score of zero. Adding RAG, prompt engineering, and agentic AI raised accuracy to the 10+% range. See Jindal6 for results on this sort of model. To get a higher score, we gave the LLM the specific tables in the from clause of the gold SQL and the actual join clauses when there were multiple tables. That generated accuracy in the 30+% range. A leaderboard for results on Beaver is available online.7 Note that this is 50+% lower in accuracy that the public benchmarks and is the difference between “the technology has promise” and “the technology does not work.”

We would welcome systems and ideas on how to make LLM/agentic AI technology work much better on real-world business applications, and we have made Beaver publicly available to assist in this process. So have at it! Our own ideas on how to do better are contained in the Rubicon system,8 so take a look.

A simple conclusion can be drawn from this discussion. Good results using traditional LLM/agentic AI technology are likely only on data warehouses with clean schemas, simple queries, and little idiosyncratic data. Otherwise, try Rubicon or your good idea.
