item.title: 10 Systemic Changes to Broaden Participation in Computing
item.dc:creator: Carla E. Brodley, Catherine Gill, Megan Giordano, and Caitlin Kidder
item.description: Systemic change is both possible and leads to increases in discovery, retention, and declaration of computing majors across all populations.
item.content:encoded:
The Center for Inclusive Computing (CIC) was established in 2019 at Northeastern University to broaden participation in computing (BPC) at U.S. universities. BPC has been a goal of the U.S. computer science (CS) community for several decades, and much work has been done to design and implement best practices. But most efforts reported in the literature explore the efficacy of BPC activities at a single institution or a handful of institutions. Further, progress in BPC nationwide has been slow; in 2019, students who identified as women and/or from races and ethnicities historically marginalized in tech continued to be underrepresented in computing relative to their representation in higher ed.4 The 2018 report “Rebooting Representation”33 stated that although there appeared to be consensus on BPC best practices, uptake was slow. The report called attention to this “paradox,” hypothesizing that university computing departments lacked sufficient incentives and resources to change. Building on previous research and with core funding from Pivotal, the CIC set out to determine which BPC practices work across different university contexts. The CIC funds changes that create a more inclusive environment for undergraduates. By inclusive environment, we mean one in which all students—including those who have never programmed—feel invited to try computing and supported to pursue a major in the field.

Key Insights

  • The Center for Inclusive Computing (CIC) launched in 2019 to partner with U.S. university computing departments to identify and remove barriers that prevent students from discovering and thriving in computing. We were given the unique opportunity to determine which interventions are most effective in removing these barriers, and to do so at a previously unheard-of scale.

  • We report results across 22 universities of the 10 systemic changes we have found most impactful and we describe how they can be adapted to different institutional contexts.

  • The results show that implementing even a subset of these changes leads to increases in retention and attraction across all populations.

At the CIC, we work with the largest U.S. universitiesa to reach as many undergraduates as possible. Our approach seeks to test two hypotheses. The first is that, by making systemic changes (e.g., to the courses and/or the degree structure), more students would try and/or be retained in computing (i.e., What happens if we focus on fixing the institution rather than fixing the student?). The second hypothesis is that, by targeting systemic changes, much of the work would be sustainable (i.e., would not require ongoing fundraising or add material cost to the department’s budget).

This article describes the results from Phase One of this experiment. Specifically, we share aggregate data from the first 22 schools funded for implementation at the undergraduate level. These 22 schools began implementation between 2020 and 2022, meaning enough time has elapsed for us to measure the impact. (Phase 2 will include results for more than 50 schools.) For each university, the CIC provides: multi-year grants of $200,000 (or more) to cover implementation costs; technical assistance through a program manager (a computing faculty member and CS-education expert); and a platform to collect and analyze the data to track the impact of changes. Each university’s grant is evaluated annually, and the next tranche of funding is contingent upon satisfactory effort and progress against the prior year’s work plan.

We begin the article by summarizing the methodology used to select the 22 schools (and schools that have joined the portfolio subsequently) and what an engagement with the CIC entails. Next, we describe 10 systemic interventions that we have found (through trial and error) to be effective in creating an inclusive environment for undergraduates, regardless of prior exposure to CS. We then map the 22 schools to the 10 interventions and share the aggregate results, including a comparison of the change in demographics of computing majors relative to the changes in overall university enrollment. Finally, we describe future plans and draw conclusions from our work.

Framework for Systemic Change

The CIC’s methodology has the following six steps:

  1. We announce the availability of funding via our website and listservs. Per the conditions of our core funding, the initial eligibility criterion was nonprofit U.S. institutions graduating 200 or more students in IPEDS CIP code 11.30 We now accept applications from schools graduating 150 or more students in CIP code 11.

  2. We meet online with each school to review their application and formulate an initial hypothesis regarding barriers and potential changes. We then decide whether to do an in-person site visit based on the level of leadership commitment, the relevance of the systemic interventions to the barriers discussed, and faculty buy-in.

  3. If we proceed, we schedule a site visit, which is a 4–6 hour, in-person (except during COVID) set of meetings with the project team, intro sequence faculty, teaching assistants (TAs), academic advisors, students, and the dean. The purpose is to hear from all stakeholders to further diagnose the barriers and assess the potential for change.

  4. We summarize the site visit in a memo that identifies key themes, connecting the findings to evidence-based interventions and pattern matching to other schools with similar institutional contexts.

  5. If we choose to fund the school, we work with the project team on a work plan and budget. We now provide costing guidelines that show the budget range for each intervention.b The work plan and budget (which includes funding for data collection and 15% overhead) are included as exhibits in the grant contract.

  6. Selected schools implement the agreed upon changes, adjusting as needed in consultation with the CIC and their program manager, and submit annual progress reports. The funding is tranched, meaning subsequent installments are contingent upon satisfactory completion of the prior year’s activities.c

Grantees (selected schools) submit data twice a year, including historic data for the two years prior to launch.d Often, faculty and departments struggle to access intersectional enrollment and outcomes data, as this data tends to be centrally held. Our experience is that the CIC funding unlocks access.4,27 Specifically, for each term,e schools submit data for CS1–3 for the following variables:

  • Count of students: non-negative integer

  • Racial identity: Hispanic/Latinx, any race; American Indian or Alaska Native, not Hispanic (AIAN); Asian, not Hispanic; Black or African American, not Hispanic; Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, not Hispanic (HPI); White, not Hispanic; Nonresident Alien, Race/Ethnicity unknown

  • Gender identity: gender X/U, men, women

  • Major: CS,f other computing, non-computing, undeclared

  • Transfer: Students who transferred from another institution during the current academic year

  • Course outcome: pass,g fail, or withdraw (PFW)

CS1–3 are defined as the first three required programming courses in the CS major that are are not taken in the same term (i.e., none are discrete math). Typically these courses are: intro to programming, object-oriented programming, and data structures. If a department does not have a required third course, then CS3 is the course taken after CS2 by the majority of CS majors. For each combination of the values of these variables, schools enter the count of students (no missing data allowed), thus ensuring the data is intersectional. The time required for the initial setup and submission averages 40 hours; subsequent submissions average 8–10 hours. Finally, we note that the data system allows schools to compare their data against 18 different peer groups of universities in the CIC’s portfolio.

10 Systemic Interventions

We have come to focus on 10 interventions through a combination of extensive literature searches on systemic changes in higher ed,21,26,35,h observations from our first two rounds of site visits, pattern recognition across schools, and data analysis of the results of the first 22 universities. To home in on these 10 interventions, we started with the literature, then noted the issues that seemed to arise at all universities related to retention and discovery. Specifically, students across the schools in our first and second rounds of site visits shared a number of concerns, including: if they were new to coding, how difficult it was to be in the same class as those with prior experience; less than optimal experiences with the TAs; that different sections of the same class taught by different professors had different levels of preparation for the next class in the sequence; that class dynamics were terrible at schools with extra barriers to major declaration; challenges engaging with some assignments; and that unless they discovered CS in their first semester it was impossible to major and graduate on time. We heard many of these same concerns from TAs and advisors, and further observed that advisors were not always able to explain different pathways (e.g., the difference between the B.S. and B.A. CS degrees at their own school), leading us to realize that advisors need to be kept in the loop. The first three interventions focus on changes to the intro sequence in order to attract students to and retain them in the major.3 The next four focus on access to the degree and the degree’s structure. The final three focus on co-curricular supports for students in the major.

1. Manage distribution of prior experience. CS is offered in 60% of high schools in the U.S., but less than 10% of high school students take CS.18 As such, universities have a significant opportunity to promote the discovery of computing in college. To do that, schools need strategies for managing the distribution of prior experience.2,5 But care must be taken because prior experience is not uniformly distributed across genders, races, and ethnicities, and high school CS classes are more often present in zip codes of economic privilege. The problem is that students without coding experience can quickly feel behind when, in reality, they have only just begun.23,34 Indeed, students have reported CS1 classes being overly difficult and unfriendly when students with and without prior experience are in the same class.25 Finally, from a faculty perspective, it is challenging to teach a class when students come with widely differing prior knowledge, and sometimes neither group is engaged.

In the June 2022 issue of CRA’s Computing Research News,11 we shared strategies for handling the distribution of prior experience. Strategies include: students take an assessment to determine where in the intro sequence they should begin (assessment can be a self- or faculty-administered evaluation); students self-select where to begin based on preference;20,i the department offers recitations for true beginners (for which they receive credits); and the department offers a CS0 course (often in Python) for non-majors and students without experience19,24,32,37,j and/or  implements two, differently paced intro sequences that merge together in CS2 or CS3.31,k

2. Implement common assessment across multi-section classes. Having shared assignments, exams,l course policies, and grading standards across sections and labs of courses in the intro sequence is key to ensuring that all students can thrive in computing.8 On the one hand, students without prior coding experience are unlikely to persist if confronted with a “super hard” CS1. On the other hand, a “super easy” CS1 will not prepare students for CS2. Common assessment in CS1–3 is therefore essential for a shared foundation, regardless of prior background and/or class instructor. Also, common assessment allows for a centralizing of resources related to TAs and graders, translating into greater coverage and more timely grading. To implement this change, the department can delegate course management to a rotating course coordinator position. It goes without saying that an added benefit to common assessment is that faculty who teach downstream can be confident as to what was covered.

3. Create assignments that show computing in the context of other fields. By contextualizing the computing curriculum in different domains, students see its applicability to real-world problems and how it connects to other disciplines. This has been extensively investigated by the CS education research community.6,7,15

4. Have CS0/CS1 fulfill a general education requirement. This promotes discovery. We acknowledge, however, that this may be infeasible in certain contexts.

5. Right-size degree requirements. Departments must evaluate whether the number of required courses and the prerequisite structure in their CS degree(s) are reasonable.22 Some departments require 20 or more semester-long computing courses plus math and science requirements. In such cases, it can be impossible for a student to discover computing and still graduate in four years. A rule of thumb is that degree requirements can be satisfied in three years—this promotes discovery and mitigates added time to graduation for transfer students. In addition, research has shown that a rigid pre- and co-requisite structure can impact the make-up of computing majors22 and student retention in the major.17 Of particular importance is the placement of math prerequisites. We recommend not requiring a math course until the content is truly needed.10 For example, calculus 1 and 2 are not needed for CS1, CS2, or discrete math.17 This change is key if a university has a high drop/fail/withdraw rate in calculus 1 and/or 2, meaning the class is functionally blocking students from progressing in the CS degree.

6. Low/no barriers to major declaration. Because of historic booming enrollments in computing,14,21,m many schools have struggled to meet student demand. Three common but problematic responses to this problem are: only allowing students to major in computing if they are admitted directly, allowing any student to take the first two to three computing courses and then deciding whether they can be admitted to the major based on their GPA in those classes, and charging more per credit for “high-demand” majors, which is a barrier for low-income students. Limiting enrollment to those admitted directly to the major excludes students from discovering computing at university. Imposing GPA-based enrollment caps favors students who arrive at university with prior coding experience. If a department feels it must cap enrollments, the CIC suggests alternative strategies that can meet the department’s needs without sacrificing the ability to attract and retain true beginners (these are discussed in Brodley12).

7. Create interdisciplinary computing majors. Often referred to as CS+X in the literature, interdisciplinary computing majors (ICMs)—majors built at the intersection of two or more fields of study—are a powerful strategy for broadening participation in computing.9,13

8. Centralize TA recruiting, training, and evaluation. At many universities, the CIC observes little to no training for TAs (and, if there is training, it is often the job of each faculty member to train those TAs assigned to them). Because a student’s experience and sense of belonging are often tied to their experience with the TAs, it is vital to train and evaluate TAs (see AIICE1 and Muzny et al.28 for publicly available TA training materials). Centralizing recruitment of TAs has the added benefit of removing the biases of individual faculty members and providing a centralized view of which TAs to rehire based on evaluation results.29

9. Align co-curricular supports. As schools make changes to their intro sequence and degrees, it is essential to update and align co-curricular supports and arm academic advisors with the information to help students understand and navigate the various pathway options. Supports also include services like tutoring and peer advising, which are scalable and low-cost methods for meeting student need.

10. Present clear degree maps on the department website. Many students will first be exposed to the major via the degree plan on the department’s website. As such, it is imperative that the site be both accurate and welcoming. We place a particular emphasis on making sure websites contain multiple sample plans of study, including plans for transfer students, students who enter university without pre-calculus, and students who discover computing in their second year of university.n

Impact

Here, we present results from the 22 universitieso that have been implementing CIC changes for three or more years. We wait three years because some changes require a year or more to go through university governance and/or be fully implemented. We first summarize the systemic changes made by the schools, then discuss the impact of the changes on who is majoring in CS, sharing data on the enrollment and pass rates in CS1. We conclude by discussing challenges that resulted in some schools being less successful than others.

Changes made across the portfolio.  In Figure 1, we list the interventions implemented by each of the 22 universities (per the terms of the CIC’s grant agreement, schools are anonymized; they are also not listed here in alphabetical order). In the figure, we indicate the level of implementation for each intervention (see legend). We explain our coding rules below. Note that we do not include interdisciplinary computing majors (ICMs) because this intervention was not added until 2024. Also note that in our five-year reportp we show detailed data for four schools.

Manage distribution of prior experience: Coded as fully implemented if the school follows one of the approaches described in the previous section, otherwise coded as not implemented, with one exception: coded as partially implemented if the school provided extra supports for students new to coding but did not give credit for the additional work.

Common assessment: Coded as fully implemented if the school has implemented common assignments and exams in CS1–3. Coded as partially implemented if common assessment is in a subset of CS1–3 and/or if this entails common exams or common assignments, but not both. For six schools, this intervention is N/A because the classes have only one section.

Computing in context: Coded as fully implemented if the department has implemented the intervention for all of CS1–3; partially implemented if only for for a subset.

CS0/CS1 fulfill a gen-ed requirement: This is either true (fully implemented) or false (not implemented).

Right-size degree requirements: Coded as fully implemented if three things are true: the number of computing credits is ≤ 60 (including discrete math but excluding other required math); calculus 1 is not a prerequisite to CS1 or CS2; and the degree’s prerequisite structure is not overly complex.q Schools are coded as partially implemented if one of the three criteria is met or if the school’s B.S. does not meet the criteria, but the institution offers a B.A. that does. We note that, across the 22 universities, the B.S. in CS requires on average 56.3 ± 12.3 computing credits and the B.A. in CS requires 40.5 ± 6.5 computing credits.

Low/no barriers to major declaration: Coded as fully implemented if one of the following is true: there are no restrictions to major declaration beyond what is dictated by the host college, or the GPA restriction is ≤ 2.5. Partially implemented means students must be able to apply to the major after entering the university and the department either uses a holistic evaluation or has a technical GPA requirement in the range (2.5, 3.2). Otherwise, coded as not implemented.

Centralized TA recruiting and training: Coded as fully implemented if both TA recruiting and training are centralized; partially implemented if only one is in place.

Co-curricular supports: Coded as fully implemented if the school offers CS tutoring, has an advisor caseload of ≤ 375 students, and has a policy requiring that students meet with advisors at key academic milestones. Partially implemented means only one or two of these criteria have been met. If none are met, then  coded as not implemented.

Clear degree maps on website: Coded as fully implemented if degree requirements and/or plan of study include pathways for all students, including external transfers, those discovering computing in their second year, and those who are not “calc-ready.” Coded as partially implemented if there is guidance for some but not all of these pathways. Otherwise, coded as not implemented.

In Figure 1, we see that most schools implemented many but not all interventions, because not all interventions are feasible in all contexts. For example, making CS0/CS1 fulfill a general education requirement or mandating common assessment requires significant faculty buy-in. Other interventions, such as centralizing TA recruiting and training and computing in context, are widely adopted. In many cases, we have provided follow-on funding after the end of the initial grant so schools can implement additional interventions. For example, University 6’s leadership did not feel ready to tackle common assessment in the early years of working with us but is now creating a policy to do so. Because at the time of this writing we have only 22 schools that implemented changes three or more years ago, an analysis of which interventions have the most impact would not be statistically valid. This is a priority area for future work. Four schools have published results from the work supported by the CIC: Rutgers,16 University of Washington,38 University of California, Riverside,31 and Colorado State University.17

Who is majoring?  The ultimate measure of impact for this work is whether the student graduates with the degree. However, graduation data means waiting four or more years from implementation. Thus, for now, our best metric is who is majoring in computing. (Note that the timing of major declaration varies by school.) Across the 22 schools, the number of majors grew between 2019 and 2024r to 42,558 men and 15,533 women.s The change in representation of who is majoring also changed over this period, with the percentage of women majors increasing from 22.4% to 26.7%. Note that results vary across the universities, as discussed in the “Challenges” section below; indeed, the mean increase in women is 4.0 points and the standard deviation is 3.2. In Figure 2, we show the changes for each race/ethnicity and gender grouping in terms of net new majors and percentage change (the darker the box, the larger the growth). We see that women majors increased by 80% and 6,914 net-new women majors were added. The most dramatic growth was for Black/African American women and Hispanic women, at 128% and 146%, respectively. The numbers for some groupings are so small (e.g., American Indian/Alaska Native) that the percentage change is not meaningful.

A question that arises is whether this growth is the result of interventions or a function of changes in overall university demographics. In Figure 3, we compare the change in representation in computing (y-axis) and the change in representation in the university (x-axis). We calculate the change in enrollment for a university using IPEDS data.t Plotting the data for each population, we see that, for all populations, the growth in computing majors increased more than the corresponding change in university enrollment. Indeed, even populations that are seeing declines in university attendance still show an increase in their representation in computing.

Improvements in pass rates.  In Table 1, we show the change in pass rates for CS1 from Fall 2019 to Fall 2024. The pass rates improved for almost every population. We show the results by genderu and race/ethnicity. In some cases, the improvements are as high as 8–10 percentage points. The variance among pass rates by race/ethnicity is smaller in 2024 than in 2019, but persists, indicating more still needs to be done.

Threats to the validity of CIC results.  Ideally the CIC would compare the results of the 22 schools to a set of similarly sized schools that did not make these changes, but there is no principled way to do this and all that is publicly available via IPEDS is graduation data. This will change in a few years, when we will be able to compare the graduation data of our 22 schools to the graduation data of a random sample from IPEDS. A limitation of the results is that we worked only with schools that graduate 200 or more CS majors a year. Thus, whether the 10 interventions would be effective at smaller schools, and liberal arts colleges in particular, is an open question.

Challenges that impacted some schools’ success.  The results above show that the portfolio as a whole made significant progress in making CS more equitably accessible. However, progress varies by school, with some schools failing to make progress despite implementing several of the recommended interventions. We have found several reasons for this. The first is a high GPA-based barrier to major declaration. When a high cap is in place, students we have met share that CS1 and CS2 are hypercompetitive and uncollegial. This environment can negatively impact students who might be considering trying CS. In schools with high (>3.5) GPA major declaration thresholds, the demographics changed little. A second confounding factor we observed at two schools was due to university-level budgetary pressure. In both cases, although enrollment in CS continued to grow, strains on university resources led many CS faculty to leave, which reduced the project team’s bandwidth to implement the changes. The final confounding variable is a lack of positional authority on the project team. Some interventions do not need much in the way of financial support but do demand that the project team have the authority to require the changes. Indeed the hardest change to make—but perhaps the most powerful—is common assessment. Faculty are often resistant to this change because they feel it infringes on their academic freedom. This has proven a valuable lesson about the importance of ensuring department leadership is bought into and able to execute on the desired changes. The CIC now requires that the department chair be on the project team.

What Is Next for the CIC?  By 2027, we project a portfolio of 50 or more schools implementing/having implemented these interventions. At that point, we will have sufficient data to more definitively show which interventions and combinations of interventions have the highest efficacy—and in which university contexts. This future research is critical for providing universities a road map for how to chart their systemic change journey once the CIC terminates operations.

What Is Next for the CIC?  In 2024, we launched an effort to understand the challenges and opportunities of interdisciplinary computing majors (ICMs). We are currently working with 10 partner schools to understand the implementation of ICMs in different institutional contexts, and to demonstrate the attractiveness of these degrees to an even broader array of students.

What Is Next for the CIC?  Finally, we are working to identify interventions that ensure equitable access to AI education. We are currently conducting a national landscape study of AI programs (see https://cicmap.ai/) and requirements at the undergraduate level, with the goal of identifying trends and best practices. Between 2025 and 2027, we will issue several RFPs to implement these best practices to ensure that the urgent adoption of AI is an opportunity for all.

Conclusion

Broadening participation in computing has been a goal of the CS community for decades, and the CIC is profoundly grateful to have been given the opportunity to advance this shared goal by testing the efficacy of interventions across universities. The framework we have developed over the past five years has led to systemic, sustainable changes at the implementing universities. Further, having made the agreed upon changes, the universities in this initial portfolio do not require ongoing funding to sustain the impact. Additionally, the CIC has been able to show how to adapt an intervention’s implementation based on a university’s particular context. The results presented here illustrate that systemic change is both possible and leads to increases in discovery, retention, and declaration of computing majors across all populations. We are excited to add to these results as we grow the number of schools in our portfolio.

Acknowledgments

This project was partially funded by Pivotal and by the National Science Foundation (awards 2216629, 2434248 and 2533723). We would like to thank CIC partner schools, our program managers and technical assistants, and Northeastern University offices of contracting, finance and grants. Christine Alvarado, Valerie Barr, and Manuel Pérez-Quiñones gave us useful feedback on an earlier version of this article.

item.title: The End of the Coder?
item.dc:creator: Logan Kugler
item.description: If AI can now write, debug, and deploy software at a competitive cost, what is the impact on human software development professionals?
item.content:encoded:
In January 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made a prediction that sent ripples through the technology sector: the world might be only six to 12 months away from AI models capable of performing all software engineering tasks end-to-end. The timeline was aggressive, but the evidence was already mounting within the walls of the major AI labs themselves. Shortly after Amodei’s statement, Boris Cherny, the head of Claude Code at Anthropic, admitted that 100% of his own code is now AI-generated.

For decades, the career of a “software developer” was defined by the ability to translate human requirements into precise, machine-readable syntax. But a rapid succession of AI releases in early 2026 has brought that definition to a breaking point.

On February 2, OpenAI launched the Codex desktop app—a tool designed to create not just simple code snippets, but also long-running, multi-agent workflows involving isolated worktrees and automated deployment. Weeks later, GPT-5.3-Codex arrived, shifting the industry’s central question from “Can the model write code?” to “Can humans direct and audit a fleet of agents fast enough?”

The impact on individual practitioners was immediate.

“I am no longer needed for the actual technical work of my job,” said Matt Shumer, co-founder of Otherside AI, in an essay that went viral on Xa in early 2026. Shumer described a workflow that has become common among advanced AI users:

“I describe what I want built, in plain English, and it just . . . appears. Not a rough draft I need to fix; the finished thing. I tell the AI what I want, walk away from my computer for four hours, and come back to find the work done; done well, done better than I would have done it myself, with no corrections needed.”

This shift raises a fundamental question for students, junior developers, and hiring managers alike: if AI can now write, debug, and deploy software at a lower cost, what is the impact on human software development professionals?

From Implementation to Strategic Oversight

The consensus among authorities is that while the “coder” may be endangered, the “engineer” remains essential, though that role is being redefined as part product manager, part reviewer, and part AI orchestrator.

James Ivers, lead of the AI Workflows and Architecture Modernization group at Carnegie Mellon University’s Software Engineering Institute, argues that the value proposition of a professional engineer has always extended far beyond syntax.

“Coding is often the easy part,” Ivers said. “Great software engineers impact much more of the software development lifecycle than just slinging code. Requirements analysis, architecture and design, effective testing strategies, planning, and stakeholder management—all of these are critical activities for project success.”

Ivers suggested a mental model that distinguishes between “coders” and “software engineers.” In this view, coders are language experts who operate within bounds defined by others, such as Jira tickets or specific designs. Software engineers, conversely, operate in ambiguous spaces to discover and create those bounds, engaging with stakeholders to determine requirements and priorities.

“Within this mental model, coders are much more likely to be impacted or even displaced by AI,” Ivers said.

Bill Nichols, lead of the Applied Measurement and Experimentation Initiative at Carnegie Mellon University, said that the differentiator is moving up the abstraction stack.

“The value proposition shifts from being a scarce source of code to being a scarce source of well-formed decisions,” Nichols said. As implementation costs drop toward zero, he said, the work shifts toward understanding domains, making tradeoffs explicit, and ensuring systems behave as intended under real-world constraints.

The Quality and Security Bottleneck

While AI can generate code at a scale that outpaces a human’s, it remains an imperfect actor. Ivers views software engineering as an evolution of practices designed to compensate for human error—finding mistakes as early as possible to reduce the cost of fixing them.

“None of these motivations go away when using AI,” he said. “We are replacing one imperfect actor with another. AI is imperfect and there will be mistakes.”

Software engineers are uniquely positioned to bring discipline to these projects by anticipating where errors can be introduced, spotting them in practice, and guiding the AI back toward intended solutions.

Amy J. Ko, a professor and Associate Dean for Academics of The Information School at the University of Washington, said there is no evidence agentic AI can devise good plans without expert human review and well-designed architectures.

“Expertise has always been marked by a deep knowledge of software qualities and how they are achieved through implementation; understanding architectural complexity; capacity to continuously learn and change practices; providing credible, honest, trustworthy information, and a long tail of other soft skills,” Ko said.

This reliance on human judgment creates a new set of bottlenecks. Nichols said the limiting factor in the software lifecycle is moving from “Can we build it?” to “Can we understand, test, and justify it?” He draws a sharp distinction between verification and validation: verification (checking if a system conforms to specs) can be automated, but validation (deciding if the system provides the right capabilities for its environment) remains a judgment-heavy human process.

Without this oversight, agent-generated codebases risk turning into unmaintainable sludge, Ko said.

The Broken Junior Pipeline

However, there is concern for some professional roles. Perhaps the most urgent relates to junior developers. Historically, entry-level roles allowed developers to build architectural proficiency through the manual trial and error of coding. With AI agents now capable of doing the work typically assigned to juniors, that foundational practice is under threat.

“We have no way of teaching, training, or educating software developers to be senior or architect-level software engineers” without that foundational experience, Ko warned. She said that industry is currently relying on existing senior talent while “deferring investing in future senior developers to instead purchase compute,” a strategy she called unsustainable. Aside from years of practice designing and building software in teams, there are no known pedagogies or research that can produce that level of high-tier skill, Ko said.

A New Pedagogy of Feedback

Despite these structural hurdles, some see the potential for a new kind of learning. Nichols said AI-assisted development could actually accelerate system-level understanding rather than hinder it.

“Manual coding has been one path to developing intuition, but it’s limited,” Nichols explained. “Feedback is often delayed and indirect, and design decisions may reveal their consequences only much later. Moreover, coding is local behavior; architecture is system behavior.”

When an engineer specifies behavior and an agent produces an implementation, the feedback loop shifts from “Did I write this correctly?” to “Did I specify this correctly?” This provides immediate feedback on whether the specification was clear and sufficient, allowing junior engineers to focus on the aspects of the system that matter most for long-term behavior.

Ivers echoed the “think beyond coding” approach. He suggested that problem decomposition and domain knowledge will be paramount for future-proofed developers.

“AI will need guidance. It also needs monitoring, which means verification and validation skills are important, and refinement, so architecting new agent workflows or improving management of new resources like tokens are huge here too,” Ivers said.

The Jevons Paradox of Code

The economic outlook for the profession remains a subject of intense debate at present. While implementation work is being commoditized, Nichols pointed to Jevons paradox,b an economic theory in which efficiency gains in a resource (such as coal or, in this case, code) lead to an increase in its total consumption.

“As the cost of implementation falls, more software tends to be built, especially lower-stakes systems that were previously uneconomical,” Nichols said. This could expand the overall scope of software work and create new entry points for early-career engineers, helping to address concerns about an empty entry-level talent pipeline.

However, the future path is more of a bend than a straight continuation. The professional’s role is evolving from progressively better implementers toward roles focused on shaping and controlling system behavior under real-world constraints. Hiring is expected to tilt toward skills in requirements, system design, risk management, and the ability to work effectively with AI tools as collaborators.

As today’s frontier models and their successors take over the keyboard, the human engineer’s most important tool is no longer the integrated development environment; it is their judgment.

item.title: Everything Everywhere All-Pervasive Augmented Reality
item.dc:creator: Holger Regenbrecht, Kushani Perera, and Nadia Pantidi
item.description: A participatory decision space should be used to rethink existing divides between the haves and the have-nots, between technology providers and users, and between regulators and citizens.
item.content:encoded:
Everyday computing technology has made its way from the office desk (PC), to the café (laptop), the pocket of your clothing (smartphone), and finally to your wrist (smartwatch). Your eyes and ears are next in line as we welcome smart glasses. Smart glasses are worn like ordinary sun- or prescription glasses and “see, hear, and locate” your environment to augment it with text, video, and 3D models, for example. No longer the province of research labs only, Big Tech companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, or Apple are now all working on this next big thing in technology. So, there just might be something to this particular development.

When you are wearing such smart glasses all the time, we call this pervasive augmented reality (AR). Those pervasive AR glasses will always be on, will augment what you see and hear, will respond to the context and your voice and gestures, and, combined with artificial intelligence, will take care of any apps to be operated. Pervasive AR will constantly and continuously provide you with information at the right place and the right time.2 Since the glasses are right in front of your eyes and near your ears, there is no longer a need for a smartphone to be pulled out of your pocket or a smartwatch to be looked at.

So, what could pervasive AR be useful for? There is the promise of a paradigm shift in how we will communicate, collaborate, work, play, educate, learn, entertain ourselves, and see the world. With this always-on and always-there technology we might make decisions faster and more accurately and explore the world while having all the information we need, accessible without effort.

Pervasive AR can be a social bonus, as you can get conversations started between you and people you do not know so well, more quickly. For instance, we have almost all been in a situation of talking to a person you have met before but have forgotten their name. Now with the latest developments, your pervasive AR glasses will subtly overlay that name into your view.

However, the introduction of pervasive AR often comes with undesired consequences, in areas such as privacy, commercial exploitation, distractions, digital inequalities, and in judging what is true and right.1 Pervasive AR will subject its users to a constant feed of tailored augmentations, of which the sources are unverified, and the access is user specific. This ability of displaying context and user-specific content is enabled by cameras, microphones, and other sensors on pervasive AR glasses capturing the world around its users continuously and often intrusively. The overlaid digital information, being within the wearer’s field of view, needs to be filtered to avoid information overload and health and safety issues, and the information provided needs to be trusted and not manipulated. To date, little is known about such perceptual effects and ethical consequences.

So, what is fundamentally different when it comes to ethical questions with pervasive AR in comparison to other emerging technologies? Regardless of the specific glasses and their applications, pervasive AR will alter the way its users see the world. In-place, in-time information will be brought to the user, unprompted, without being incited by the user.2 This also carries the risk of distorting reality perception in a subtle and unprecedented way. Existing research has often discussed how prolonged AR use can blur the distinction between reality and augmentations, leading to users being misled. Furthermore, continuously wearing AR eyeglasses will potentially lead to health and safety issues not seen with other technologies, such as increased cognitive load, fatigue, eye strain, and potential physical harm from manipulated augmentations.5 In addition, we already see software applications running on AR glasses for law-enforcement agencies, which demonstrate the new level of issues surrounding privacy and dignity that will certainly develop when those glasses become commonplace and pervasive. Those ethical examples demonstrate a need to have a closer look at pervasive AR.

Anticipated implications of the so called metaverse will also impact pervasive AR,1 such as users being unwillingly subjected to corporate-mandated content. Similarly, pervasive AR further exacerbates the already problematic situation of existing racial and sexist biases due to lack of inclusivity in the development of technologies. This includes research that has specifically focused on identifying social implications of everyday use of AR, often exploring themes of privacy concerns,3 commonly stemming from the always-on nature of cameras.

In our research, we are using the power of empirical studies with guiding questions8 for ethical impact assessment of pervasive AR. We can anticipate future real-world use through technology probes, that is, tangible implementations of potential pervasive AR systems, and empirically testing them with people in selected scenarios such as socializing in public.7 Hence, we can receive intuitive feedback from the public instead of relying purely on the opinions of the designers and engineers of such technology. A reoccurring theme is the issue of asymmetry in the future use of pervasive AR—the divide between the technology haves and the have-nots. We have explored this asymmetry in terms of how pervasive AR can transform public settings by augmenting not only the space,6,7 but, also those sharing the space by showing pervasive AR eyeglass wearers information about their bystanders. Asymmetry is multifaceted and raises the questions of who will be able to afford these eyeglasses and who gets which information? Who is controlling the information? Are there new kinds of power imbalance that will potentially develop here? Are we willing to leave this level of decision making to the big tech companies, or should we all try to actively shape the future of pervasive AR? Here, we strongly propose the latter choice.

One of the fundamental questions arising is whether realities of alternative facts will be promoted through the use of pervasive AR. As Chalmers in his Reality+ book provokes: Will there be an “Apple Reality, Facebook Reality, and Google Reality”? Recently, Meta released their latest iteration of AR glasses, partnered with Ray-Ban. These devices exacerbate privacy concerns, as subtle, spectacle-like AR devices with always-on cameras are increasingly thrust upon societies.3,4 However, it is not only Meta; Samsung, Apple, Google, Snap, and Alibaba have enthusiastically announced their devices will be the new future. That makes one wonder about Chalmers’ proposition on the emergence of developer-driven technologies, are the users at the mercy of the developers? After all, shouldn’t users’ concerns count for more than another pixel upgrade or another boost to a company’s bottom line?

The million-dollar question is how to ethically shape the future of pervasive AR. Moshe Y. Vardi9 on multiple occasions over many years argued for technology serving humanity, that Big Tech is becoming too powerful and their power must be curtailed, and that their business models are unethical and must be regulated, and finally asks the question whether it is even outright unethical to work for Big Tech. As a way out of this ongoing dilemma we propose a co-responsibility model where computing professionals adopt a position of supporting the public good and genuinely co-designing pervasive AR. Such a model allows computing professionals to participate in the future-shaping process without having to either shoulder the whole responsibility for all ramifications or otherwise to retreat to a position of ethical neglect.

We propose what we call a pervasive AR civics space: a participatory platform to design pervasive AR technology with and for people, potentially leading to high usability and utility, transparency, and meaningful regulation. We have seen how participatory design in the 1970s and 1980s shifted the balance of power between workers and managers by advocating for workers having the ability to influence the design of the computer systems they were expected to use. The foundations of participatory design were, and still remain, greatly political, supporting the empowerment of vulnerable and marginalized groups, and rooted in democratic values; the right of people to co-determine and be active agents of their living conditions. Within this frame, a participatory decision space would leverage principles and practices from digital civics10 and networked participatory publics to advocate for the pervasive AR user being able to influence the design of, or better control, their immersion at every layer of manipulation. This space should be used to rethink existing divides between the haves and the have-nots, between technology providers and users, and between regulators and citizens to enter into a constructive dialogue about the future of this potentially omnipresent and transformative technology.

However, given pervasive AR is already in place as part of our socio-technical infrastructure, and ‘publics’ are heterogeneous and in conflict, this is not an easy task. It may require a participatory design strategy, where practices and technologies undergo change at the same time, and therefore require continuous alignment of actors’ conflicting interests and matters of concern. The exact methods to be used are still a matter of debate, but there are existing approaches that can serve as starting points or used in localized contexts, such as Speculative Design or the Living Labs concept that has been successfully applied in contexts such as rural health solutions, urban tourism, and others to support co-design and open innovation. Whatever the method, it will certainly require a multi- and interdisciplinary approach, between technologists, designers, social scientists, businesses, regulators, and of course end users and other stakeholders.

A truly participatory process can be initiated, implemented, and maintained at any type and level of pervasive AR research, design, and development. It allows leaders, line managers, interface designers, software developers, and all other professionals involved in decision making, big or small, to influence the way we will be surrounded by and see the world through pervasive AR. Co-responsibility and initiative have to be developed inside, with, as well as outside of Big Tech. Based on our experience, moral intuition and explicit morality of non-experts and experts alike play a major role here.

A civics space for pervasive AR with computing professionalism at its core can interrogate power relations and changing hierarchies and at the same time bring participative and dialogue-based processes to the forefront of discussions about how such technologies are developed, implemented, regulated, and held accountable. We need informed digital citizens to engage with those processes to confidently welcome pervasive AR to our everyday lives—let’s shape smart glasses for a smart future.
